This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah, and we have previously discussed it many times, and that Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah say: the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is with letters and sound.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the high status of this Quran, due to His saying: ﴿those are the verses﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the Quran is a sign and evidence of its Revealer, due to His saying: ﴿the verses of the Book﴾. We have previously noted that the idāfa (construction) is with the sense of "min" (of), so it is a genus idāfa. The Quran is a sign of its Revealer, Exalted is He, from which aspect? From the truthfulness of its reports and their agreement with reality, and from the excellence of its narratives and their love in souls, and that they never bore people, for there is no speech that is repeated but it becomes tiresome, except the Quran. Third: from the aspect of its rulings, since they are just rulings beneficial to the servants in their livelihood and their hereafter. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-Anʿām 115].
* Among its benefits: that the Quran is written as it is recited, due to His saying: ﴿those are the verses of the Book﴾.
* Among its benefits: praise of the Quran with this great attribute, which is al-Ḥakīm (the Wise).
* Also among its benefits: that there is no report in the Quran that is stated in vain, nor a ruling established in vain. From where do we derive this? From al-Ḥakīm (the Wise), since vanity contradicts wisdom, and it is impossible for there to be anything in vain in the Quran, neither a report nor a ruling.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a guidance and mercy for the good-doers﴾. It has two readings, as previously mentioned: ﴿hudan wa raḥmatun﴾ and ﴿hudan wa raḥmatan﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to this Quran, due to His saying: ﴿a guidance and mercy﴾. Each of us seeks guidance and mercy: it is guidance in knowledge and mercy in action, since the one who acts by it attains the mercy of Allah, and the one guided by it is upon guidance and insight.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Noble Quran combines all good: it is beneficial knowledge, what else? And righteous action. It is beneficial knowledge by His saying: ﴿guidance﴾, and righteous action by His saying: ﴿mercy﴾, because mercy is not attained except through righteous action.
* Among its benefits: encouragement to ihsān (excellence), due to His saying: ﴿for the good-doers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that ihsān is a cause of attaining knowledge and righteous action, since He made it ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ for whom? ﴿for the good-doers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whenever the servant's ihsān increases, his knowledge and righteous action increase, because when a ruling is attached to an attribute, it increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease, as has previously been explained.
* Among the benefits of the verse that follows: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give zakāt, and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾. Among its benefits: that establishing the prayer is part of ihsān, since what follows is its explanation: ﴿those who establish﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the prayer is the most beloved of deeds to Allah, since Allah placed it before giving zakāt, even though giving zakāt has benefit extending to others; yet the prayer is more beloved to Allah than it and more excellent.
* Among its benefits: encouragement to establishing the prayer. From where do we derive it? From Allah's praise of those who establish it, and praise is only given for doing something loved and desired by Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of giving zakāt, and that it follows the prayer in excellence, due to His saying: ﴿and give zakāt﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the one who has certainty in the Hereafter, due to His saying: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of resurrection (al-baʿth), ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾.
* It is derived from this noble verse that those characterized by what was mentioned are those upon guidance. Consequently, another benefit follows: whoever opposes what was mentioned is not upon guidance, and he has lost of guidance to the extent that he has lost of action and certainty.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the grace of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon these excellent people, due to His saying: ﴿from their Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the lordship (rubūbiyya) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is of two types: general and specific. The general is for all creation: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [Maryam 65], and the specific is for the believers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that through these virtuous and sublime deeds and beneficial beliefs, success (falāḥ) is attained, due to His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾.
* Among its benefits: that there is no path to success except by this, and its aspect is restriction (ḥaṣr), due to His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ (...)
Now we move to the new lesson, at His saying: (Surat al-Sajda).
Surat al-Sajda: this is an idāfa, and the idāfa here is explanatory (bayāniyya), meaning the surah in which prostration is mentioned. Prostration will come, God willing, within it. It is Meccan, thirty verses. Every surah that begins with alphabetic letters is Meccan, except two surahs: which are they? al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān, for they are Medinan. Otherwise, every surah that begins with alphabetic letters is Meccan.
* A student: Its being named "Sajda" is this (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the Prophet used to recite in the dawn prayer of Friday "Alif Lām Mīm, the Revelation" (al-Sajda).
* A student: In it (...) meaning evidence that it (...).
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: This (...) that it is disputed whether one prostrates in it, or... it is the same surah (...).
* The Shaykh: He said: (﴿Alif Lām Mīm﴾ Allah knows best what He means by it). We have previously mentioned that the scholars divided into three groups on this. One group claimed that these letters have meanings and are symbols for those meanings; this is a view with no evidence, weak, indeed invalid. The second view: they have meanings, but Allah knows them, so they are among the ambiguous matters known only to Allah. The third group says: they have no meaning at all, because the Quran was revealed in the Arabic tongue, and these letters in the Arabic tongue never have meanings. This is the view of Mujāhid, and it is the correct one: they have no meanings.
If someone says: How do you assert that they have no meaning, when negation requires proof? We say: we assert that because the Quran was revealed in clear Arabic tongue.

This is a discipline from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for the Prophet ﷺ and for others as well: that a person should be patient, and let not those who do not have certainty (in what Allah has promised to the patient) make him hasty. This happens to many people. You find that some people, for example, experience what befalls them of matters, and then the foolish and their likes come to them and say: "Do this, do that, do that." Suppose, for example, that he has a neighbour who harms him; some people come and say: "How can you bear this harm from your neighbour?" Or: "How can you bear this harm from your companion, or from your family, or the like?" So they make him hasty, and he does not show patience. But what is fitting for the sensible person is that he not be made hasty by those people who do not have certainty in what Allah has promised to the patient, but rather that he be patient and not concern himself with people's talk until Allah fulfills for him what He has promised. With this, the Surah of ar-Rum ends, and we move on after it to the Surah of Luqman.

He says: (It is Meccan). The most preferred of the opinions, which the majority hold, is that whatever was revealed after the Messenger ﷺ arrived in Madinah is Madani, even if it was revealed in Makkah, and whatever was revealed before his arrival in Madinah is Meccan. This is the preponderant opinion. So based on this, is the criterion time or place? Time. And this is also easier for a person.

He says: (Meccan, except ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27]). In another copy: (or except). There is a difference between them, because the author's saying "except and if" is a restriction to one opinion and a firm judgment on it, whereas on the second copy, "or except," it is an indication that there are two opinions on the matter and that he did not firmly decide on either. The correct view, as we have already mentioned, is that if a Surah is Meccan, we do not exclude anything from it except with a clear and explicit text, and if it is Madani, likewise we do not exclude anything from it except with a clear and explicit text. This is because the basic principle is that a Surah is continuous, and that the Messenger ﷺ placed every verse in its place or commanded its placement. Based on this, we say: if someone establishes that the saying ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27] was revealed after the Hijrah, and establishes that by an explicit text, then it is upon the eye and head (we accept it gladly); otherwise, the basic principle is that the Surah in its entirety is Meccan.

He says: (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [Luqman: 1] Allah knows best what He means by it). Has the discussion of the basmalah been covered grammatically, in meaning, and in ruling, or not?

Its grammatical analysis: it is a prepositional phrase (jar and majrur) related to a deleted element, a verb placed later that suits the context. The deleted element is a verb placed later that suits the context. Now, when we recite this Surah, the estimate would be: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I recite." When we want to explain, we say: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I explain." When a person wants to perform wudu, he says: "In the name of Allah, I perform wudu." Has this come up for us? Why did we estimate it as a verb? Why did we choose that its estimate be a verb?

* Student: It has not come up for us.
* Shaykh: It has not come up?
* Student: I did not hear it.
* Another student: Because the estimate indicates an answer (...) its estimate as a verb, meaning; as for the nominal sentence, it indicates continuity.
* Shaykh: No. The original principle regarding the governing element is that it be a verb, especially since it is deleted. That is one point. Why did we estimate it as specific? We did not say, for example, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I begin." Rather we said: if you are reciting, estimate "I recite"; if you want to eat, estimate "I eat"; if you want to drink, estimate "I drink." So why did we choose that its estimate be specific?
* Student: So that it suits each particular situation.
* Shaykh: In order that it suit each particular situation; and because the Messenger ﷺ said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1960/3), from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abdullah]. This indicates that the deleted verb is estimated in a way that suits the verb with which one begins. And why did we choose that its estimate be placed later?
* Student: Beginning with the name of Allah.
* Shaykh: Good. Does anyone else have something?
* Student: He mentioned it.
* Shaykh: What did he mention? Tell us.
* Student: Beginning with the name of Allah.
* Shaykh: Beginning with the name of Allah. And what else? And to convey restriction and exclusivity, because fronting the object conveys restriction and exclusivity. It is as if you were saying: "I begin only with the name of Allah." This is the reason we estimate it as placed later: for the sake of beginning with the name of Allah, and to convey restriction and exclusivity.

"Ism" is a construct noun, and the word "Allah" is the genitive complement; "ar-Rahman" is an attribute of Allah, and "ar-Rahim" is also an attribute of Allah. Is this clear? That is its grammatical analysis. As for its ruling, it is a verse from the Book of Allah, which Allah spoke, and which He sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ. However, it is not a verse of the Surah; rather, it was made a marker of the end of the preceding Surah and the beginning of the following Surah, or, more correctly, a marker of the beginning of the Surah only, so that the Fatihah is not an exception, since nothing precedes it. So it is a marker of the beginning of the Surah and not part of it. You will find in the mushafs that no number was written on it except in the Fatihah, where it was numbered. The reason is that many scholars held that the basmalah is part of the Fatihah, while the correct view is that it is not part of it, like the rest (of the Surahs), and that the first verse of the Surah al-Fatihah is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds (2), the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful (3), Sovereign of the Day of Recompense (4), You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help (5), Guide us to the straight path (6)﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2–6]. How many verses are these?
* Students: Five.
* Shaykh: Five. The Fatihah has seven verses. Where is the seventh?
* Students: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7].
* Shaykh: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is the sixth. ﴿Not of those who have evoked (Your) anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ is the seventh, correct? Yes. This is the correct view, although you find in the mushafs ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have evoked (Your) anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] as one verse, based on the view that the basmalah is the first verse.
* Student: I have seen some Pakistani mushafs written as you have said.
* Shaykh: Yes, amazing! This is the preponderant view. As for its ruling regarding its recitation in prayer: if we say it is part of the Fatihah, then it is a verse of it and must be recited, and it is recited aloud as the Fatihah is recited aloud. If we say it is not part of it, then its recitation is not obligatory and it is not recited aloud.
* Student: Recitation outside prayer, is it recited aloud outside prayer (...)?
* Shaykh: He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [Luqman: 1]. Allah knows best what He means by it. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ are three alphabetic letters. The author says: "Allah knows best what He means by it," and in this is an affirmation that Allah intended something by it, but it is not known.

From this statement of the author, or from his statement, we take that he holds these letters have a meaning, but Allah knows it. Some scholars said: they have a meaning, and they fumbled about this meaning, making them symbols for what they assigned them to. Mujahid said: they have no meaning. We say: in principle they have no meaning. We do not say "Allah knows what He intended," because the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 195], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 3]. And in the Arabic language these letters have no meaning. Based on this, we say they have no meaning. We say this because this is what the Arabic language, in which the Qur'an was revealed, requires.

If someone says: if you say they have no meaning, how is it permissible for you to be certain in negating meaning?
I say: yes, it is permissible for me, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and these alphabetic letters, according to the requirements of the Arabic language, have no meaning, so I am certain of that, because the Qur'an is in Arabic. If the matter is so, what is the benefit of their presence in the Qur'an? This is the point on which we may say: Allah knows best. However, some scholars sought a wisdom for this, that it is an indication that this Qur'an which has defeated you did not come with new letters so that you would say, "By Allah, these are not from our letters"; rather, it is from the letters of which Arabic speech is composed, and yet it has defeated you.

They said: this is why the opening with these alphabetic letters is never without the mention of the Qur'an or what is among its distinctive features: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1–2]. Reflect on it and it will flow with you.

Some surahs are like: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) The Romans have been defeated﴾ [ar-Rum: 1–2], ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) Do people think they will be left alone﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–2]. These do not contain a mention of the Qur'an, but they contain a mention of what is among its distinctive features: ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ is a matter of the unseen, known only through revelation; and ﴿Do people think they will be left alone, to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2] is an informing about those who came before, which is also a matter of the unseen: ﴿And We did test those before them, so Allah will surely know those who are truthful and will surely know the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3].

In any case, what we have mentioned last is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah adopted, and az-Zamakhshari preceded him to it in his book al-Kashshaf. He said: ﴿Tilka﴾ means: these, i.e., these verses are the verses of the Book, the wise Qur'an, possessing wisdom; and the idafah is in the sense of "min" (of).

﴿Tilka āyātu al-kitāb﴾ ("These are the verses of the Book"). ﴿Tilka﴾: the one indicated is the verses of the Qur'an. You will find that the demonstrative here is in the form of the distant, and the Qur'an is not distant, since it is before our hands; but it is elevated in rank, so the distant demonstrative was used for it.

And His saying: ﴿āyātu al-kitāb﴾ means: the written, which is the Qur'an. We mentioned earlier that it is written in three places: in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and in the scrolls in our hands.

And His saying: ﴿Tilka āyātu al-kitāb﴾, the idafah here, the author says, is according to an estimate of "min," meaning verses from the Book. The verses, as we have already gone over, are cosmic and legislative. The verses of the Book are of the legislative kind, or of the cosmic kind? Legislative.

And His saying: ﴿al-Hakim﴾. The author said: (possessing wisdom). But it may be said: possessing wisdom and also judgment, because it is the reference of people in judgment, and because it includes wisdom. It is also suitable to be taken in the sense of "muhkam" (perfected), so that fa'il is in the sense of mufa'al. The Qur'an, then, is wise for including wisdom and judgment between people: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [an-Nisa: 105].

And His saying: ﴿﴿Hudan wa rahmah﴾﴾ (in the nominative). Its place in grammar is that it is the predicate of a deleted subject, which the author estimated with his saying: (it is guidance and mercy). Huda means indication/guidance, and rahmah means that Allah showed mercy to creation by sending it down to them. So the Qur'an is guidance and mercy: whoever holds fast to it is saved and guided. Thus, one who holds to this Qur'an will not go astray nor be wretched, because it is guidance and mercy. Based on this, we say to every person who seeks knowledge: upon you is the Qur'an, because it is guidance; and to every person who seeks mercy: upon you is the Qur'an, because it is guidance.

﴿Hudan wa rahmatan﴾ [Luqman: 3]. But ﴿for the doers of good﴾: those who did good in worshipping Allah and did good to the servants of Allah. Ihsan is the opposite of evil-doing, and evil-doing is either by abandoning an obligation or by doing a forbidden thing. Whoever abandons what Allah has obligated upon him for himself, such as prayer and other things, is not a doer of good; whoever does what Allah has forbidden him is not a doer of good; whoever abandons what is due to people, such as maintaining family ties, dutifulness to parents, and kindness to them, is not a doer of good; and whoever transgresses against them is not a doer of good.

And His saying: ﴿lil-muhsinin﴾ indicates that the more a person increases in ihsan, the more he benefits from the Qur'an in guidance and mercy, based on the principle mentioned earlier, that when a ruling is linked to an attribute, it grows stronger in proportion to the presence of that attribute.

And His saying: ﴿Hudan wa rahmatan lil-muhsinin﴾. Then are those who are not doers of good not guided by it nor shown mercy? Yes, because the doers of good are those who benefit from it. Otherwise, it is guidance for all people, a source of guidance for everyone, but only those who did good benefit from it.

(And in the recitation of the common readers, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) from the verses.) This expression of the author is strange: (in the recitation of the common readers). Someone who does not know the terminology might understand from it: who is meant by "the common readers"?
* Student: Those other than the scholars.
* Shaykh: The common people, other than the scholars. That is not so. What he means by "the common" is the majority of readers, apart from one reader who recited in the nominative. Most readers, and the majority of them, read it in the accusative: ﴿Hudan wa rahmatan﴾ (in the accusative, as a circumstantial from the verses, governed by what is in that of the sense of indication). ﴿Tilka āyātu al-kitābi al-hakim﴾ [Luqman: 2], in the state of being guidance and mercy.

If someone says: a circumstantial needs a governing element, like an adverb, a prepositional phrase, or a direct object; so what is the governing element? The governing element is what is in ﴿Tilka﴾ of the sense of indication.

﴿Tilka﴾ is a noun, rigid and not derived, but it carries the meaning of "pointed to." So when you say "This is Zayd," the meaning is "he is pointed to." Thus ﴿Tilka āyātu﴾ means "these verses are pointed to." Since it contains the meaning of a verb, it is suitable to govern a circumstantial.

﴿Alladhina yuqimuna al-salah﴾ [Luqman: 4] (an explanation of "the doers of good"). Based on this, it is not a descriptive attribute (na't); rather it is an explanation (bayan), i.e., an appositive (atf bayan). Who are the doers of good? ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾: meaning they perform it upright and complete. ﴿Al-salah﴾ includes the obligatory and the voluntary. Establishing it is by performing the obligations and avoiding what nullifies it; likewise, establishment is completed by performing the complements and recommended acts. And ﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah﴾: they give it. And zakah, as has been said, is a portion legally determined in a specific property for a specific category.

Where is the second object of ﴿yu'tuna﴾? Its second object is deleted. The estimate: ﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah ahlaha﴾ (and they give zakah to its people). It was permissible to delete it because it is a superfluous element, and it has been mentioned before that all superfluous objects may be deleted.

And His saying: ﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah﴾: this paid property is called zakah because by it the character of the one who pays is purified (tazku), and the property also grows and increases, because zakah in the language means growth and increase.

﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned among the actions only prayer and zakah, and their pairing in the Qur'an is frequent, because they are the most emphasized pillars of Islam after the two testimonies. Abandoning both together necessitates disbelief. Abandoning one of them: regarding prayer, the correct view is that one becomes a disbeliever; regarding zakah, the correct view is that one does not become a disbeliever. This has been discussed before.

﴿wa hum bil-akhirati hum yuqinun﴾ [Luqman: 4]. ﴿Hum﴾ is the subject, ﴿bil-akhirah﴾ is a prepositional phrase related to ﴿yuqinun﴾, and the second ﴿hum﴾: the author says: (the second hum is emphasis). Emphasis of what? Of the first ﴿hum﴾. Is the first one verbal or semantic emphasis? Verbal. Ibn Malik said:

And of verbal emphasis is what comes repeated, like your saying: "Idruji, idruji" (walk on, walk on).

His saying: ﴿hum yuqinun bil-akhirah﴾. By "the Hereafter" is meant the Day of Resurrection, and it is called "the last" because it is the final thing that will occur. A person has four stages: the first stage is in his mother's womb; the second stage is in this world; the third stage is in the barzakh; and the fourth and last stage is the Day of Resurrection.

And His saying: ﴿bil-akhirati hum yuqinun﴾. Faith in the Hereafter does not mean merely that you believe the Resurrection will take place. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in al-Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah: Faith in the Last Day includes faith in everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will occur after death. This includes the trial of the grave, the punishment of the grave, the bliss of the grave, the Sirat, the reckoning, the Scale, the books that will be distributed on the Day of Resurrection, and other matters.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

He said: ﴿They are certain of the Hereafter. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾ [Luqman 4–5]. The Noble Quran sometimes repeats verses exactly. The exact repetition of verses is found in the Quran; this one is repeated in Surah al-Baqarah, although there is a slight difference in the verse before it. As for His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 4–5], it is one verse.

His saying: ﴿upon guidance from their Lord﴾ uses ʿalā (upon), which indicates elevation. That is, they are upon guidance, which they follow, and they are elevated above it because of the height of their rank.

As for His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 5], this sentence is a nominal sentence whose predicate is emphasized by the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), which is His saying: ﴿hum al-mufliḥūn﴾ (they are the successful). Indeed, hum is a pronoun of separation, and we have previously mentioned that the pronoun of separation conveys three benefits (...)

These are three benefits of the pronoun of separation. If you say: Zayd al-qāʾim (Zayd the standing one), this is a subject and predicate, but it may be that al-qāʾim is an adjective of Zayd, and the predicate is awaited, as in: Zayd al-qāʾim fāḍilun (Zayd the standing one is excellent), for example. But if you say: Zayd huwa al-qāʾim (Zayd, he is the standing one), it becomes definite that al-qāʾim is the predicate; you have now separated the adjective from the predicate. Likewise, if you say: Zayd huwa al-qāʾim, it conveys restriction (ḥaṣr): Zayd, he, meaning not other than him, is the standing one. Likewise, your saying Zayd huwa al-qāʾim is more emphatic than your saying Zayd al-qāʾim; it is more forceful in emphasis.

So here: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 5] means not other than them. The author says that al-mufliḥ (the successful) is "al-fāʾiz" (the victorious). And what is the meaning of al-fāʾiz? Al-fāʾiz is the happy one (al-saʿīd). And what is the meaning of al-saʿīd?
* A student: One who attains the good of this world and the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: They say: al-mufliḥ is one who attains what he seeks and is saved from what he fears. This is the successful one: one who attains what he seeks, which is what he desires, and is safe from what he does not want.
﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 5]. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who purchases idle talk﴾ [Luqman 6]. (Min) is for partitive (tabʿīḍ). ﴿And among the people﴾ and so on (...)
* A student: The narrator dominated (...).
* The Shaykh: In any case (...), we proceed with clear evidences and leave this doubtful matter.
* * *
Allah the Exalted said, in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful: ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm. Those are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in sending down these alphabetic letters, which are ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm﴾ and what is similar to them.
* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, speaks with letters and also with sound, since ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm﴾ is from the speech of Allah and consists of letters. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah, and we have previously discussed it many times, and that Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah say: the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is with letters and sound.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the high status of this Quran, due to His saying: ﴿those are the verses﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the Quran is a sign and evidence of its Revealer, due to His saying: ﴿the verses of the Book﴾. We have previously noted that the idāfa (construction) is with the sense of "min" (of), so it is a genus idāfa. The Quran is a sign of its Revealer, Exalted is He, from which aspect? From the truthfulness of its reports and their agreement with reality, and from the excellence of its narratives and their love in souls, and that they never bore people, for there is no speech that is repeated but it becomes tiresome, except the Quran. Third: from the aspect of its rulings, since they are just rulings beneficial to the servants in their livelihood and their hereafter. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-Anʿām 115].
* Among its benefits: that the Quran is written as it is recited, due to His saying: ﴿those are the verses of the Book﴾.
* Among its benefits: praise of the Quran with this great attribute, which is al-Ḥakīm (the Wise).
* Also among its benefits: that there is no report in the Quran that is stated in vain, nor a ruling established in vain. From where do we derive this? From al-Ḥakīm (the Wise), since vanity contradicts wisdom, and it is impossible for there to be anything in vain in the Quran, neither a report nor a ruling.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a guidance and mercy for the good-doers﴾. It has two readings, as previously mentioned: ﴿hudan wa raḥmatun﴾ and ﴿hudan wa raḥmatan﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to this Quran, due to His saying: ﴿a guidance and mercy﴾. Each of us seeks guidance and mercy: it is guidance in knowledge and mercy in action, since the one who acts by it attains the mercy of Allah, and the one guided by it is upon guidance and insight.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Noble Quran combines all good: it is beneficial knowledge, what else? And righteous action. It is beneficial knowledge by His saying: ﴿guidance﴾, and righteous action by His saying: ﴿mercy﴾, because mercy is not attained except through righteous action.
* Among its benefits: encouragement to ihsān (excellence), due to His saying: ﴿for the good-doers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that ihsān is a cause of attaining knowledge and righteous action, since He made it ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ for whom? ﴿for the good-doers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whenever the servant's ihsān increases, his knowledge and righteous action increase, because when a ruling is attached to an attribute, it increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease, as has previously been explained.
* Among the benefits of the verse that follows: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give zakāt, and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾. Among its benefits: that establishing the prayer is part of ihsān, since what follows is its explanation: ﴿those who establish﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the prayer is the most beloved of deeds to Allah, since Allah placed it before giving zakāt, even though giving zakāt has benefit extending to others; yet the prayer is more beloved to Allah than it and more excellent.
* Among its benefits: encouragement to establishing the prayer. From where do we derive it? From Allah's praise of those who establish it, and praise is only given for doing something loved and desired by Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of giving zakāt, and that it follows the prayer in excellence, due to His saying: ﴿and give zakāt﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the one who has certainty in the Hereafter, due to His saying: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of resurrection (al-baʿth), ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾.
* It is derived from this noble verse that those characterized by what was mentioned are those upon guidance. Consequently, another benefit follows: whoever opposes what was mentioned is not upon guidance, and he has lost of guidance to the extent that he has lost of action and certainty.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the grace of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon these excellent people, due to His saying: ﴿from their Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the lordship (rubūbiyya) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is of two types: general and specific. The general is for all creation: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [Maryam 65], and the specific is for the believers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that through these virtuous and sublime deeds and beneficial beliefs, success (falāḥ) is attained, due to His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾.
* Among its benefits: that there is no path to success except by this, and its aspect is restriction (ḥaṣr), due to His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ (...)
Now we move to the new lesson, at His saying: (Surat al-Sajda).
Surat al-Sajda: this is an idāfa, and the idāfa here is explanatory (bayāniyya), meaning the surah in which prostration is mentioned. Prostration will come, God willing, within it. It is Meccan, thirty verses. Every surah that begins with alphabetic letters is Meccan, except two surahs: which are they? al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān, for they are Medinan. Otherwise, every surah that begins with alphabetic letters is Meccan.
* A student: Its being named "Sajda" is this (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the Prophet used to recite in the dawn prayer of Friday "Alif Lām Mīm, the Revelation" (al-Sajda).
* A student: In it (...) meaning evidence that it (...).
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: This (...) that it is disputed whether one prostrates in it, or... it is the same surah (...).
* The Shaykh: He said: (﴿Alif Lām Mīm﴾ Allah knows best what He means by it). We have previously mentioned that the scholars divided into three groups on this. One group claimed that these letters have meanings and are symbols for those meanings; this is a view with no evidence, weak, indeed invalid. The second view: they have meanings, but Allah knows them, so they are among the ambiguous matters known only to Allah. The third group says: they have no meaning at all, because the Quran was revealed in the Arabic tongue, and these letters in the Arabic tongue never have meanings. This is the view of Mujāhid, and it is the correct one: they have no meanings.
If someone says: How do you assert that they have no meaning, when negation requires proof? We say: we assert that because the Quran was revealed in clear Arabic tongue.

This is a discipline from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for the Prophet ﷺ and for others as well: that a person should be patient, and let not those who do not have certainty (in what Allah has promised to the patient) make him hasty. This happens to many people. You find that some people, for example, experience what befalls them of matters, and then the foolish and their likes come to them and say: "Do this, do that, do that." Suppose, for example, that he has a neighbour who harms him; some people come and say: "How can you bear this harm from your neighbour?" Or: "How can you bear this harm from your companion, or from your family, or the like?" So they make him hasty, and he does not show patience. But what is fitting for the sensible person is that he not be made hasty by those people who do not have certainty in what Allah has promised to the patient, but rather that he be patient and not concern himself with people's talk until Allah fulfills for him what He has promised. With this, the Surah of ar-Rum ends, and we move on after it to the Surah of Luqman.

He says: (It is Meccan). The most preferred of the opinions, which the majority hold, is that whatever was revealed after the Messenger ﷺ arrived in Madinah is Madani, even if it was revealed in Makkah, and whatever was revealed before his arrival in Madinah is Meccan. This is the preponderant opinion. So based on this, is the criterion time or place? Time. And this is also easier for a person.

He says: (Meccan, except ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27]). In another copy: (or except). There is a difference between them, because the author's saying "except and if" is a restriction to one opinion and a firm judgment on it, whereas on the second copy, "or except," it is an indication that there are two opinions on the matter and that he did not firmly decide on either. The correct view, as we have already mentioned, is that if a Surah is Meccan, we do not exclude anything from it except with a clear and explicit text, and if it is Madani, likewise we do not exclude anything from it except with a clear and explicit text. This is because the basic principle is that a Surah is continuous, and that the Messenger ﷺ placed every verse in its place or commanded its placement. Based on this, we say: if someone establishes that the saying ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27] was revealed after the Hijrah, and establishes that by an explicit text, then it is upon the eye and head (we accept it gladly); otherwise, the basic principle is that the Surah in its entirety is Meccan.

He says: (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [Luqman: 1] Allah knows best what He means by it). Has the discussion of the basmalah been covered grammatically, in meaning, and in ruling, or not?

Its grammatical analysis: it is a prepositional phrase (jar and majrur) related to a deleted element, a verb placed later that suits the context. The deleted element is a verb placed later that suits the context. Now, when we recite this Surah, the estimate would be: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I recite." When we want to explain, we say: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I explain." When a person wants to perform wudu, he says: "In the name of Allah, I perform wudu." Has this come up for us? Why did we estimate it as a verb? Why did we choose that its estimate be a verb?

* Student: It has not come up for us.
* Shaykh: It has not come up?
* Student: I did not hear it.
* Another student: Because the estimate indicates an answer (...) its estimate as a verb, meaning; as for the nominal sentence, it indicates continuity.
* Shaykh: No. The original principle regarding the governing element is that it be a verb, especially since it is deleted. That is one point. Why did we estimate it as specific? We did not say, for example, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I begin." Rather we said: if you are reciting, estimate "I recite"; if you want to eat, estimate "I eat"; if you want to drink, estimate "I drink." So why did we choose that its estimate be specific?
* Student: So that it suits each particular situation.
* Shaykh: In order that it suit each particular situation; and because the Messenger ﷺ said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1960/3), from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abdullah]. This indicates that the deleted verb is estimated in a way that suits the verb with which one begins. And why did we choose that its estimate be placed later?
* Student: Beginning with the name of Allah.
* Shaykh: Good. Does anyone else have something?
* Student: He mentioned it.
* Shaykh: What did he mention? Tell us.
* Student: Beginning with the name of Allah.
* Shaykh: Beginning with the name of Allah. And what else? And to convey restriction and exclusivity, because fronting the object conveys restriction and exclusivity. It is as if you were saying: "I begin only with the name of Allah." This is the reason we estimate it as placed later: for the sake of beginning with the name of Allah, and to convey restriction and exclusivity.

"Ism" is a construct noun, and the word "Allah" is the genitive complement; "ar-Rahman" is an attribute of Allah, and "ar-Rahim" is also an attribute of Allah. Is this clear? That is its grammatical analysis. As for its ruling, it is a verse from the Book of Allah, which Allah spoke, and which He sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ. However, it is not a verse of the Surah; rather, it was made a marker of the end of the preceding Surah and the beginning of the following Surah, or, more correctly, a marker of the beginning of the Surah only, so that the Fatihah is not an exception, since nothing precedes it. So it is a marker of the beginning of the Surah and not part of it. You will find in the mushafs that no number was written on it except in the Fatihah, where it was numbered. The reason is that many scholars held that the basmalah is part of the Fatihah, while the correct view is that it is not part of it, like the rest (of the Surahs), and that the first verse of the Surah al-Fatihah is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds (2), the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful (3), Sovereign of the Day of Recompense (4), You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help (5), Guide us to the straight path (6)﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2–6]. How many verses are these?
* Students: Five.
* Shaykh: Five. The Fatihah has seven verses. Where is the seventh?
* Students: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7].
* Shaykh: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is the sixth. ﴿Not of those who have evoked (Your) anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ is the seventh, correct? Yes. This is the correct view, although you find in the mushafs ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have evoked (Your) anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] as one verse, based on the view that the basmalah is the first verse.
* Student: I have seen some Pakistani mushafs written as you have said.
* Shaykh: Yes, amazing! This is the preponderant view. As for its ruling regarding its recitation in prayer: if we say it is part of the Fatihah, then it is a verse of it and must be recited, and it is recited aloud as the Fatihah is recited aloud. If we say it is not part of it, then its recitation is not obligatory and it is not recited aloud.
* Student: Recitation outside prayer, is it recited aloud outside prayer (...)?
* Shaykh: He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [Luqman: 1]. Allah knows best what He means by it. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ are three alphabetic letters. The author says: "Allah knows best what He means by it," and in this is an affirmation that Allah intended something by it, but it is not known.

From this statement of the author, or from his statement, we take that he holds these letters have a meaning, but Allah knows it. Some scholars said: they have a meaning, and they fumbled about this meaning, making them symbols for what they assigned them to. Mujahid said: they have no meaning. We say: in principle they have no meaning. We do not say "Allah knows what He intended," because the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 195], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 3]. And in the Arabic language these letters have no meaning. Based on this, we say they have no meaning. We say this because this is what the Arabic language, in which the Qur'an was revealed, requires.

If someone says: if you say they have no meaning, how is it permissible for you to be certain in negating meaning?
I say: yes, it is permissible for me, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and these alphabetic letters, according to the requirements of the Arabic language, have no meaning, so I am certain of that, because the Qur'an is in Arabic. If the matter is so, what is the benefit of their presence in the Qur'an? This is the point on which we may say: Allah knows best. However, some scholars sought a wisdom for this, that it is an indication that this Qur'an which has defeated you did not come with new letters so that you would say, "By Allah, these are not from our letters"; rather, it is from the letters of which Arabic speech is composed, and yet it has defeated you.

They said: this is why the opening with these alphabetic letters is never without the mention of the Qur'an or what is among its distinctive features: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1–2]. Reflect on it and it will flow with you.

Some surahs are like: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) The Romans have been defeated﴾ [ar-Rum: 1–2], ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) Do people think they will be left alone﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–2]. These do not contain a mention of the Qur'an, but they contain a mention of what is among its distinctive features: ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ is a matter of the unseen, known only through revelation; and ﴿Do people think they will be left alone, to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2] is an informing about those who came before, which is also a matter of the unseen: ﴿And We did test those before them, so Allah will surely know those who are truthful and will surely know the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3].

In any case, what we have mentioned last is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah adopted, and az-Zamakhshari preceded him to it in his book al-Kashshaf. He said: ﴿Tilka﴾ means: these, i.e., these verses are the verses of the Book, the wise Qur'an, possessing wisdom; and the idafah is in the sense of "min" (of).

﴿Tilka āyātu al-kitāb﴾ ("These are the verses of the Book"). ﴿Tilka﴾: the one indicated is the verses of the Qur'an. You will find that the demonstrative here is in the form of the distant, and the Qur'an is not distant, since it is before our hands; but it is elevated in rank, so the distant demonstrative was used for it.

And His saying: ﴿āyātu al-kitāb﴾ means: the written, which is the Qur'an. We mentioned earlier that it is written in three places: in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and in the scrolls in our hands.

And His saying: ﴿Tilka āyātu al-kitāb﴾, the idafah here, the author says, is according to an estimate of "min," meaning verses from the Book. The verses, as we have already gone over, are cosmic and legislative. The verses of the Book are of the legislative kind, or of the cosmic kind? Legislative.

And His saying: ﴿al-Hakim﴾. The author said: (possessing wisdom). But it may be said: possessing wisdom and also judgment, because it is the reference of people in judgment, and because it includes wisdom. It is also suitable to be taken in the sense of "muhkam" (perfected), so that fa'il is in the sense of mufa'al. The Qur'an, then, is wise for including wisdom and judgment between people: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [an-Nisa: 105].

And His saying: ﴿﴿Hudan wa rahmah﴾﴾ (in the nominative). Its place in grammar is that it is the predicate of a deleted subject, which the author estimated with his saying: (it is guidance and mercy). Huda means indication/guidance, and rahmah means that Allah showed mercy to creation by sending it down to them. So the Qur'an is guidance and mercy: whoever holds fast to it is saved and guided. Thus, one who holds to this Qur'an will not go astray nor be wretched, because it is guidance and mercy. Based on this, we say to every person who seeks knowledge: upon you is the Qur'an, because it is guidance; and to every person who seeks mercy: upon you is the Qur'an, because it is guidance.

﴿Hudan wa rahmatan﴾ [Luqman: 3]. But ﴿for the doers of good﴾: those who did good in worshipping Allah and did good to the servants of Allah. Ihsan is the opposite of evil-doing, and evil-doing is either by abandoning an obligation or by doing a forbidden thing. Whoever abandons what Allah has obligated upon him for himself, such as prayer and other things, is not a doer of good; whoever does what Allah has forbidden him is not a doer of good; whoever abandons what is due to people, such as maintaining family ties, dutifulness to parents, and kindness to them, is not a doer of good; and whoever transgresses against them is not a doer of good.

And His saying: ﴿lil-muhsinin﴾ indicates that the more a person increases in ihsan, the more he benefits from the Qur'an in guidance and mercy, based on the principle mentioned earlier, that when a ruling is linked to an attribute, it grows stronger in proportion to the presence of that attribute.

And His saying: ﴿Hudan wa rahmatan lil-muhsinin﴾. Then are those who are not doers of good not guided by it nor shown mercy? Yes, because the doers of good are those who benefit from it. Otherwise, it is guidance for all people, a source of guidance for everyone, but only those who did good benefit from it.

(And in the recitation of the common readers, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) from the verses.) This expression of the author is strange: (in the recitation of the common readers). Someone who does not know the terminology might understand from it: who is meant by "the common readers"?
* Student: Those other than the scholars.
* Shaykh: The common people, other than the scholars. That is not so. What he means by "the common" is the majority of readers, apart from one reader who recited in the nominative. Most readers, and the majority of them, read it in the accusative: ﴿Hudan wa rahmatan﴾ (in the accusative, as a circumstantial from the verses, governed by what is in that of the sense of indication). ﴿Tilka āyātu al-kitābi al-hakim﴾ [Luqman: 2], in the state of being guidance and mercy.

If someone says: a circumstantial needs a governing element, like an adverb, a prepositional phrase, or a direct object; so what is the governing element? The governing element is what is in ﴿Tilka﴾ of the sense of indication.

﴿Tilka﴾ is a noun, rigid and not derived, but it carries the meaning of "pointed to." So when you say "This is Zayd," the meaning is "he is pointed to." Thus ﴿Tilka āyātu﴾ means "these verses are pointed to." Since it contains the meaning of a verb, it is suitable to govern a circumstantial.

﴿Alladhina yuqimuna al-salah﴾ [Luqman: 4] (an explanation of "the doers of good"). Based on this, it is not a descriptive attribute (na't); rather it is an explanation (bayan), i.e., an appositive (atf bayan). Who are the doers of good? ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾: meaning they perform it upright and complete. ﴿Al-salah﴾ includes the obligatory and the voluntary. Establishing it is by performing the obligations and avoiding what nullifies it; likewise, establishment is completed by performing the complements and recommended acts. And ﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah﴾: they give it. And zakah, as has been said, is a portion legally determined in a specific property for a specific category.

Where is the second object of ﴿yu'tuna﴾? Its second object is deleted. The estimate: ﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah ahlaha﴾ (and they give zakah to its people). It was permissible to delete it because it is a superfluous element, and it has been mentioned before that all superfluous objects may be deleted.

And His saying: ﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah﴾: this paid property is called zakah because by it the character of the one who pays is purified (tazku), and the property also grows and increases, because zakah in the language means growth and increase.

﴿wa yu'tuna al-zakah﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned among the actions only prayer and zakah, and their pairing in the Qur'an is frequent, because they are the most emphasized pillars of Islam after the two testimonies. Abandoning both together necessitates disbelief. Abandoning one of them: regarding prayer, the correct view is that one becomes a disbeliever; regarding zakah, the correct view is that one does not become a disbeliever. This has been discussed before.

﴿wa hum bil-akhirati hum yuqinun﴾ [Luqman: 4]. ﴿Hum﴾ is the subject, ﴿bil-akhirah﴾ is a prepositional phrase related to ﴿yuqinun﴾, and the second ﴿hum﴾: the author says: (the second hum is emphasis). Emphasis of what? Of the first ﴿hum﴾. Is the first one verbal or semantic emphasis? Verbal. Ibn Malik said:

And of verbal emphasis is what comes repeated, like your saying: "Idruji, idruji" (walk on, walk on).

His saying: ﴿hum yuqinun bil-akhirah﴾. By "the Hereafter" is meant the Day of Resurrection, and it is called "the last" because it is the final thing that will occur. A person has four stages: the first stage is in his mother's womb; the second stage is in this world; the third stage is in the barzakh; and the fourth and last stage is the Day of Resurrection.

And His saying: ﴿bil-akhirati hum yuqinun﴾. Faith in the Hereafter does not mean merely that you believe the Resurrection will take place. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in al-Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah: Faith in the Last Day includes faith in everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will occur after death. This includes the trial of the grave, the punishment of the grave, the bliss of the grave, the Sirat, the reckoning, the Scale, the books that will be distributed on the Day of Resurrection, and other matters.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

He said: ﴿They are certain of the Hereafter. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾ [Luqman 4–5]. The Noble Quran sometimes repeats verses exactly. The exact repetition of verses is found in the Quran; this one is repeated in Surah al-Baqarah, although there is a slight difference in the verse before it. As for His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 4–5], it is one verse.

His saying: ﴿upon guidance from their Lord﴾ uses ʿalā (upon), which indicates elevation. That is, they are upon guidance, which they follow, and they are elevated above it because of the height of their rank.

As for His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 5], this sentence is a nominal sentence whose predicate is emphasized by the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), which is His saying: ﴿hum al-mufliḥūn﴾ (they are the successful). Indeed, hum is a pronoun of separation, and we have previously mentioned that the pronoun of separation conveys three benefits (...)

These are three benefits of the pronoun of separation. If you say: Zayd al-qāʾim (Zayd the standing one), this is a subject and predicate, but it may be that al-qāʾim is an adjective of Zayd, and the predicate is awaited, as in: Zayd al-qāʾim fāḍilun (Zayd the standing one is excellent), for example. But if you say: Zayd huwa al-qāʾim (Zayd, he is the standing one), it becomes definite that al-qāʾim is the predicate; you have now separated the adjective from the predicate. Likewise, if you say: Zayd huwa al-qāʾim, it conveys restriction (ḥaṣr): Zayd, he, meaning not other than him, is the standing one. Likewise, your saying Zayd huwa al-qāʾim is more emphatic than your saying Zayd al-qāʾim; it is more forceful in emphasis.

So here: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 5] means not other than them. The author says that al-mufliḥ (the successful) is "al-fāʾiz" (the victorious). And what is the meaning of al-fāʾiz? Al-fāʾiz is the happy one (al-saʿīd). And what is the meaning of al-saʿīd?
* A student: One who attains the good of this world and the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: They say: al-mufliḥ is one who attains what he seeks and is saved from what he fears. This is the successful one: one who attains what he seeks, which is what he desires, and is safe from what he does not want.
﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman 5]. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who purchases idle talk﴾ [Luqman 6]. (Min) is for partitive (tabʿīḍ). ﴿And among the people﴾ and so on (...)
* A student: The narrator dominated (...).
* The Shaykh: In any case (...), we proceed with clear evidences and leave this doubtful matter.
* * *
Allah the Exalted said, in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful: ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm. Those are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in sending down these alphabetic letters, which are ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm﴾ and what is similar to them.
* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, speaks with letters and also with sound, since ﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm﴾ is from the speech of Allah and consists of letters. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah, and we have previously discussed it many times, and that Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah say: the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is with letters and sound.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the high status of this Quran, due to His saying: ﴿those are the verses﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the Quran is a sign and evidence of its Revealer, due to His saying: ﴿the verses of the Book﴾. We have previously noted that the idāfa (construction) is with the sense of "min" (of), so it is a genus idāfa. The Quran is a sign of its Revealer, Exalted is He, from which aspect? From the truthfulness of its reports and their agreement with reality, and from the excellence of its narratives and their love in souls, and that they never bore people, for there is no speech that is repeated but it becomes tiresome, except the Quran. Third: from the aspect of its rulings, since they are just rulings beneficial to the servants in their livelihood and their hereafter. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-Anʿām 115].
* Among its benefits: that the Quran is written as it is recited, due to His saying: ﴿those are the verses of the Book﴾.
* Among its benefits: praise of the Quran with this great attribute, which is al-Ḥakīm (the Wise).
* Also among its benefits: that there is no report in the Quran that is stated in vain, nor a ruling established in vain. From where do we derive this? From al-Ḥakīm (the Wise), since vanity contradicts wisdom, and it is impossible for there to be anything in vain in the Quran, neither a report nor a ruling.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a guidance and mercy for the good-doers﴾. It has two readings, as previously mentioned: ﴿hudan wa raḥmatun﴾ and ﴿hudan wa raḥmatan﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to this Quran, due to His saying: ﴿a guidance and mercy﴾. Each of us seeks guidance and mercy: it is guidance in knowledge and mercy in action, since the one who acts by it attains the mercy of Allah, and the one guided by it is upon guidance and insight.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Noble Quran combines all good: it is beneficial knowledge, what else? And righteous action. It is beneficial knowledge by His saying: ﴿guidance﴾, and righteous action by His saying: ﴿mercy﴾, because mercy is not attained except through righteous action.
* Among its benefits: encouragement to ihsān (excellence), due to His saying: ﴿for the good-doers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that ihsān is a cause of attaining knowledge and righteous action, since He made it ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ for whom? ﴿for the good-doers﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whenever the servant's ihsān increases, his knowledge and righteous action increase, because when a ruling is attached to an attribute, it increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease, as has previously been explained.
* Among the benefits of the verse that follows: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give zakāt, and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾. Among its benefits: that establishing the prayer is part of ihsān, since what follows is its explanation: ﴿those who establish﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the prayer is the most beloved of deeds to Allah, since Allah placed it before giving zakāt, even though giving zakāt has benefit extending to others; yet the prayer is more beloved to Allah than it and more excellent.
* Among its benefits: encouragement to establishing the prayer. From where do we derive it? From Allah's praise of those who establish it, and praise is only given for doing something loved and desired by Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of giving zakāt, and that it follows the prayer in excellence, due to His saying: ﴿and give zakāt﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the one who has certainty in the Hereafter, due to His saying: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of resurrection (al-baʿth), ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾.
* It is derived from this noble verse that those characterized by what was mentioned are those upon guidance. Consequently, another benefit follows: whoever opposes what was mentioned is not upon guidance, and he has lost of guidance to the extent that he has lost of action and certainty.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the grace of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon these excellent people, due to His saying: ﴿from their Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the lordship (rubūbiyya) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is of two types: general and specific. The general is for all creation: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [Maryam 65], and the specific is for the believers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that through these virtuous and sublime deeds and beneficial beliefs, success (falāḥ) is attained, due to His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾.
* Among its benefits: that there is no path to success except by this, and its aspect is restriction (ḥaṣr), due to His saying: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ (...)
Now we move to the new lesson, at His saying: (Surat al-Sajda).
Surat al-Sajda: this is an idāfa, and the idāfa here is explanatory (bayāniyya), meaning the surah in which prostration is mentioned. Prostration will come, God willing, within it. It is Meccan, thirty verses. Every surah that begins with alphabetic letters is Meccan, except two surahs: which are they? al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān, for they are Medinan. Otherwise, every surah that begins with alphabetic letters is Meccan.
* A student: Its being named "Sajda" is this (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the Prophet used to recite in the dawn prayer of Friday "Alif Lām Mīm, the Revelation" (al-Sajda).
* A student: In it (...) meaning evidence that it (...).
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: This (...) that it is disputed whether one prostrates in it, or... it is the same surah (...).
* The Shaykh: He said: (﴿Alif Lām Mīm﴾ Allah knows best what He means by it). We have previously mentioned that the scholars divided into three groups on this. One group claimed that these letters have meanings and are symbols for those meanings; this is a view with no evidence, weak, indeed invalid. The second view: they have meanings, but Allah knows them, so they are among the ambiguous matters known only to Allah. The third group says: they have no meaning at all, because the Quran was revealed in the Arabic tongue, and these letters in the Arabic tongue never have meanings. This is the view of Mujāhid, and it is the correct one: they have no meanings.
If someone says: How do you assert that they have no meaning, when negation requires proof? We say: we assert that because the Quran was revealed in clear Arabic tongue.

This is a divine discipline from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for the Prophet ﷺ and for others as well: that a person should be patient and not let those who have no certainty be light-headed about them. (Cf. ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and let not those who do not have certainty make you impatient﴾ [al-Rum: 60].) This happens to many people. You find that some people, for example, experience certain matters, and then the foolish and their like come to them and say: "Do this, do that, do that." Suppose someone has a neighbour who harms him. Some people come and say: "How do you tolerate this harm from your neighbour?" or "How do you tolerate this harm from your companion, or from your family, or the like?" They make him light-headed, so he does not remain patient. But what is fitting for the sensible person is that he should not be swayed by those people who have no certainty about what Allah has promised to the patient; rather, he should be patient and not concern himself with people's words until Allah makes true for him what He has promised. With this, Surat al-Rum comes to an end, and we move on after it to Surat Luqman.

He says: (It is Meccan). The most preferred of the opinions, held by the majority, is that whatever was revealed after the Messenger ﷺ arrived in Medina is Medinan, even if it was revealed in Mecca, and whatever was revealed before his arrival in Medina is Meccan. This is the preferred opinion. Based on this, is the criterion time or place? Time. And this is also easier for a person.

He says: (Meccan, except ﴿And if all the trees on earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27]). In another copy: (or except). There is a difference between them. The author's statement "except and if..." is a restriction to a single opinion and a definite judgement on it. As for the second copy, "or except", it indicates that there are two opinions on the matter and that he did not decide on either. The correct view, as has already been mentioned to us, is that if a surah is Meccan, we do not exclude anything from it except by a clear and explicit text; and if it is Medinan, we do not exclude anything from it except by a clear and explicit text. This is because the basic principle is that a surah is continuous, and that the Messenger ﷺ placed each verse in its place or commanded its placement. Accordingly, we say: if someone establishes that the verse ﴿And if all the trees on earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27] was revealed after the Hijrah, if he establishes this by a text, then it is upon the eye and the head (we accept it gladly); otherwise, the basic principle is that the surah in its entirety is Meccan.

He says: (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem﴾ [Luqman: 1]. Allah knows best what He means by it). Has the discussion of the basmalah, in terms of its grammatical analysis, meaning and ruling, already taken place or not?

Its grammatical analysis is that it is a prepositional phrase related to a deleted element: a verb, postponed, suited to the context. The deleted element is a postponed verb suited to the context. Now, when we recite this surah, the estimate is: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I recite." When we want to explain, we say: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I explain." When a person wants to perform wudu, he says: "In the name of Allah, I perform wudu." Has this been covered for us? Why did we estimate it as a verb? Why did we choose that its estimate be a verb?

* Student: It has not been covered for us.
* The Shaykh: It has not been covered?
* Student: I did not hear it.
* Another student: Because the estimate indicates an answer (...) its estimate being a verb means, whereas a nominal sentence indicates continuity.
* The Shaykh: No. The basic principle regarding the operator is that it be a verb, especially since it is deleted. That is one reason. Why did we estimate it as specific? We did not just say, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I begin," but rather we said: if you are reciting, estimate "I recite"; if you want to eat, estimate "I eat"; if you want to drink, estimate "I drink." So why did we choose that its estimate be specific?
* Student: So that it suits each particular situation.
* The Shaykh: In order that it suits each particular situation; and because the Messenger ﷺ said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1960/3), from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abdullah]. This is an indication that the deleted verb is estimated in a way that suits the verb with which one begins. And why did we choose that its estimate be postponed?
* Student: The beginning with the name of Allah.
* The Shaykh: Good. Does anyone else have something?
* Student: Mentioning it.
* The Shaykh: What did the one who mentioned it tell us?
* Student: The beginning with the name of Allah.
* The Shaykh: The beginning with the name of Allah. And another reason? And to convey exclusivity, because fronting the object conveys restriction and exclusivity. It is as if you were saying: "I begin only with the name of Allah." This is the reason we estimate it as postponed: for the beginning with the name of Allah, and to convey restriction and exclusivity.

"Ism" is a noun in construct, and the word "Allah" is the noun in the genitive. "Al-Rahman" is an adjective of Allah, and "al-Rahim" is also an adjective of Allah. Is that clear? This is its grammatical analysis. As for its ruling, it is a verse of the Book of Allah, spoken by Allah and revealed by Him upon the Messenger ﷺ. However, it is not a verse of the surah; rather, it was made a marker for the end of the preceding surah and the beginning of the following surah, or, more correctly, a marker for the beginning of the surah only, so that the Fatihah is not an objection to us, since nothing precedes it. So it is a marker for the beginning of the surah and not part of it. You will find in the mushafs that no number was written on it except in al-Fatihah, where it was numbered. The reason is that many scholars held that the basmalah is part of al-Fatihah, but the correct view is that it is not part of it, like the rest of the surahs, and that the first verse of al-Fatihah is the Most High's saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds (2), The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful (3), Sovereign of the Day of Recompense (4), It is You we worship and You we ask for help (5), Guide us to the straight path (6)﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2-6]. How many are there?
* Students: Five.
* The Shaykh: Five. Al-Fatihah has seven verses. Where is the seventh?
* Students: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7].
* The Shaykh: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is the sixth. ﴿Not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾ is the seventh. Is that right? Yes. This is the correct view, although you find in the mushafs: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] as a single verse, based on the view that the basmalah is the first verse.
* Student: I have seen some Pakistani mushafs written as you said.
* The Shaykh: Yes, how strange! This is according to the preferred view. As for its ruling with regard to recitation in prayer: if we say it is part of al-Fatihah, then it is a verse of it and it must be recited, and it is recited aloud as al-Fatihah is recited aloud. If we say it is not part of it, then it is not obligatory to recite it and it is not recited aloud.
* Student: Recitation outside prayer, is it recited aloud outside prayer (...)?
* The Shaykh: He said ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem﴾ [Luqman: 1], "Allah knows best what He means by it." ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem﴾ are three alphabetic letters. The author says: "Allah knows best what He means by it," and in this there is an affirmation that Allah intends something by it, but it is not known.

From this statement of the author, or from his words, we take that he holds that these letters have a meaning, but Allah knows it best. Some scholars said: they have a meaning, and they groped about this meaning, making them symbols for what they assigned them to. Mujahid said: they have no meaning. We say: in principle they have no meaning, and we do not say "Allah knows best what He intends." This is because the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, as He Most High said: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 195], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3]. And in the Arabic language these letters have no meaning. Accordingly, we say they have no meaning; we say that because this is what the Arabic language, in which the Qur'an was revealed, requires.

If someone says: If you say they have no meaning, how is it permissible for you to affirm with certainty the negation of meaning?

I say: Yes, it is permissible for me to do so, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and these alphabetic letters, according to the requirements of the Arabic language, have no meaning, so I affirm that with certainty, because the Qur'an is in Arabic. If the matter is so, what is the benefit of their presence in the Qur'an? This is the question for which we might say: Allah knows best. But some scholars sought a wisdom for it: that it is an indication that this Qur'an which has defeated you did not come with new letters, so that you might say, "By Allah, these are not from our letters"; rather, it is made of the letters from which Arabic speech is composed, and yet it has defeated you.

They said: For this reason, no opening with these alphabetic letters occurs except that after it there is mention of the Qur'an or of something that is among the characteristics of the Qur'an: ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem (1). That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1-2]. Reflect on it and it will fit together with it.

In some surahs, such as ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem (1). The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 1-2], and ﴿Alif, Lam, Meem (1). Do people think they will be left [to say, "We believe," and not be tested?]﴾ [al-Ankabut: 1-2], there is no mention of the Qur'an, but there is mention of something among its characteristics. ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ is a matter of the unseen, known only through revelation. And ﴿Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-Ankabut: 2] is an announcement about those who came before, which is also a matter of the unseen: ﴿And We did test those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-Ankabut: 3].

In any case, what we have just mentioned last is the view adopted by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and it was preceded to it by al-Zamakhshari in his book al-Kashshaf. He said: ﴿Tilka﴾, that is, these verses, the verses of the Book, the wise Qur'an; and the idafah (construction) is in the sense of "min" (of/from).

﴿That is the verses of the Book﴾: ﴿That﴾ refers to the verses of the Qur'an. You will find that the pointing here is in the form of the distant, and the Qur'an is not distant, since it is before our hands; but it is elevated in rank, so it is pointed to with the distant demonstrative.

His saying ﴿verses of the Book﴾ means the written, which is the Qur'an. We mentioned earlier that it is written in three places: in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and in the scrolls in our hands.

His saying ﴿That is the verses of the Book﴾: the author says the idafah here is by estimate of "min" (of), meaning verses from the Book. And the verses, as has passed for us, are cosmic and legislative. Are the verses of the Book among the legislative or the cosmic? Among the legislative.

His saying ﴿the wise﴾: the author said "possessing wisdom," but it may be said: possessing wisdom and also judgement, since it is the reference for people in judgement, and since it comprises wisdom. It is also suitable to be taken in the sense of "muhkam" (firm, perfected), so that fa'il is in the sense of maf'ul. Therefore the Qur'an is wise because it contains wisdom and judgement between people: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [al-Nisa: 105].

His saying ﴿﴿Guidance and mercy﴾﴾ (in the nominative): its place in grammar is that it is the predicate of a deleted subject, which the author estimated by his saying: "It is guidance and mercy." Guidance means indication, and mercy means that Allah showed mercy to creation by sending it down to them. So the Qur'an is guidance and mercy. Whoever holds fast to it is saved and guided, so one who holds to this Qur'an does not go astray and does not become wretched, because it is guidance and mercy. Based on this, we say to every person who wants knowledge: upon you is the Qur'an, because it is guidance; and to every person who wants mercy: upon you is the Qur'an, because it is guidance.

﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ [Luqman: 3], but for ﴿the doers of good﴾: those who do good in the worship of Allah and do good to the servants of Allah. Good (ihsan) is the opposite of evil (isa'ah), and evil occurs either by leaving an obligation or by doing a prohibited act. Whoever leaves what Allah has obligated upon him for himself, such as prayer and other things, is not a doer of good; whoever does what Allah has forbidden him is not a doer of good; whoever leaves what is due to people, such as maintaining kinship ties, dutifulness to parents and kindness to them, is not a doer of good; and whoever transgresses against them is not a doer of good.

His saying ﴿for the doers of good﴾ implies that the more a person increases in good, the more he benefits from the Qur'an in guidance and mercy, based on the earlier rule that when a ruling is linked to an attribute, it grows stronger in proportion to the presence of that attribute.

His saying ﴿Guidance and mercy for the doers of good﴾: well, and those who are not doers of good are not guided by it and not shown mercy? Yes; because the doers of good are those who benefit from it. Otherwise it is guidance for all people, a source of guidance for everyone, but only those who do good benefit from it.

(And in the recitation of the common readers, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the verses.) This expression of the author is strange: "and in the recitation of the common readers." One who does not know the terminology would understand from it: who is meant by "the common"?

* Student: Those other than the scholars.
