On His saying ﴿Show me﴾: the mufassir explained "show" here as "inform." But it is better to keep it on its apparent meaning, that the intended "showing" is: let me see, show me something that anyone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has created.

And His saying ﴿Show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11] is more forceful than the mufassir's explanation "tell me," because the challenge in it is evident. It is possible that they could inform him of a matter while lying, saying: "Yes, in such-and-such there is something, its creation is such-and-such." But when he says "Show me," challenging with what can be seen, then they are silenced.

As for His saying "Show me," he said: (O people of Makkah). This is based on the view that every address in a Meccan surah that concerns the disbelievers is directed to the people of Makkah. The correct view is that it is general, so that this challenge can now be applied in our present age. The imperative here in "Show me," for what purpose? For what? For incapacitation (ta'jiz) and threat.

(﴿what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11] — other than Him, i.e., your gods, that you have associated with Him, may He be exalted.) That is, show me what they created. If you show me that they created something, it may be an excuse for you to associate them with Allah, the Exalted, in worship. But since the matter is not so, and no creator can exist other than the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, it is not permissible to worship anything along with Him. For if you acknowledge that there is no creator but Allah, you must acknowledge that there is no deity but Allah, and just as you have acknowledged His lordship, you must acknowledge His divinity.

On His saying ﴿what He created﴾: he says: "(mā) is an interrogative of denial, a subject (mubtada'), and (dhā) means (alladhī) with its relative clause as the predicate, and (ara) is suspended from acting, and what follows it fills the place of the two objects."

On His saying ﴿what those besides Him have created﴾: the mufassir parsed it correctly. "(mā khalaqa)": he says: (mā) is an interrogative noun, (dhā) is a relative noun built on quiescence in the place of nominative, (khalaqa) is a past-tense verb, and the clause is the relative clause having no place in i'rab. The returning pronoun is omitted, and the estimate is: "what did those besides Him create." The clause ﴿what those besides Him have created﴾ is an interrogative clause suspended from action, suspended from the action of what? (Show me).

As for his saying "and what follows it fills the place of the two objects": this holds if we say that seeing means knowing. But if we say that seeing means sight with the eye, then what follows it fills the place of only one object. Does Ibn Malik's words in the Alfiyya indicate this parsing that the mufassir mentioned? What is it?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He parsed it as not cancelled (mulghah). Is it permissible to cancel it? The answer: yes, it is permissible, indeed it may be said that cancelling it is preferable, because if you cancel it you make ﴿mādhā﴾ a fronted object of ﴿khalaqa﴾, and then we do not need this, and the original is non-omission. You have previously learned that cancelling it has two aspects: either you say (mā) is an interrogative noun and (dhā) is superfluous, or you say ﴿mādhā﴾ together is an interrogative noun.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11], i.e., those other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is a challenge, and every challenge in the Qur'an cannot be something that exists, for if the thing were possible the challenge would be idle, with no benefit in it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿But﴾. The mufassir said: (for transition) ﴿the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11] (clear in their associating others, while you are among them). That is, the matter is clear, that there is no creator but Allah, and that no one can exist who creates. But the persistence of the polytheists in their polytheism is considered wrongdoing and manifest error. For this reason He said: ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., the polytheists who associated others with Allah in worship, although they believe that He has no partner in creation, ﴿are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11]. The mufassir said: (clear, بَيِّن).

The word ﴿mubīn﴾ comes with the meaning of "bayyin," i.e., apparent, and with the meaning of "muzhir" (making manifest), since it is derived from the quadriliteral (abāna). The quadriliteral abāna comes transitive and comes intransitive. So abāna comes with the meaning of bāna, i.e., became apparent, and then it is intransitive; and it comes with the meaning of azhara, abāna al-shay' means he made it manifest, and then it is transitive. In this verse, ﴿the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11]: is it from the intransitive or the transitive? From the intransitive. For this reason he explained it with "bayyin." We want an example of it from the transitive. What is it?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the transitive.
* Student: ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 77]; ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [Yusuf 1]. Both meanings are permissible: clear in itself, or making the truth clear.
* Shaykh: Yes, and similarly: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 195], i.e., making clear. The conclusion is that you should not assume that ﴿mubīn﴾ is always transitive; it may be intransitive in the sense of "clear," and it may be transitive in the sense of "making manifest."

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 12]: among it knowledge, religiosity, and correctness in speech, and his sayings are many and transmitted.) ﴿And We had certainly﴾: this sentence is emphasized by three emphatics. What are they?

* Student: The lam, qad, and the oath.
* Shaykh: Yes, the lam, qad, and the oath. His saying ﴿ātaynā﴾ means "a'taynā," we gave, and this giving is a cosmic giving: Allah gave him the thing by a cosmic giving.

His saying ﴿Luqmān﴾ is the name of a man. Most scholars hold that he was a man whom Allah gave wisdom and insight into affairs, and that he was not a prophet. Ibn Kathir said: most people hold that he was not a prophet, and it is related from 'Ikrimah, if it is authentically from him, that he said he was a prophet.[[Mentioned by Ibn Kathir (6/334).]] But the correct view is that he was not a prophet; rather he was a wise man of sound judgment, whom Allah gave this wisdom, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah 269].

* Student: Shaykh, (...) some say: is Luqman the wise the same as this one or another?
* Shaykh: No, this is him.
* Student: How is that, is it a report from the Messenger or Israelite narrations?
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: (...) Luqman the wise, did Luqman the wise say (...)?
* Shaykh: This is among what is transmitted about his wisdom (...) is it correct or not?

He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 12]. What is wisdom? Wisdom in origin is agreement with what is correct. Close to this is their saying: it is putting things in their proper places. So the person of sound opinion and right conduct is considered wise, because he puts things in their places. Is that right? What did we mention about wisdom, its explanation?

* Student: (...) putting things in their places.
* Shaykh: That is one. And the second?
* Student: (...) the wise (...).
* Shaykh: No, we want wisdom only, not the wise. What is wisdom? It has been said: it is putting things in their places, that is one. And it has been said?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Did you not go right or left? It has been said: it is agreement with what is correct, and they have one meaning, because agreement with the correct is placing a thing in its proper place. Good. He says: among it is knowledge.
* Student: Is this its content or an explanation, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, this is its meaning. Among it is knowledge and religiosity. Is knowledge wisdom or not? Or is wisdom attained by it? Wisdom is attained by it.
Second: religiosity, yes, it is wisdom.
Third: correctness in speech, and this too is wisdom. Likewise correctness in action is wisdom.

He said: (And his sayings are many and transmitted: he used to give legal rulings before the mission of Dawud, and he lived to see his mission, and took knowledge from him, and gave up issuing rulings, and said concerning that: "Shall I not be content when I am spared?" It was said to him: Which of people is the worst? He said: The one who does not care if people see him doing evil.) (...) He said: "I was spared." This is from wisdom: that a person, when he is spared, should be content, because if he is spared and then works on what he was spared from, he will gain nothing but wasting time and effort.

As for "Which of people is the worst? He said: The one who does not care if people see him doing evil," this may be disputed, because one who does not care if people see him doing evil is considered merely lacking shame, and is not considered the worst of people. The worst of people, in reality, is the one who associates others with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; this is the worst of people, for he is the greatest wrongdoer, so he is the worst of people.

Furthermore, this saying the mufassir mentioned, or these two sentences, may be correct as going back to Luqman, and may be incorrect; that is, one cannot be certain, because there is no authentic connected chain to Luqman, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not inform of it. Like all earlier reports, if they do not come through the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, they must be examined, because they reach us without a chain and are taken from the People of the Book, who are not trustworthy.

* Student: Shaykh, is no wisdom taken from them?
* Student: Then he gave up issuing rulings (...) David, according to the mufassir's words (...).
* Shaykh: And he said: (...) yes, in everything a person is asked for a ruling, he has no need to be involved with it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know; Ibn Kathir did not mention this report.
* Student: Shaykh, his saying: "Narrate from the Children of Israel and there is no harm" (...).
* Shaykh: It may be (...) from him, and it may be (...); because the Children of Israel have a book and a remnant of knowledge, whereas others may have nothing. But all reports about earlier peoples fall into three conditions, as is known: either they agree with the Shari'ah, or they contradict it, or there is neither agreement nor contradiction. What agrees with the Shari'ah is accepted, what contradicts it is rejected, and what has neither agreement nor contradiction is neither confirmed nor denied.

He says: (﴿That﴾ i.e., and We said to him: ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾ [Luqman 12] for what He gave you of wisdom.)

His saying: (﴿We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 12]). Then He said: (﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾). If someone said that His saying "Be grateful to Allah" is an explanation of the wisdom, meaning "that" here explains the wisdom, it would not be far-fetched. But the mufassir holds that it is the object of an omitted verb whose estimate is: "We said to him: that be grateful to Allah," meaning for what He gave you of wisdom. As for the first possibility, which is the apparent sense of the Qur'an and needs no estimate, the matter is evident: that gratitude for Allah's blessing is part of wisdom, indeed it is its head.

His saying ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾: the lam here is for exclusivity and entitlement, because gratitude in the absolute sense is exclusively for Allah, and only Allah, glory be to Him, deserves absolute gratitude. Gratitude is the performance of obedience to the Benefactor, acknowledged in the heart, praised by the tongue, and obeyed by the limbs. The objects of gratitude are three: the tongue, the heart, and the limbs; its cause is one, namely the blessing. For this reason there is a general and specific relation between it and praise (hamd): in terms of cause, praise is more general; in terms of its objects, gratitude is more general. How so? Praise has two causes: the perfection of the one praised, and the bounty of the one praised. So you praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for His perfection, and you praise Him for His bounty. But praise is specific to what, in terms of its object? It is specific to the tongue only. As for gratitude, in terms of cause it is more specific, because it occurs only in return for a blessing; but in terms of its objects it is more general, occurring by the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. On this is the poet's saying:

Three blessings have been granted you from me: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart.

His saying ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾ [Luqman 12]. We said: the lam here is for exclusivity, and what else? And entitlement. So it is obligatory upon the servant to sincerely direct gratitude to Him, and to believe in his heart that none deserves absolute gratitude but Allah.

He said: (﴿And whoever is grateful, it is only for himself﴾ [Luqman 12], because the reward of his gratitude returns to him. ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ — the blessing — ﴿indeed Allah is Free of need﴾ from His creation, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ in His doing.)

﴿And whoever is grateful﴾: this sentence is conditional. The verb of the condition is jussive by "man," and the answer of the condition is the sentence ﴿it is only for himself﴾; "innamā" is a particle of restriction, and ﴿yashkuru﴾ is an imperfect verb. But is it said that ﴿yashkuru﴾ is the answer, or the whole sentence? The whole sentence.

His saying ﴿it is only for himself﴾: how did He say "Be grateful to Allah" and then say "it is only for himself"? One would expect the phrase "whoever is grateful, it is only for Allah." But we say, as the mufassir said: the meaning of "it is only for himself" is that the reward of gratitude returns to him, so it is for his own benefit, and gratitude does not return to Allah so that He benefits from it; for He, glory be to Him, does not benefit from obedience nor is He harmed by disobedience, but it returns to you yourself.

﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, which is the opposite of gratitude, ﴿indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾: Free of need of him, when he disbelieves the blessing of Allah.

﴿Praiseworthy﴾ is on the pattern of faʿīl in the sense of maf'ūl, and it may be that ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ means fā'il (one who praises), so He, glory be to Him, is praised and is also one who praises, because He, glory be to Him, describes those who deserve perfect attributes with what they deserve; for this reason He praised His prophets and His friends, and this is praise of them, and He is also praised by His servants; so it is faʿīl in the sense of fā'il and in the sense of maf'ūl. The connection of the answer-clause to the condition is: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 12]. Its connection to the condition is evident: whoever disbelieves will not harm Allah, nor diminish His dominion, because He is Free of need. Likewise, this does not reflect any deficiency in His wisdom, because He, majestic and exalted, is Praiseworthy: the existence of the grateful and the existence of the disbelievers are both things for which Allah is praised. Had it not been so, the worth of gratitude would not be known, nor would the harm of disbelief be known; without this, people would be on one level, and the good would not be distinguished from the bad.

﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾: Al-Ghanī (the Free of need) is one of Allah's names, and al-Ḥamīd (the Praiseworthy) is also one of His names.

He said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾ [Luqman 14], and mention when he said.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, "whoever disbelieves" is general, but since it is within the context of the wisdom given to Luqman, the mufassir, by his explanation, restricted it to wealth, saying: mention ﴿And when Luqman said to his son﴾ [Luqman 13].
* Student: He says: "Praiseworthy in His doing" only.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is a deficiency. The mufassir says that ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ means "praiseworthy in His doing," whereas the correct view is that He is praiseworthy in His doing and His legislation, and in all His attributes; so He is praised for His perfect attributes, for His acts, and for His legislation.

He said: (Mention ﴿when Luqman said to his son while he was advising him: "O my son"﴾ [Luqman 13], a diminutive of affection, ﴿"Do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is great injustice"﴾ [Luqman 13], so he returned to Him and submitted.)

His saying: (Mention "when") — the mufassir informed us that "idh" is an object of an omitted verb, or an adverb dependent on an omitted verb, meaning: mention this time when Luqman said to his son, and so on to the end.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 11–14 (part 2 of 4):

His saying: ﴿When Luqman said to his son, while he was admonishing him: "O my son..."﴾ The clause ﴿while he was admonishing him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), a state (hal) of the subject of ﴿said﴾, who is Luqman. That is, the situation was that he was admonishing his son. Al-maw'iza (admonition) is a reminder coupled with warning or encouragement. He said to him: ﴿O my son﴾. The author (al-Mu'allif) said that it is a diminutive of affection (taṣghīr ishfāq), and so it is, not a diminutive of belittlement (taṣghīr iḥtiqār), because the context does not call for that; rather, it is a diminutive expressing compassion toward him.

﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah﴾: this is the content of the saying in His words ﴿and when he said﴾. ﴿Do not associate anything with Allah﴾ means: do not make a partner with Him in what? In worship, in creation and decree, and in His names and attributes. This is because tawhid, as is well known among the scholars, is divided into three categories: tawhid al-rububiyya (Lordship), tawhid al-uluhiyya (worship/divinity), and tawhid al-asma' wa al-sifat (names and attributes). Associating partners with Allah means associating someone with Him in one of these categories. Whoever believes that there is a creator besides Allah has committed shirk in Lordship; whoever believes that there is someone besides Allah who deserves to be worshipped has committed shirk in worship; and whoever believes that Allah has a like in His names and attributes has committed shirk in names and attributes. He said: (﴿Do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association [with Him] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]). Luqman emphasized that shirk is a wrong by using two emphasizers: ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ and the lam (of emphasis).

His saying: ﴿Indeed, association is surely a great wrong﴾: this clause is a justification for what precedes it, namely ﴿do not associate anything with Allah﴾. Thus Luqman combined in his advice the ruling and the wisdom: he forbade him from shirk and explained that it is a great wrong. Dhulm (wrong), in its original sense, means deficiency, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens yielded its produce and did not fall short (lam taẓlim) of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33], meaning it did not diminish. In the Sharia, wrong is the diminishing of every possessor of a right of his right; accordingly, shirk is a deficiency in the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying: ﴿surely a great wrong﴾: this is a way of magnifying shirk and warning against it. No wrong is greater than shirk, because whatever else it may be, the wrong of shirk is greater than anything. He who created you brought you into existence from nothingness; He who provides you with what sustains your life is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; He who prepared you and made you ready to benefit from what is beneficial is Allah. He is the Originator (al-Mujid), the Preparer (al-Mu'idd), and the Supplier (al-Mumidd). If this is so, is there anyone whose right over you is greater than Allah's? There is none. So when you diminish Allah's right, that is the greatest wrong. For this reason, the one who has done you more good, if you wrong him, your wrong toward him is greater than toward another. He who does good to you, gives to you and raises you, then you wrong him, is greater than if you had wronged someone who had not done that.

(﴿Indeed, association is surely a great wrong﴾) so he returned and embraced Islam. Who returned? The son. In any case, we do not know whether this matter is as the author said, that the son was a polytheist, and when his father admonished him he returned and became a Muslim; or that the son, fearing for him from shirk, his father forbade him from it and explained to him that association is a great wrong. The prohibition of shirk does not necessarily imply that the person has committed it, because one may be forbidden from something out of fear that it may occur, not as a removal of what has already happened. This is a common and consistent matter in the Qur'an, in the Sunnah, and in human speech. You say, for example, to a man: "Do not keep company with the wicked." Does this prohibition imply that he is keeping their company? It does not. It may be a prohibition against what one fears may happen. Thus the words ﴿do not associate anything with Allah﴾ are not explicit that the son had fallen into shirk, such that one would say he returned and embraced Islam. Rather, his father may have forbidden him from shirk out of fear that he would fall into it. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents﴾ [Luqman: 14]. This sentence is not part of Luqman's speech; rather, it is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is an interjection between Luqman's first speech (...). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always links the right of parents with His own right: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isra': 23]; ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you not associate anything with Him, and to parents, good treatment"﴾ [al-An'am: 151].

(﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents﴾ [Luqman: 14]: We commanded him to honor them.) "We commanded him": the author explained wasiyya (enjoining) as amr (command). But it is more specific than an absolute command. Wasiyya is a binding charge concerning what must be given careful attention; it is not merely a command but a charge about what deserves to be taken seriously. (...) in nourishment. For this reason a pregnant woman needs more food, and therefore the Sharia permitted her to break her fast in Ramadan, so that her nourishment is not diminished, lest she become exhausted and the fetus be harmed. This is from the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, weakness befalls her at the time of labor. Does it or not? Labor causes pain and suffering, and is no small matter, because labor—by Allah's permission—comes so that the fetus turns in order to prepare to come out. The fetus, now in its mother's womb, is positioned with its head toward the mother's head and its face toward the mother's back, and its back toward her belly; it is inverted relative to its mother in orientation. This is part of the wisdom, because when its face is toward the back, the back becomes a protection for it, since the bones protect the face of the fetus. If the fetus's face were toward its mother's face, there would be nothing protecting it, and even a small blow or something striking its face would harm it. But from the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He made it so. For this reason the scholars said: If a non-Muslim, Scripturalist woman pregnant with a child by a Muslim dies, how is she to be buried?

* A student: Her back is placed toward the qibla.
* The Shaykh: She is buried on her right side with her back toward the qibla.
* The student: The right or the left? Shouldn't it be on the left?
* The Shaykh: No, the right. Not the right?
* The student: It becomes the left?
* Another student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, on her left side, if she can be buried alone, neither in the cemetery of Muslims nor in the cemetery of disbelievers, which is preferable. If that is impossible, then she is buried in the cemetery of the Muslims on her left side, so that the child lies on the right side facing the qibla.

Now, labor occurs when this child turns; this child will turn at the time of delivery so that its head is foremost to come out. The first thing to emerge from the fetus is the head. The woman suffers from this labor without doubt; then at delivery, does she also suffer or not? Yes, she suffers, and weakness befalls her, and perhaps fainting and exhaustion, and perhaps she dies. So Allah, the Exalted, reminds man of the mother's condition in these states, all of which are states of weakness upon weakness.

* A student: Some say it turns in the seventh month...
* The Shaykh: No, what is known is that it turns at the time of delivery, and that this is the labor pain.

He said: (﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾ [Luqman: 14]: that is, she became weak due to pregnancy, weak due to labor, and weak due to delivery.) ﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾ [Luqman: 14]: that is, his weaning. The author says: "his weaning," but is the period of pregnancy added to it or not? Is the period of pregnancy added to it, or is the period of pregnancy excluded from it?

* The student: Excluded.
* The Shaykh: The period of pregnancy is excluded from it, because Allah says in another verse: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. So if we subtract the minimum period of pregnancy, six months, twenty-four months remain, which are two years.

* A student: ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾: the meaning of "upon" (...).
* The Shaykh: The meaning of "upon" is elevation; that is, weakness added upon weakness, just as you say, for example: "I placed a bag upon a bag, and a brick upon a brick," and similar things.

* The student: And the weakness (...) an old weakness, or a new weakness (...) due to pregnancy, weakness...
* The Shaykh: It is all due to pregnancy. He said: But that one is at its rearing, the second at labor, and the third at delivery.

﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years﴾ [Luqman: 14]. (And We said to him: ﴿Be grateful to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqman: 14]) ("his weaning in two years"): that is, he is not separated from his mother except after two years, so the period of weaning is added to the period of pregnancy. Is there hardship in the period of weaning? There is no doubt there is hardship: she nurses him, stays awake for his wakefulness, her heart aches for his suffering, she cares for his affairs, cleaning him and cleaning his clothes, carrying him when he cries, and other things. Thus she is in hardship from the time he is carried until he is weaned after his birth, over two years. Allah, glorified and exalted, did not mention anything concerning the father. So what do you say? Explain.

Because the father is generally respected and feared, there is no need to describe what he endures from his son, so that it serves as a motive for the son to fulfill his duty to him. But since the mother is weak, and a person may neglect her right, Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned among her conditions what would be a cause for the son to perform his obligation. You see this often in the Qur'an: that which is feared to be neglected is emphasized. An example is bequest (wasiyya) and debt in the estate: which takes precedence? Debt takes precedence over bequest by consensus. Yet Allah mentioned bequest before debt in the verses on inheritance; He placed it first in mention before debt. Why? Because bequest is a right that heirs may neglect, whereas debt, if the heirs neglect it, is backed by...

* A student: The one who demands it.
* The Shaykh: The one who demands it, its owner. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may reinforce things that are feared to be neglected with descriptions that move one to do what should be done. Here, since the mother is weak, and a person may transgress against her and her right more than against the father's, Allah mentioned among the causes that make her kindness obligatory what He did not mention concerning the father. I think we all know that a son often mistreats his mother with abuse and insults, and perhaps with beating, but toward his father he cannot do so, and he does not transgress against him as he transgresses against his mother. And if he fails to fulfill his duty, his father can compel him to do so. Therefore Allah mentioned these attributes of the mother, to be an incitement for us to fulfill her right (...).

* * *

﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you see﴾ [Luqman: 10].
* Benefits drawn from it: the affirmation that Allah created the heavens. Derived from this benefit is the refutation of the philosophers' claim that the celestial spheres are eternal. The philosophers say that the celestial spheres are eternal and do not change, because for them "eternal" is that which has no beginning, and what has no beginning has no end. Thus in this there is a refutation of the philosophers' claim that the spheres are eternal and unchanging. Consequently they vehemently denied the splitting of the moon, and said: "The moon cannot split, because it is one of the spheres." They claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1] is merely that the truth of the message is evident, and they denied the hadiths narrated on this matter, which the Ummah received with acceptance.
* And from this noble verse is derived: the demonstration of Allah's power in creating these great heavens ﴿And the heaven We constructed with power, and indeed We are expanding it﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47].
* And from it is derived: the demonstration of power from another aspect, namely that these great heavens and wide canopy are without pillars, by His saying ﴿without pillars that you see﴾ [Luqman: 10]. I think if we saw a wide building without any columns, we would marvel at how such a wide building could stand without columns, when the heaven is wider and greater, and yet is without pillars.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse ﴿And He cast into the earth firmly set mountains﴾: the demonstration of Allah's wisdom and mercy in placing the mountains. Is that so? And (His mercy) so that the earth would not sway with its creatures.
* And from the noble verse is derived: that the earth rotates.
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Alright, let us now put the metal on the fire, melt it, and see the counterfeit from the genuine.
* From the verse it is derived that the earth rotates. How so? They say: because His saying ﴿lest it sway with you﴾ [Luqman: 10] indicates the existence of the basic movement, for the negation of the more specific implies the existence of the more general. Have you not considered His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103], where it was evidence for the existence of the basic act of seeing or not? Is His saying ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ not evidence that seeing exists?

The people of the Sunnah use this verse to affirm the seeing of Allah, and the people of innovation use it to deny the seeing of Allah. But the correct position is that of the people of the Sunnah, because the negation of the more specific implies the existence of the more general. It is not reasonable that the more specific be negated while the more general is not negated; if the more general were nonexistent, it would be necessary to negate the more general so that the more specific would be included. Had Allah been unseen, He would have said: "Vision does not see Him," so that seeing is negated; and perception is negated a fortiori, is it not so? When He said ﴿does not perceive Him﴾, it became known that the basic act of seeing exists but He is not perceived, glorified and exalted.

Here, when He said ﴿lest it sway with you﴾, and "mayadan" means agitation, it became known that the basic movement exists, but these mountains are for the balance of the movement, so that it does not become agitated. This is the reasoning of one who holds that the verse is evidence that the earth rotates. As for those who say the verse is evidence that the earth does not rotate, they say: "We do not concede that mayadan means agitation; rather, we say that mayadan means movement: ﴿He cast into the earth firmly set mountains﴾ [Luqman: 10], so that it settles and does not move." They interpret mayadan as a basic movement or as movement in general. If this is the case, then it is obligatory to return to the Arabic language. If the Arabic language indicates that mayadan means agitation, we say the verse contains evidence for the existence of basic movement; and if the Arabic language says that mayadan is movement, we say it contains evidence that the earth does not rotate.

When we say that it rotates, Allah does not diminish anything; rather, in reality, it is an increase in His power, glorified and exalted, since this earth rotates with all that is in it of seas, rivers, trees, clay, stone, and everything, rotating yet maintaining this wonderful balance that does not change. This is evidence of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, just as its stillness while resting on water is evidence of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted. But the matter that must be denied, so that it becomes clear to us like the sun, is the claim that the alternation of night and day is due to the rotation of the earth. We do not accept this. Rather, we say that the alternation of night and day is due to the sun's revolving around the earth, because this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and we cannot move from it except by evidence that we can see, like the sun. For Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, attributed the action to the sun: ﴿And you see the sun when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾ [al-Kahf: 17], and did not say: "when the cave rises over it, inclining." He attributed ﴿inclines﴾ to the sun, and if the movement were of the earth, it would be the earth that inclines.

﴿and when it sets﴾ [al-Kahf: 17] is the third verb. If it were the earth that rotates, by whose rotation the alternation of night and day occurs, He would have said: "and when the earth sets," or "a part of the earth becomes hidden," or something similar. And "taqriduhum" (it cuts them off) is the same kind of action. The Prophet ﷺ, when he said to Abu Dharr: "Do you know where it goes?" (1) — when the sun set — informed that it goes by itself. So the correct position is undoubtedly this, unless we find evidence like the sun, in which case these verses could be interpreted to mean that it "set" and "rose" in terms of the viewer's perception, even if the viewer is the one moving. You are traveling in a car, and in the course of your travel a camel appears before you; do you say, "The camel appeared before me," or not? While I was walking, a camel appeared before me... you say "appeared before me," even though you are the one who approached it. This is linguistically possible. But as long as we are not certain of this matter, and these are merely theories of people who do not believe in the Qur'an or the revealed laws, we do not accept it from them, but take the apparent meaning of the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

If someone says: "Does your statement contradict your statement that the rotation of the earth is possible? For if the rotation of the earth is possible, it must be that the alternation of night and day is due to its rotation." —

---
(1) Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3199) and Muslim (159 / 250), from the hadith of Abu Dharr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah 31, verses 11–14 (part 3 of 4):

So we say: this does not bind us, because it is possible that this revolves and that revolves, and the sun's movement and its rotation are faster. If it is faster, it follows that it orbits the earth even while the earth rotates. That is, it is possible for the earth to rotate slowly while the sun rotates more, so the sun can circle around the earth.

The conclusion is that these matters, without doubt, require the believer to adhere to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the Sunnah. This is the obligation regarding unseen matters and matters that he cannot perceive through the senses. Then, if it becomes clear to him through the senses that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is not what is intended, it is permissible for us, indeed obligatory, to interpret the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Why? Because the Qur'an cannot contradict reality; this is impossible. If we allowed that by reason, it would follow that the Qur'an contains falsehood, because falsehood is that which contradicts reality, and this is impossible.

Therefore, O brothers, we must regard these theories as we regard the narrations of the Children of Israel: whatever agrees with the Qur'an is true and we accept it. However, we do not accept it on the basis that it is what established the matter, but on the basis that the Qur'an is what established it. We say this so that they will not have a favour over us.

Second: whatever contradicts the Qur'an, we must reject.

Third: what we do not know to agree or disagree with the Qur'an. Here, reason and the Sharia require that we suspend judgement and say: we neither affirm nor deny. At that point, the student of knowledge needs to probe deeply, reflect, and examine the texts of the Book and the Sunnah very carefully, so that he does not rule that reality contradicts them, for that would be a reactionary response to those who do not believe in Islam. That is, for example, if someone rejected such theories without reflecting on the indication of the Book and the Sunnah, rejecting them immediately as some of the common people do, this is, in reality, not serving Islam. It is like a person taking a dagger in his hand and stabbing his own chest while not realising it. Therefore, the obligation regarding these matters, as I told you, is that we present them to the Book and the Sunnah. Whatever agrees with the Book and the Sunnah is true, because it agrees with the Book and the Sunnah, and whatever contradicts them is false. Whatever we do not know to agree or disagree with them, the obligation regarding it is to suspend judgement, and a person should say: if it becomes clear to me according to my own understanding, and even if my knowledge in these sciences is limited, I will affirm it. If it does not become clear to me, I am not obliged to affirm or deny it. I take the stance of a neutral party. This is what reason and the Sharia demand.

* Student: O Shaykh, this theory contradicts the Qur'an.
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: Because they say: the sun is stationary, and the earth is what revolves around it.
* Shaykh: We did not say that the sun is stationary and then refute it. We said: this is not permissible.
* Student: Alright, is this a theory?
* Shaykh: We refute this, although they say that the sun is not stationary.
* Student: How?
* Shaykh: It revolves in a high orbit, travelling a tremendous course. I read a small booklet called *Ancient Astronomy*, which says that it moves at, I do not know by God, thousands of millions of miles per second. Yes, but this...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We do not know...
* Student: Sometimes they say: stationary, and sometimes they say...
* Shaykh: By God, I have not seen anyone say: stationary.
* Student: The word *maydan* (...) the difference (...).
* Shaykh: What appears to me from its wording, and I have not in fact consulted the books of lexicography, is that (*mada, yameed*) means to be disturbed, to move with agitation. In any case, we now place this in your hands to consult whatever lexicons are available, and God willing, you will bring us the result afterwards.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in dispersing these creatures on the earth. This is based on His saying: ﴿And He dispersed therein every kind of creature﴾ [Al-Baqarah 164], meaning He spread them. The way it indicates power is the variation of these creatures in their kinds, types, forms, and conditions. Is that not so? We have previously explained some of the wisdom behind creating the harmful ones among them, and I think we mentioned how many wisdoms?
* Student: Three.
* Shaykh: No, it is either six or seven. We mentioned several wisdoms in the creation of this harmful kind.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: also the demonstration of Allah's power, wisdom, and mercy in sending down water from the sky. Power: we find this water descending from above, which means that great bodies of water float around the earth between the sky and the earth. Allah, the Exalted, has said in another verse: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail﴾ [An-Nur 43]. Glory be to Allah! Mountains between the sky and the earth made of hail, from which these pieces are released until they descend onto the earth. Had Allah willed, He could have made the mountain fall entirely upon the earth.
* We have also said in this regard: it is evidence of mercy, since its descent is from above, in order that it encompass both the elevated and the low-lying.
* And in it also: evidence of mercy, that this water has two great benefits for us: the growth of what grows from it, and second, its storage in the earth. ﴿And We sent down water from the sky and gave you to drink from it, and you are not its retainers﴾ [Al-Hijr 22]. And Allah said in another verse: ﴿And He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. And Allah said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or are We the sender?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 68–69]. Thus in it is the material of human life, in its food and in its drink.
* Student: ﴿And We settled it in the earth﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 18].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Among the benefits of the verse also: the affirmation of causes, based on His saying: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [Luqman 10]. From where do we derive the affirmation of causes? From the *fa'* of causation in ﴿fa-anbatna﴾ ("and caused to grow"). The affirmation of causes is part of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever denies causes, without doubt, is casting doubt on the wisdom of Allah, because Allah is Wise, Exalted is He.
The power is that whoever finds this descending from above, it means that great bodies of water float around the earth between the sky and the earth. Allah, the Exalted, has said in another verse: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail﴾ [An-Nur 43]. Glory be to Allah! Mountains of hail between the sky and the earth, from which these pieces are released until they descend onto the earth. Had Allah willed, He could have made the mountain fall entirely upon the earth.
We have said: in it there is also evidence of mercy, since its descent is from above, so that it encompasses the elevated and the low-lying. In this is evidence of mercy. As for this water, it has two great benefits for us: the growth of what grows from it, and second, its storage in the earth. ﴿And We sent down water from the sky and gave you to drink from it, and you are not its retainers﴾ [Al-Hijr 22]. And Allah said in another verse: ﴿And He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. And Allah said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or are We the sender?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 68–69]. Thus in it is the material of human life, in it is his food, and in it is his drink.
* Among the benefits of the verse also: the affirmation of causes, based on His saying: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky, and We caused to grow﴾ [Luqman 10]. From where do we derive the affirmation of causes? From the *fa'* of causation in ﴿fa-anbatna﴾. The affirmation of causes is part of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever denies causes is, without doubt, casting doubt on the wisdom of Allah, because Allah is Wise, Exalted is He. Everything has a cause with Him, so that things subsist and proceed in an orderly system.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in making this vegetation diverse, even though its land is one and its water is one. This is from His saying: ﴿of every pair﴾, meaning of every kind. You see this tree is large and that one small, this one green and that one brown, this one's flower is white and that one is yellow of another colour. Various colours, though the water is one and the land is one. This is evidence of the perfect power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this growth has two benefits for us: looking at it, and the joy and pleasure in it. For this reason, when a person stands in a grassy meadow, where the winds sway its flowers, he finds joy and delight.
Second: the benefits that come from this vegetation for us and for our livestock. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then We split the earth, splitting [it open], and caused to grow therein grain, and grapes and herbage, and olive and palm trees, and gardens dense with trees, and fruit and grasses, as provision for you and your grazing livestock﴾ [Abasa 26–32]. (...)

In His saying: ﴿He created the heavens﴾, [it indicates] that the heavens are open celestial bodies. Whoever denies them denies that the sky (...), and is one who denies the Qur'an. One who denies the Qur'an becomes a disbeliever, and this is a grave matter, because those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day do not acknowledge that there are celestial bodies. They say: orbs, galaxies, stars, and what is similar to that, and they do not acknowledge the sky. Whoever agrees with them in that denies the Qur'an, and thus becomes a disbeliever in it, God forbid (...).

* * *

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿This is the creation of Allah; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11].
* This noble verse indicates: deriving proof of the oneness of Lordship (*tawhid al-rububiyyah*, affirming Allah's sole lordship over creation) as evidence for the oneness of worship (*tawhid al-uluhiyyah*, affirming that Allah alone is to be worshipped). This is based on His saying: ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾, meaning what is created, and they acknowledge that it is the creation of Allah. If they acknowledge this, they are bound to acknowledge the oneness of worship. Accordingly, we say: from this verse is derived the argument from the oneness of Lordship to the oneness of worship. There are parallels to this in the Qur'an, among them His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 21]. He said: ﴿worship your Lord who created you﴾. He derives from His being Lord and Creator that worship must be directed to Him alone. This is a compelling rational proof.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: deriving proof from what is more evident to that which the opponent acknowledges. This is an argument from a clear and manifest matter to a matter that the opponent denies, namely the denial that Allah is singular in divinity.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the use of challenge in debate, based on His saying: ﴿so show me what those other than Him have created﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that those who deny the oneness of divinity are wrongdoers and in manifest error, based on His saying: ﴿But the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the inability of all worshipped idols to create the like of Allah's creation, based on His saying: ﴿so show me what those other than Him have created﴾. If they are unable to create, then they do not deserve worship. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿O mankind, an example has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah could not create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ [Al-Hajj 73]. And beyond that: ﴿And if the fly should steal from them something, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom, [saying], "Be grateful to Allah"﴾ [Luqman 12], and the verse continues to its end. In this noble verse is a demonstration of Allah's favour upon Luqman in granting him wisdom: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾.
* Among its benefits: wisdom may be attained by one who is not a prophet, because Luqman, according to the majority of scholars, was not a prophet.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of gratitude to Allah, based on His saying: ﴿"Be grateful"﴾.
* And among them, that is, among the benefits: that thanking Allah is part of wisdom, because His saying: ﴿"Be grateful"﴾ is an explanation of wisdom. Thanking Allah is without doubt part of wisdom, because wisdom is conforming to what is correct, or placing a thing in its proper place, and there is no doubt that thanking Allah conforms to what is correct, and it is placing a thing in its proper place.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the grateful person's reward is for himself: ﴿And whoever is grateful, is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself﴾.
* And among them: that Allah, the Exalted, does not benefit from the obedience of the obedient. The obedience of the obedient is for their own souls. It follows from this benefit that the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His servants to worship Him is purely a kindness to them, because the benefit is theirs. It is like when you raise a child and say: eat this food, wear this garment, drink this water. You are commanding him, but the command is for his own benefit.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the disbeliever does not harm Allah in any way, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free of need and praiseworthy﴾. In a sacred hadith: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were as righteous as the most wicked heart of one man among you, that would not decrease My dominion in the least."[[Recorded by Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of these two names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: Al-Ghani (the Self-Sufficient) and Al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy), and the affirmation of the attributes included in them, namely self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness, whether He is the one who praises or the one who is praised.
* Among its benefits: that Allah, the Exalted, is described by an attribute composed of two qualities, namely self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness. Not every self-sufficient person is praised, and not every praised person is self-sufficient. As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, both self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness are combined in His right, owing to the perfection of His generosity and bounty, Glorified and Exalted is He.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Allah's favour upon Luqman with wisdom.
* Student: That means every wise person... (...) he did not say...
* Shaykh: It may be derived from His saying: ﴿"Be grateful to Allah"﴾ [Luqman 12], just as He commanded him to give thanks for being granted wisdom. It may be said that it follows from this that whoever Allah has favoured with wisdom must thank Allah more than others.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The praise of wisdom. We mentioned Allah's favour upon Luqman with wisdom, and this is a blessing. As for its praise, it is evident in it that wisdom is among the best things a person can be given.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And [mention] when Luqman said to his son while he was instructing him, "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah"﴾ [Luqman 13].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing gentleness to the one addressed in order to encourage his acceptance of what is directed to him, based on His saying: ﴿O my son﴾, for this is a matter of gentleness.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the importance of this advice, because it came from a compassionate father to his son, so it is among the most important of counsels.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of associating partners with Allah, based on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah﴾. Is it sufficient to express this by saying: the prohibition of shirk?
* Student: Mostly...
* Shaykh: No, and I think later. We say: yes, it is sufficient, because Allah says: ﴿Say, "My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has not sent down any authority"﴾ [Al-A'raf 33].
One might say: if he hears me say that shirk is forbidden, he might say: is it sufficient to say merely "forbidden"? It is sufficient, because Allah said it. But it is the gravest of forbidden things in sin and wrongdoing.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of affirming the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because the prohibition of shirk necessarily requires the obligation of tawhid.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that shirk is a great wrong, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾.
* And among its benefits: that it is appropriate to join rulings with their reasons, because of the benefits mentioned earlier. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿Do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verses 11–14 (part 4 of 4):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: one of the most important things to attend to is focusing on *tawhid* (affirming the oneness of God) and avoiding *shirk* (associating partners with God). He said, ﴿Do not associate anything with Allah﴾, beginning with it before anything else. When the Messenger ﷺ sent someone to call people to Islam, he would instruct him to begin the call with *tawhid*, because it is the foundation. If a person does not have *tawhid*, whom will he worship? One must focus on *tawhid*, but every situation has its own discourse. If we are in a place where *shirk* is widespread, our speech should concentrate more on *tawhid*. If it is the opposite, but they have violations in other matters, we should focus more on those. This is drawn from the method of the Qur'an.
In Makkah, the verses focused more on *tawhid*, while in Madinah they focused more on transactions and the forms of worship. So every situation has its own discourse. For this reason, some people may object and say: Why do you not speak more about *tawhid*? (...) Especially in the matter of (...)?
We say: Speaking about *tawhid* is undoubtedly important, and it is the most important of matters. But if we are among a people who have affirmed the oneness of God, praise be to Allah, and who know the matter and are far from *shirk*, and who only oppose in other matters short of *shirk*, then we focus on the violations they have. However, if something (...) of *tawhid* emerges, it must be focused on, as has appeared recently, some *shirk*-based and *bid'ah* (innovation) matters, such as (...) those that contain litanies and devotional recitations which are all lies, or mostly lies. These must be focused on.
Likewise, there have appeared amulets that are hung, copper amulets, which are said to benefit from rheumatism. This too is a type of *shirk*. Similarly, there is the matter of the *dabla* (engagement ring) and what is connected to it: a man writes his name on his wife's ring, and she writes her name on her husband's ring, and they believe this causes love and union, as if it were a bond. This too is *shirk*, and it is of the type of *tiwalah* (a form of love-magic).
When such matters emerge, they must be opposed, focused upon, and spoken about extensively, so that they do not spread. The main point is that every situation has its own discourse, as it is said.
* It may be derived from this noble verse: the giving of admonitions from fathers to their children, and that this is from wisdom, or not?
Because of His saying: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son while he was advising him﴾ [Luqman 13].
* Among its benefits: a person who gives guidance should combine his guidance with admonition, because of His saying: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son while he was advising him﴾. So is it sufficient, for example, to tell a person: This is forbidden, or this is obligatory? Or does one consider the condition of the person? Yes, one considers the condition of the person. Some people are sufficed by being told that something is forbidden or obligatory, and they comply. Others are not sufficed by being told that something is forbidden or obligatory until it is accompanied by an admonition, so you say: Fear Allah! How can you persist in this when it is disobedience to Allah and His Messenger? And similar things.
The main point is that every situation has its own discourse. Likewise, you mention the threats that have come in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, as when you give advice to a man who is deeply involved in usury: it is not enough to say, "It is forbidden," because he knows that. Nobody doubts that usury is forbidden, but he needs an admonition that softens his heart toward the truth and brings him closer to Allah.
* * *
Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (care) for his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾ [Luqman 14].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the care of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for the treatment of parents. For this reason He enjoined it as a commandment (*wasiyyah*).
* Among its benefits: He, glory be to Him, is more merciful to parents than their children are, or not? Because Allah enjoined children regarding their parents, so He is more merciful to parents than children are. As we said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [an-Nisa 11], that in the verse there is evidence that Allah is more merciful to the child than the parents are.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the explanation of the great rights of parents. For this reason Allah made it a commandment (*wasiyyah*). A *wasiyyah*, as was mentioned earlier in the tafsir, is entrusting a person with an important matter, in addition to the great rights of parents.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one being addressed should be reminded of what motivates him to carry out what has been entrusted to him, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the weaker side should be strengthened with what strengthens it. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years﴾. Allah mentioned what the mother undergoes, as an incentive to fulfill her right, and did not mention what the father undergoes, because, as we said in the tafsir, the mother is weak and needs someone to strengthen her side.
Can it be derived from this that the right of the mother is more binding than the right of the father?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: How?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the hadith is clear, but from the verse.
* A student: The scholars mentioned (...).
* The Shaykh: Because He mentioned the hardships the mother endures, as an indication that she has the greater claim. As for the father, he does not experience in his child these hardships. Rather, it is the mother who experiences them. It is true that the father may bear other hardships, such as providing sustenance and similar things. But the mother, the physical pain, does not befall the father.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a mother should be patient with the hardship of pregnancy, because it is a natural matter, because of His saying: ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾.
* Branching from this benefit: the explanation of the error of some women today who cannot bear the weakness of pregnancy. You find a woman who uses pills to prevent pregnancy, saying: Because pregnancy is exhausting and burdensome, and similar things.
Some women try to give birth by surgery, saying: Because it is easier. All of this is an escape from the weakness with which women are created during pregnancy, during labor, and at delivery. Yes, if the matter requires surgery, there is no harm in it out of necessity. Otherwise, it is not appropriate, because this goes against the nature with which Allah created women.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, from His saying: ﴿and his weaning is in two years﴾. And Allah, Exalted is He, said in Surah al-Ahqaf: ﴿His carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf 15]. So if you subtract two years from thirty months, how many remain?
* A student: Six.
* The Shaykh: Six months remain. Ibn Qutaybah mentioned in *al-Ma'arif* that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan was born after six months, and he was the astute caliph, as is well known. He was born after six months. Experts in these matters say that if a child is born after six months it is possible that he survives, but if born after seven months he may not survive. This is wisdom (...).
* A student: The possibility that he does not survive.
* The Shaykh: (...).
Gratitude to parents is required just as gratitude to Allah is required, because of His saying: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾.
* Among them: the gratitude owed to Allah, Exalted is He, takes precedence over other gratitude, because He placed it first in His saying: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾. So He placed gratitude to Himself before gratitude to parents, despite the great rights of the parents.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: all matters return to Allah, in His saying: ﴿To Me is the final return﴾. The placement of the predicate before the subject indicates restriction, that the return is to Allah alone.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning and a threat against opposition, because His saying: ﴿To Me is the final return﴾ means: I will hold you accountable, O human. So the connection of this sentence to what precedes it is that it conveys a threat and a warning to the one who opposes.

This is the commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verses 11–14 (part 1 of 4):

He said: ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqman 11]. The one indicated (by "this") is what preceded: the creation of the heavens without pillars, the placing of firm mountains in the earth, and the spreading of creatures upon it. ﴿And He spread therein from every creature [that moves]﴾ [al-Baqarah 164], and the sending down of water from the sky, and the growing therein of every noble pair. These are five things that are observed and perceptible. For this reason He indicated them with a sensory pointing, saying: (﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾, i.e., His creation). It is thus a case of using the verbal noun (maṣdar) to mean the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), and the intended meaning is not the "creation of Allah" which is His act, since His act is not observed; what is observed is His created thing.

(﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾, i.e., His creation. ﴿Show me﴾ — he said: tell me, O people of Makkah, ﴿what those besides Him have created﴾.)

On His saying ﴿Show me﴾: the mufassir explained "show" here as "inform." But it is better to keep it on its apparent meaning, that the intended "showing" is: let me see, show me something that anyone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has created.

And His saying ﴿Show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11] is more forceful than the mufassir's explanation "tell me," because the challenge in it is evident. It is possible that they could inform him of a matter while lying, saying: "Yes, in such-and-such there is something, its creation is such-and-such." But when he says "Show me," challenging with what can be seen, then they are silenced.

As for His saying "Show me," he said: (O people of Makkah). This is based on the view that every address in a Meccan surah that concerns the disbelievers is directed to the people of Makkah. The correct view is that it is general, so that this challenge can now be applied in our present age. The imperative here in "Show me," for what purpose? For what? For incapacitation (ta'jiz) and threat.

(﴿what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11] — other than Him, i.e., your gods, that you have associated with Him, may He be exalted.) That is, show me what they created. If you show me that they created something, it may be an excuse for you to associate them with Allah, the Exalted, in worship. But since the matter is not so, and no creator can exist other than the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, it is not permissible to worship anything along with Him. For if you acknowledge that there is no creator but Allah, you must acknowledge that there is no deity but Allah, and just as you have acknowledged His lordship, you must acknowledge His divinity.

On His saying ﴿what He created﴾: he says: "(mā) is an interrogative of denial, a subject (mubtada'), and (dhā) means (alladhī) with its relative clause as the predicate, and (ara) is suspended from acting, and what follows it fills the place of the two objects."

On His saying ﴿what those besides Him have created﴾: the mufassir parsed it correctly. "(mā khalaqa)": he says: (mā) is an interrogative noun, (dhā) is a relative noun built on quiescence in the place of nominative, (khalaqa) is a past-tense verb, and the clause is the relative clause having no place in i'rab. The returning pronoun is omitted, and the estimate is: "what did those besides Him create." The clause ﴿what those besides Him have created﴾ is an interrogative clause suspended from action, suspended from the action of what? (Show me).

As for his saying "and what follows it fills the place of the two objects": this holds if we say that seeing means knowing. But if we say that seeing means sight with the eye, then what follows it fills the place of only one object. Does Ibn Malik's words in the Alfiyya indicate this parsing that the mufassir mentioned? What is it?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He parsed it as not cancelled (mulghah). Is it permissible to cancel it? The answer: yes, it is permissible, indeed it may be said that cancelling it is preferable, because if you cancel it you make ﴿mādhā﴾ a fronted object of ﴿khalaqa﴾, and then we do not need this, and the original is non-omission. You have previously learned that cancelling it has two aspects: either you say (mā) is an interrogative noun and (dhā) is superfluous, or you say ﴿mādhā﴾ together is an interrogative noun.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11], i.e., those other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is a challenge, and every challenge in the Qur'an cannot be something that exists, for if the thing were possible the challenge would be idle, with no benefit in it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿But﴾. The mufassir said: (for transition) ﴿the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11] (clear in their associating others, while you are among them). That is, the matter is clear, that there is no creator but Allah, and that no one can exist who creates. But the persistence of the polytheists in their polytheism is considered wrongdoing and manifest error. For this reason He said: ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., the polytheists who associated others with Allah in worship, although they believe that He has no partner in creation, ﴿are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11]. The mufassir said: (clear, بَيِّن).

The word ﴿mubīn﴾ comes with the meaning of "bayyin," i.e., apparent, and with the meaning of "muzhir" (making manifest), since it is derived from the quadriliteral (abāna). The quadriliteral abāna comes transitive and comes intransitive. So abāna comes with the meaning of bāna, i.e., became apparent, and then it is intransitive; and it comes with the meaning of azhara, abāna al-shay' means he made it manifest, and then it is transitive. In this verse, ﴿the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾ [Luqman 11]: is it from the intransitive or the transitive? From the intransitive. For this reason he explained it with "bayyin." We want an example of it from the transitive. What is it?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the transitive.
* Student: ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 77]; ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ [Yusuf 1]. Both meanings are permissible: clear in itself, or making the truth clear.
* Shaykh: Yes, and similarly: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 195], i.e., making clear. The conclusion is that you should not assume that ﴿mubīn﴾ is always transitive; it may be intransitive in the sense of "clear," and it may be transitive in the sense of "making manifest."

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 12]: among it knowledge, religiosity, and correctness in speech, and his sayings are many and transmitted.) ﴿And We had certainly﴾: this sentence is emphasized by three emphatics. What are they?

* Student: The lam, qad, and the oath.
* Shaykh: Yes, the lam, qad, and the oath. His saying ﴿ātaynā﴾ means "a'taynā," we gave, and this giving is a cosmic giving: Allah gave him the thing by a cosmic giving.

His saying ﴿Luqmān﴾ is the name of a man. Most scholars hold that he was a man whom Allah gave wisdom and insight into affairs, and that he was not a prophet. Ibn Kathir said: most people hold that he was not a prophet, and it is related from 'Ikrimah, if it is authentically from him, that he said he was a prophet.[[Mentioned by Ibn Kathir (6/334).]] But the correct view is that he was not a prophet; rather he was a wise man of sound judgment, whom Allah gave this wisdom, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah 269].

* Student: Shaykh, (...) some say: is Luqman the wise the same as this one or another?
* Shaykh: No, this is him.
* Student: How is that, is it a report from the Messenger or Israelite narrations?
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: (...) Luqman the wise, did Luqman the wise say (...)?
* Shaykh: This is among what is transmitted about his wisdom (...) is it correct or not?

He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 12]. What is wisdom? Wisdom in origin is agreement with what is correct. Close to this is their saying: it is putting things in their proper places. So the person of sound opinion and right conduct is considered wise, because he puts things in their places. Is that right? What did we mention about wisdom, its explanation?

* Student: (...) putting things in their places.
* Shaykh: That is one. And the second?
* Student: (...) the wise (...).
* Shaykh: No, we want wisdom only, not the wise. What is wisdom? It has been said: it is putting things in their places, that is one. And it has been said?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Did you not go right or left? It has been said: it is agreement with what is correct, and they have one meaning, because agreement with the correct is placing a thing in its proper place. Good. He says: among it is knowledge.
* Student: Is this its content or an explanation, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, this is its meaning. Among it is knowledge and religiosity. Is knowledge wisdom or not? Or is wisdom attained by it? Wisdom is attained by it.
Second: religiosity, yes, it is wisdom.
Third: correctness in speech, and this too is wisdom. Likewise correctness in action is wisdom.

He said: (And his sayings are many and transmitted: he used to give legal rulings before the mission of Dawud, and he lived to see his mission, and took knowledge from him, and gave up issuing rulings, and said concerning that: "Shall I not be content when I am spared?" It was said to him: Which of people is the worst? He said: The one who does not care if people see him doing evil.) (...) He said: "I was spared." This is from wisdom: that a person, when he is spared, should be content, because if he is spared and then works on what he was spared from, he will gain nothing but wasting time and effort.

As for "Which of people is the worst? He said: The one who does not care if people see him doing evil," this may be disputed, because one who does not care if people see him doing evil is considered merely lacking shame, and is not considered the worst of people. The worst of people, in reality, is the one who associates others with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; this is the worst of people, for he is the greatest wrongdoer, so he is the worst of people.

Furthermore, this saying the mufassir mentioned, or these two sentences, may be correct as going back to Luqman, and may be incorrect; that is, one cannot be certain, because there is no authentic connected chain to Luqman, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not inform of it. Like all earlier reports, if they do not come through the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, they must be examined, because they reach us without a chain and are taken from the People of the Book, who are not trustworthy.

* Student: Shaykh, is no wisdom taken from them?
* Student: Then he gave up issuing rulings (...) David, according to the mufassir's words (...).
* Shaykh: And he said: (...) yes, in everything a person is asked for a ruling, he has no need to be involved with it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know; Ibn Kathir did not mention this report.
* Student: Shaykh, his saying: "Narrate from the Children of Israel and there is no harm" (...).
* Shaykh: It may be (...) from him, and it may be (...); because the Children of Israel have a book and a remnant of knowledge, whereas others may have nothing. But all reports about earlier peoples fall into three conditions, as is known: either they agree with the Shari'ah, or they contradict it, or there is neither agreement nor contradiction. What agrees with the Shari'ah is accepted, what contradicts it is rejected, and what has neither agreement nor contradiction is neither confirmed nor denied.

He says: (﴿That﴾ i.e., and We said to him: ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾ [Luqman 12] for what He gave you of wisdom.)

His saying: (﴿We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman 12]). Then He said: (﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾). If someone said that His saying "Be grateful to Allah" is an explanation of the wisdom, meaning "that" here explains the wisdom, it would not be far-fetched. But the mufassir holds that it is the object of an omitted verb whose estimate is: "We said to him: that be grateful to Allah," meaning for what He gave you of wisdom. As for the first possibility, which is the apparent sense of the Qur'an and needs no estimate, the matter is evident: that gratitude for Allah's blessing is part of wisdom, indeed it is its head.

His saying ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾: the lam here is for exclusivity and entitlement, because gratitude in the absolute sense is exclusively for Allah, and only Allah, glory be to Him, deserves absolute gratitude. Gratitude is the performance of obedience to the Benefactor, acknowledged in the heart, praised by the tongue, and obeyed by the limbs. The objects of gratitude are three: the tongue, the heart, and the limbs; its cause is one, namely the blessing. For this reason there is a general and specific relation between it and praise (hamd): in terms of cause, praise is more general; in terms of its objects, gratitude is more general. How so? Praise has two causes: the perfection of the one praised, and the bounty of the one praised. So you praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for His perfection, and you praise Him for His bounty. But praise is specific to what, in terms of its object? It is specific to the tongue only. As for gratitude, in terms of cause it is more specific, because it occurs only in return for a blessing; but in terms of its objects it is more general, occurring by the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. On this is the poet's saying:

Three blessings have been granted you from me: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart.

His saying ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾ [Luqman 12]. We said: the lam here is for exclusivity, and what else? And entitlement. So it is obligatory upon the servant to sincerely direct gratitude to Him, and to believe in his heart that none deserves absolute gratitude but Allah.

He said: (﴿And whoever is grateful, it is only for himself﴾ [Luqman 12], because the reward of his gratitude returns to him. ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ — the blessing — ﴿indeed Allah is Free of need﴾ from His creation, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ in His doing.)

﴿And whoever is grateful﴾: this sentence is conditional. The verb of the condition is jussive by "man," and the answer of the condition is the sentence ﴿it is only for himself﴾; "innamā" is a particle of restriction, and ﴿yashkuru﴾ is an imperfect verb. But is it said that ﴿yashkuru﴾ is the answer, or the whole sentence? The whole sentence.

His saying ﴿it is only for himself﴾: how did He say "Be grateful to Allah" and then say "it is only for himself"? One would expect the phrase "whoever is grateful, it is only for Allah." But we say, as the mufassir said: the meaning of "it is only for himself" is that the reward of gratitude returns to him, so it is for his own benefit, and gratitude does not return to Allah so that He benefits from it; for He, glory be to Him, does not benefit from obedience nor is He harmed by disobedience, but it returns to you yourself.

﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, which is the opposite of gratitude, ﴿indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾: Free of need of him, when he disbelieves the blessing of Allah.

﴿Praiseworthy﴾ is on the pattern of faʿīl in the sense of maf'ūl, and it may be that ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ means fā'il (one who praises), so He, glory be to Him, is praised and is also one who praises, because He, glory be to Him, describes those who deserve perfect attributes with what they deserve; for this reason He praised His prophets and His friends, and this is praise of them, and He is also praised by His servants; so it is faʿīl in the sense of fā'il and in the sense of maf'ūl. The connection of the answer-clause to the condition is: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 12]. Its connection to the condition is evident: whoever disbelieves will not harm Allah, nor diminish His dominion, because He is Free of need. Likewise, this does not reflect any deficiency in His wisdom, because He, majestic and exalted, is Praiseworthy: the existence of the grateful and the existence of the disbelievers are both things for which Allah is praised. Had it not been so, the worth of gratitude would not be known, nor would the harm of disbelief be known; without this, people would be on one level, and the good would not be distinguished from the bad.

﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾: Al-Ghanī (the Free of need) is one of Allah's names, and al-Ḥamīd (the Praiseworthy) is also one of His names.
