He is the One who will call them to account for their deeds. For this He said: ﴿then We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. ﴿We will inform them﴾: We will tell them.

When they are informed of it, are they recompensed for it? Yes: the disbeliever must be recompensed for his sin, but he is recompensed with justice; for this reason the Fire has levels according to the crimes of the disbelievers, and the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire.

So His saying ﴿We will inform them﴾ means: We will tell them, as a form of rebuke and humiliation, then We will recompense them according to what they deserve.

His saying: ﴿to Us﴾ and ﴿We will inform them﴾ is a plural pronoun, but what is meant by it?
* Student: Glorification (ta'lil).
* Shaykh: Glorification, without doubt. The meaning is the glorification [of Allah].

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [Luqman 23]: this completes the warning; that is, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts. And what are "what is within the breasts"? "What is within the breasts" are the hearts, because He said: ﴿But it is hearts that grow blind which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj 46].

So the meaning of (dhāt al-ṣudūr) is: the owners of the breasts, which are the hearts.

He said: ﴿dhāt al-ṣudūr﴾ here means the hearts, because what is inside the chest is hidden from creation and only Allah the Mighty and Majestic knows it; for this He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾.

In His saying: ﴿Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ there is evidence that the disbeliever is held accountable for the deeds of the heart, and this is so: the disbeliever is held accountable for it, because if he were not to be held accountable, His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ would have no great benefit.

* Student: His saying ﴿then let not grieve you his disbelief﴾: the second conditional's answer, is it not a request (talabiyya)?
* Shaykh: It is not a request, because (lā) is a prohibitive. Correct: ﴿then let not grieve you﴾ is a prohibition; it is not a request.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verses 15–25 (part 6 of 6):

Then He said: ﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little, then We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾ [Luqman 24]. I seek refuge in Allah. ﴿We will let them enjoy themselves﴾ means: We will make them enjoy themselves, eating what they wish, wearing what they wish, riding what they wish, dwelling where they wish, and taking pleasure in every delight of this world. But this is little, little, little. The Messenger ﷺ said: "The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it" [al-Bukhari (2892), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd]. The place of a whip is better than the world. What is the world? With all its people, from its beginning to its end, that is "the world and all that is in it." These people, and we seek refuge in Allah, enjoy themselves for a little while, and how little is the world and its enjoyment! Everything that has passed of the world up to this present hour of yours is as though it had never been, as if it were a jumble of dreams. A person may live in it as long as he lives, yet ﴿On the Day they see what they are promised, it will seem to them they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf 35]. So they enjoy themselves a little, and the littleness here is considered both in terms of the kind of enjoyment and in terms of its duration. So, the kind of enjoyment, compared to what is in the Hereafter, is it little or much?

* Students: Little.

* Shaykh: Very little, and it cannot even be compared. Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in the Hereafter except the names" [al-Bayhaqi, al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur (332)].

Likewise with regard to its duration: the duration is short, is it not? And it cannot be compared to the everlasting time of the Hereafter.

﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little﴾. Allah, exalted is He, has explained the nature of this enjoyment in another verse, when He said, glorified is His remembrance: ﴿Those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their abode﴾ [Muhammad 12]. This is the description of this enjoyment: they are slaves of desire, having no concern except the desire of the belly and the desire of the private parts, just as cattle do exactly.

He said: ﴿Then We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾ [Luqman 24]. ﴿Then﴾ means: after this little enjoyment, (﴿We will drive them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿to a harsh punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire, from which they will find no escape).

﴿We will drive them﴾ means: We will compel them. ﴿But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah 173], meaning: whoever is forced. This is originally derived from being compelled into harm, because (idtarra, "to be compelled") originally comes from nudtarru ("we compel"). Therefore, everything that compels a person is called a darurah ("necessity"), because it compels him toward that thing.

As for His saying ﴿We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾, it is because they do not want it. They do not want the Fire, nor do they want this punishment, but they are forced into it, and we seek refuge in Allah, because they performed its causes.

As for His saying (﴿We will drive them﴾ in the Hereafter): what is meant by "the Hereafter"? Is it what comes after the Day of Resurrection, or even the grave?

* A student: Even the grave.

* Shaykh: Even the grave. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah: "Among what enters into belief in the Last Day is everything the Prophet ﷺ informed about that occurs after death. All of it is from the Last Day." So after this enjoyment they will be driven to punishment, and we seek refuge in Allah.

As for His saying ﴿We will drive them to a punishment﴾: "punishment" means chastisement. The author says "harsh" means: "it is the punishment of the Fire." What is the opposite of "harsh"? Its opposite is "gentle." The harshness of the punishment of the Fire is in its manner and in its kind, and we seek refuge in Allah.

As for its manner: Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa' 56]. And He says regarding what they are punished with: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 97]. And we seek refuge in Allah, this is regarding its manner.

As for its kind: it does not occur to the mind, nor can imagination grasp it. They are given to drink boiling water. When they cry for help and die of thirst, and seek relief, what are they given for relief? They are given water like molten brass, which is melted lead, and we seek refuge in Allah. It scorches the faces: when it approaches the face, it scorches the face. When it descends into the intestines, they are given boiling water which cuts their intestines to pieces. Sometimes they are given drink of pus: ﴿They gulp it down but can hardly swallow it, and death comes to him from every direction, yet he will not die, and before him is a harsh punishment﴾ [Ibrahim 17]. This punishment, and we seek refuge in Allah, with its severe, great kinds, deserves to be described as a harsh punishment, without any gentleness or kindness. Rather, it is harsh and severe.

As for His saying ﴿They will find no escape from it﴾ [al-Nisa' 121]: this is how it is in the Qur'an, meaning they will find no place of flight. ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are about to fall into it, and will find no escape from it﴾ [al-Kahf 53]. Not even this; rather, they, and we seek refuge in Allah, will come to it as thirsty herds rushing to water, and it will appear to them as a mirage. The thirsty person, when he sees water, even if it is a mirage, thinks it is water, due to his intense longing for water. So they will approach it in this manner, and we seek refuge in Allah, and they will fall into it.

﴿And if﴾: the lam of oath. ﴿If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman 25].

Regarding His saying ﴿And if﴾: he says "lam of oath" is joined with what? With the conditional ("in," "if"). Was the answer of the condition omitted, or the answer of the oath? The answer of the condition was omitted and the answer of the oath remained. Where is the answer? ﴿They would surely say, "Allah"﴾. Ibn Malik's saying has already passed us:

"When the condition and the oath come together, omit the answer of whichever is placed later, and it is what is required."

And His saying ﴿If you asked them﴾: does it mean the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or whoever may be addressed? It may be either.

﴿Who created the heavens﴾: this is the form of the question. Who created the heavens and the earth? Did al-Lat create them? Al-'Uzza? Manat? Hubal? Who?

The answer: ﴿They would surely say, "Allah"﴾. They acknowledge that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, mighty and majestic.

As for His saying ﴿They would surely say﴾: it is the answer of the oath. (The nun of the nominative was deleted because of the succession of similar letters, and the waw of the pronoun because of the meeting of two quiescent letters.) Its original form is: liyaqulunanna, correct? Because this is a present-tense verb of the "five verbs," which must include the waw and the nun. So we say: (liyaqulun), then add the emphatic nun with it: (liyaqulunanna). Now three nuns have gathered, all of them additional. Do we draw lots among them, or distinguish between them by a ruling? We distinguish between them by a ruling. We say: if we delete the nun of the nominative, the emphatic nun remains; if we delete the emphatic nun, the nun of the nominative remains. Which one? We delete the nun of the nominative, for two reasons.

The first reason: the nun of the nominative is customarily deleted when the verb is in the subjunctive or the jussive, is that correct? Rather, it may also be deleted outside the two states of subjunctive and jussive, deleted for lightness, as in the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise until you believe" [Abu Dawud (5193), al-Tirmidhi (2688), Ibn Majah (68), and it is originally in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise." "You will not enter" here has neither a governing particle nor a jussive particle, and it was deleted for lightness. Its original form is: "you will not enter Paradise" (la tadkhuluna al-jannah), so the nun was deleted for lightness.

The nun is also often deleted together with the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah). So it is more deserving of deletion, and the emphatic nun remains. For if we deleted the emphatic nun, the intended purpose would be lost, while we want to emphasize the verb. And the emphasis of the verb here, and we have studied this in a new lesson in grammar, is it obligatory or not obligatory (liyaqulunanna)?

* A student: Obligatory.

* Shaykh: Obligatory, because it affirms a future oath.

* A student: It is not separated.

* Shaykh: It is not separated. Nothing separates its lam from its verb, so its emphasis is obligatory.

So we keep the nun. If the nun of the nominative says, "Let us all remain," and we all become (liyaqulunanna), can we keep what contradicts it?

We say: it is not possible, because the nun of the nominative is additional and the emphatic nun is additional, so three letters, all additional, cannot gather in one place. We can bear one letter or two letters at most.

So we say: one of you must be deleted, and you, O nun of the nominative, are more deserving of deletion. Go! Then the waw comes together with the emphatic nun. The waw here is quiescent. You say: quiescent, and the emphatic nun is doubled, so the first of them is quiescent. Two quiescent letters have come together, and two quiescent letters cannot come together. Why? Because quiescence and vowel are opposites, so one quiescent letter and another quiescent letter cannot come together. Therefore we must perform an action that frees us from the meeting of two quiescent letters. What is the action? If the letter before the quiescent letter is sound, what do we do with it? We vowel it with kasrah. If the letter before the quiescent letter is not sound, but a soft letter (harf layn), then we delete it. Ibn Malik said:

"If two quiescent letters meet, vowel what precedes them with kasrah. If it is a soft letter, deletion is deserved."

So here, is the first quiescent letter (the waw) a soft letter or a sound one?

* A student: A soft letter.

* Shaykh: Then we delete it, so the lam meets the nun: (liyaqulunna). So in this verb there are now two deletions: deletion of the nun, with the reason being the succession of similar letters; deletion of the waw of the nominative, with the reason being the meeting of two quiescent letters. On this basis the author says: "The nun of the nominative was deleted because of the succession of similar letters, and the waw of the pronoun because of the meeting of two quiescent letters."

What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying ﴿Allah﴾ in ﴿They would surely say, "Allah"﴾? It is the subject of a deleted verb. The estimate is: "Allah created them." This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 9]. "They would surely say: created them." So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the verb. So here, what is the deleted element?

* A student: A verb.

* Shaykh: The verb? Yes. Is it correct to say the deleted element is a noun, with the estimate "He is Allah"? It is correct, but it is contrary to what is preferable, because the question is in conflict with the answer. And the question was in the form of a verb: "Who created?" So it requires that the answer be like the question in verb form: "He created them, such-and-such."

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾ [Luqman 25]. ("Say") means: when they acknowledge and confess. ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾. ﴿The praise﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿to Allah﴾ is its predicate. Praise be to Allah for what? For the clarity of the proof and the clarity of the way. Now they have confessed to what? That they are in error in their polytheism.

So ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ here is for the clarification and manifestation of the proof, and that they have been refuted by it. For when they acknowledge and confess that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, and that these idols do not create, then they have testified against themselves that these idols do not deserve worship. For this reason, ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾. Also, the praise here may be understood as: "Praise be to Allah for creating the heavens and the earth, that He is the Creator, mighty and majestic, alone, and therefore He is praised for His attributes of perfection and His beautiful acts."

He says: (﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ for the manifestation of the proof against them).

﴿The praise﴾ has been mentioned here many times, and it is the description of the one praised with perfection, together with love and exaltation.

The lam in His saying ﴿to Allah﴾ is the lam of entitlement and exclusivity. Entitlement, because He is the one entitled to praise, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Possessor of praise and glory" [Muslim (477/205), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Second, exclusivity: because who is the one who deserves absolute praise? He is Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾. ("But" here) is the transitional retraction (idrab intiqali), not the cancelling retraction (idrab ibtali). It is a transition from what preceded to recording their complete ignorance. For this reason he says: (﴿But most of them do not know﴾) its obligation upon them, meaning tawhid (monotheism). The negation of knowledge from them is because of what? Because its benefit is absent, and a thing may be negated because its benefit is absent. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21]. He negated hearing from them, because its benefit is absent with regard to them.

So His saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ negates knowledge from them, although they acknowledge that Allah is the Creator, but they did not benefit from this knowledge. And which of the two is more abominable: an ignorant person who does not know, or a knowledgeable person who did not benefit?

* Students: The latter.

* Shaykh: The latter is more severe and more abominable, because he is a compound ignorant person, while the other is a simple ignorant person. And because he is stubborn and arrogant, while the other is a misguided person who is not stubborn. Compound ignorance is more abominable, and stubbornness born of knowledge is worse than stubbornness born of ignorance. A poet said two verses:

"Whoever seeks the sciences without a teacher will go astray from the straight path,
and the sciences will become confused for him until he becomes more misguided than Tuma the sage."

Tuma is a compound ignorant person whom they called "the sage." But what deceived him is that they called him "the sage," and he began to issue rulings on everything, until he ruled that whoever gives his daughter in charity to a man will enter Paradise. He said, (the third verse):

"He gave away daughters in charity to men,
desiring by that the gardens of bliss."

Is this ignorance or not?

* A student: Is this like fornication?

* Shaykh: Yes. You are a young man in need of marriage and you have no dowry or anything, so if I gave you charity, [they say] yes indeed. Ignorance may measure with its mind and say: instead of giving him dirhams and having him go to propose, we cut the road, saying: this one is without dirhams.

* A student: We want an explanation of this compound and simple.

* Shaykh: Listen to the compound and the simple in the next two verses:

"The donkey of the sage Tuma said..."

Did he not say: more misguided than Tuma the sage?

"The donkey of the sage Tuma said: If fate were just, I would be the one riding.
Because I am a simple ignorant one, and my companion is a compound ignorant one."

Did you understand the difference now?

* A student: Yes, it is known, the verse, that is...

* Shaykh: Fine, it is known, finished.

* The student: I am saying: what is the difference...?

* Shaykh: The donkey says: he is a simple ignorant one, and his companion, who is Tuma, is a compound ignorant one. The compound ignorant one is the one who does not know that he is ignorant: ignorant and unaware that he is ignorant, this is compound. And the simple one is the ignorant one who knows that he is ignorant. It becomes clear through an example: someone says to you, "When was the Battle of Badr?" and you say, "I do not know." What is this called?

* A student: Simple.

* Shaykh: This is simple ignorance. The person does not know, and he knows that he does not know, and he says: "I do not know."

Another man says to someone else, "When was the Battle of Badr?" He says, "Praise be to Allah who has opened [knowledge] to the ignorant. The Battle of Badr was in Jumada al-Akhirah in the ninth year after the Hijrah (...)."

Did you understand the difference now?

* A student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...).

* The student: No, I am saying: what is the difference...

* Shaykh: The donkey says he is a simple ignorant one, and his companion, who is Tuma, is a compound ignorant one. The compound ignorant one is the one who does not know that he is ignorant: ignorant and unaware that he is ignorant, this is compound. And the simple one is the ignorant one who knows that he is ignorant. It becomes clear through an example: someone says to you, "When was the Battle of Badr?" and you say, "I do not know." What is this called?

* A student: Simple.

* Shaykh: This is simple ignorance: the person does not know, and he knows that he does not know, and he says, "I do not know."

Another man says to someone else, "When was the Battle of Badr?" He says, "Praise be to Allah who has opened [knowledge] to the ignorant. The Battle of Badr was in Jumada al-Akhirah in the ninth year after the Hijrah." What do you say about this?

* A student: This is compound ignorance.

* Shaykh: Now, he is ignorant, and he does not know that he is ignorant. For this reason he began with his saying: "Praise be to Allah who has opened [knowledge] to the ignorant." It is said to him: "Allah has not opened [knowledge] to you, because you are ignorant."

* A student: I mean "compound." What is the meaning of "compound"?

* Shaykh: It is compounded of two ignorances: his ignorance of the reality and his ignorance of his own state. The compound ignorant one is ignorant of the reality and ignorant of his own state. Clear?

* A student: Yes.

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verses 15–25 (part 1 of 6):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them﴾ [Luqman 15]. ﴿If they strive with you﴾: The pronoun in His saying ﴿they strive with you﴾ is the subject pronoun referring to the two parents. The meaning of ﴿jahadaka﴾ (they strive with you): the author mentioned its meaning, but its meaning is: they exerted effort with you. Exerted effort over what? ﴿To make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾, meaning: to make you set up with Me a partner of which you have no knowledge.

His saying ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾ is a qualifier to describe the reality, not a qualifier of restriction (ihtirazi), because it is impossible for knowledge to exist that Allah the Exalted has a partner. This is like His saying: ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another god, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun 117].

If someone says: What is the benefit of this qualifier, when it is known that it will never exist?

We say: The benefit in it is to belittle this matter, so that no one attempts to deny it and seek knowledge or proof that Allah the Exalted has a partner. It is as if He is saying: this is the reality of the situation, and what is a reality cannot be otherwise. This is the benefit of His saying ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾.

His saying ﴿mā laysa﴾: the ﴿mā﴾ here may be a relative pronoun, meaning "that which you have no knowledge of," and it may be an indefinite qualified noun, meaning: to associate with Me a partner of which you have no knowledge.

His saying ﴿then do not obey them﴾ is the answer to the conditional, which is ﴿if they strive with you﴾: if they strive with you, then do not obey them.

Consider His saying ﴿then do not obey them﴾. He did not say "then do not be dutiful to them," nor did He say "then disobey them." This is because the expression "do not obey them" is easier on the soul than the expression "disobey them." This is why the statement of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to his father was: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43], which is gentler than saying: "O my father, indeed you are ignorant of what I possess." Therefore he said ﴿there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾, because negating perfection is easier on souls than affirming deficiency.

It is mentioned that a king saw in a dream that his teeth had fallen out, so he said: Call for me an interpreter who will interpret this vision. They brought a man to interpret it, and he related the dream to him. He said: Your family will die. When he said "your family will die," the king was alarmed, terrified and panicked, and said: Flog him. They flogged him and he left. He said: Bring me someone else. They brought another man and he related the dream to him. He said: The king will be the longest-lived of his family. So he honored him and lavished blessings upon him. The meaning of both is close, since if he is the longest-lived of them, it means they will die before him.

The conclusion is that interpretation has an effect on the soul. The expression "do not obey them" is easier than the expression "disobey them."

Then His saying "do not obey them": He did not say "do not be dutiful to them" or "do not fulfill their right." Their right is obligatory even if they command you to associate partners with Allah. If the two parents have an obligatory right even when they command you to associate partners with Allah, then how much more so when they command you to do something less than shirk? For this reason, the right of parents is not a small matter. ﴿So do not obey them﴾. Why should you not obey them? Because there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator. The right of Allah is more binding than the right of the parents. It is He who made their right obligatory, so how can we neglect His right for the sake of their right?

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [Luqman: 15]). He says: "in agreement with reality." This is an explanation of His saying ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾, that this is the actual situation: you have no knowledge of it. ﴿Then do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾; that is, with what is customary: goodness and maintaining ties.

﴿Accompany them in this world﴾: The word ﴿fi al-dunya﴾ (in this world): the ﴿fi﴾ here is undoubtedly locative. But what is meant by "in this world"? Is it meant as a time period, or as matters of worldly affairs? It may mean matters: that is, in worldly affairs, accompany them kindly, but in religious matters, do not transgress what Allah has commanded you. It may also mean "in this worldly life," but the first meaning is more eloquent, because it is known that companionship between parents and child only occurs in this world, so there is no need for the qualification. The apparent meaning is that ﴿accompany them in this world﴾ means: in matters related to worldly affairs, accompany them ﴿kindly (ma'ruf)﴾. The author said: "with kindness (bil-ma'ruf)."

The meaning of this explanation is that ﴿ma'rufan﴾ (kindly) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (nasb bi-nazi'l-khafid). Accusative by removal of the preposition with anything other than "an" (that) is not consistent; rather, it is irregular (shadh). Since this is the case, the Qur'an should not be referred to it. If it were said that ﴿ma'rufan﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, the estimate being: "accompany them with a kind companionship," meaning a known companionship with no harshness, no rebuke, no blame, and no lack of what is owed to them, this would be better.

The author said: "with righteousness and maintaining ties (bil-birr wa's-sila)." Righteousness (birr) is abundance of good, and maintaining ties (sila) is not severing. So the meaning is: maintain ties with them and be good to them according to what they deserve from you, but only in worldly matters.

﴿And follow the way of him who turns back to Me﴾. ﴿Follow the way (sabil)﴾: path. ﴿Him who turns back to Me (anaba ilayya)﴾: returned to Me in obedience.

His saying ﴿and follow the way of him who turned back﴾: ﴿man﴾ here is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun conveys generality. So is it general, meaning: follow the way of whoever among them turns back to Me, or of anyone else? Or is it general but intended to be specific, meaning: whoever among them turns back to Me? The better view is that we say it is general: ﴿and follow the way of him who turns back to Me﴾ from all people.

Accordingly, if one of the parents turns back to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, then following his way is all the more fitting. His saying ﴿and follow the way of him who turns back to Me﴾: ﴿anaba﴾ means "returned." Returned from where? From disobedience to obedience, from polytheism to monotheism, and from sinfulness to uprightness and piety.

It is said that when Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him) embraced Islam, his mother said to him: "What is this religion that you have brought?" He said: "This is the truth." She said to him: "You will either abandon it, or I will refuse food and drink until I die, and you will be shamed because of me." He said: "This is the truth, and I will not abandon it." So she abstained from food and drink for a full day. When morning came, she was exhausted, meaning weakened by hunger and thirst. Her son asked her to eat and drink, and said: "I will not return from this religion." But she refused. On the second day, she was even more exhausted, and he said to her as he had said the first time: "I will not abandon this religion." She remained stubborn. When the third day came, she was severely exhausted. He said to her: "O mother, you know that this is the truth. By Allah, even if you had a hundred souls and every soul died, by Allah, I would not abandon this religion." (...). When she saw that the man was resolved, she ate.

In a situation like this, is it permissible for a person, if he sees that his mother wants to die or his father wants to die, to commit shirk?

Student: No.

Shaykh: If someone said: what if he wanted to say that he is a polytheist with his tongue, interpreting it figuratively?

Student: If it depends on (...) this, then only out of necessity.

Another student: I think it is permissible, except for one who is coerced while his heart is (...).

Shaykh: That does not contradict, but this is someone who is coerced into something. Here, he is not coerced into anything.

Student: But this involves saving a life.

Shaykh: This is saving a disbelieving soul that commands disbelief. So figurative interpretation is not permissible, even by interpretation.

Student: This is a satanic soul.

Shaykh: Yes. It is not permissible, not even by interpretation. Let him be patient and say: "I have not harmed you in anything. Whatever you want of worldly matters, I am ready for it; I have not harmed you. If you wish (...), if you wish, eat, and if you wish, do not eat."

Student: And that figurative interpretation may be a help to disbelief.

Shaykh: Yes, indeed, there are undoubtedly corruptions in it. The main point is that it is not permissible to say it, even figuratively. Yes, but if he feared for his own self, and there is a difference between one who fears for the soul of another and one who fears for his own soul. If he feared for his own self, that he would be killed, then he may say it figuratively, based on His saying ﴿except one who is forced while his heart is secure in faith﴾ [al-Nahl 106]. However, regarding the last matter, it is not permissible if it involves support for Islam. If maintaining his position is support for Islam, and conforming outwardly is abandonment of Islam, then it is forbidden for him to do that, because in that case it falls under the category of jihad. This is what happened to Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him). He was called to say that the Qur'an is created, and others were also called to say that the Qur'an is created. Some scholars interpreted and outwardly answered what they were called to say. Others insisted and were killed. Others insisted and Allah protected them from being killed, like Imam Ahmad. Imam Ahmad did not answer them even by interpretation, because people watch what Imam Ahmad says. If he had said that the Qur'an is created, even figuratively, what would the common people say? They would say: "It is created," and this innovation would deceive the general Muslims. So he, may Allah have mercy on him, saw that it was not permissible to interpret in that situation, because of what that entails of abandoning truth and establishing falsehood.

Student: (...) People narrate the story of the man who killed a fly, and there was something in his soul for other than Allah, and he said: "No..."

Shaykh: "I would not offer anything to anyone other than Allah." This was covered for us in the Book of Tawhid, and we said that the hadith is weak. Even if it were authentic, this man would have approached with a heart at peace with disbelief, having expanded his breast to disbelief.

Student: He was afraid of being killed, because they had killed his companion.

Shaykh: Yes, that is not contradictory. But when he feared being killed, was his act a defense, or did he do it at peace?

Student: In the hadith, the last one who was killed.

Shaykh: (...) was killed. In this case we say: this first man who approached (...) regarding the first. Because the first, when he approached, it seems he approached with his breast expanded to disbelief, and this is not beneficial, because if a person is coerced, his coercion must be that he intends, by the deed or the word, to repel the coercion, and (...) for it. But if he does it with his breast expanded by it, or when he was coerced and sees that the matter is serious and decisive, his breast is expanded by this thing.

Student: Shaykh, what is the indication of the expansion of the breast?

Shaykh: (...) carrying it in agreement with the verse (...). As an answer to this, it should be said: this hadith [[narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah (33583) and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (9/457), from the hadith of Salman al-Farsi.]] is first of all weak and not authentic. Second, even if it were authentic, it should be understood in a way that agrees with the noble verse, because it is impossible for something authentically from the Messenger to contradict the Qur'an.

Student: What is the meaning of (...) "let him go his way"? What is the meaning of his saying: "I have nothing to offer"? They said: "Offer a fly for him," so he offered a fly immediately.

Shaykh: So offering a fly means his breast expanded to disbelief.

Student: Yes, he did not say "offer a fly" or force him.

Shaykh: The main point is that he expanded his breast to disbelief when he was coerced into this.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: Yes, but if the hadith is authentic from the Messenger, its meaning is that it is a lesson, just as he related to us about previous nations, so that we may take a lesson from them.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No, not for this reason. The reason is that when the Messenger relates to us a story of previous nations, it does not mean merely "listen to it and do not take a lesson from it." Its meaning is for taking a lesson. But the hadith, as we said to you in the explanation of Tawhid, is weak and not authentic.

Student: (...) to repel coercion (...).

Shaykh: "And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, then do not obey them." What is the meaning of His saying ﴿jahadaka﴾ (...)?

﴿Then﴾: This sequencing indicates that after He mentioned that if they command shirk, do not obey them, and that it is obligatory for you to follow the way of those who turn back to Allah, He said ﴿then﴾: meaning, after these attempts by them to make you associate partners with Allah, and after you obey, the return is to Allah.

His saying ﴿to Me is your return﴾ is a nominal sentence of information in which the predicate was placed first to indicate exclusivity. ﴿To Me﴾: not to other than Me. ﴿Your return (marji'kum)﴾: meaning your return (mardudkum), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Baqarah 210].

﴿Then I will inform you of what you used to do﴾: He says ﴿then I will inform you﴾, meaning I will tell you ﴿of what you used to do﴾. This informing entails recompense, though there may not be recompense. This is why Allah the Mighty and Majestic always expresses it as informing, that is, notifying, because He may recompense or may not recompense. He will meet His believing servant in private, inform him of his sins, and make him acknowledge them. Then after that He says: I covered them for you in this world, and I forgive them for you today.

His saying ﴿then I will inform you of what you used to do﴾ means: of that which you used to do. This includes everything a person does, small and great, but not what he did not do. If he intended something and did not do it, he is not recompensed for it. However, he may be rewarded for it if it was a sin that he abandoned for the sake of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because he is rewarded for that abandonment. He said: (Then I will recompense you for it. The sentence of the injunction and what follows it is a parenthetical interjection). The author said: "Then I will recompense you for it," as if he made recompense a necessary consequence of informing.

But I told you: it is not necessary. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic expressed it as informing, so that the matter may be permissible or may be in between being recompensed for it and not being recompensed for it.

His saying: (the sentence of the injunction and what follows it is a parenthetical interjection). The injunction begins with His saying ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾. It is a parenthetical interjection within the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and it is not from the words of Luqman to his son, because the one who enjoined parents to kindness, and the reason for kindness, is Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This injunction came after the mention of shirk because disobedience to parents comes after the right of Allah the Exalted. In the injunction there is also another parenthetical sentence. What is it? It is His saying ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years﴾, because His saying ﴿that give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ is what is enjoined. ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾ ﴿that give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾. Now we have how many parenthetical interjections? (...).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: So we say in this: the injunction is a parenthetical interjection between the words of Luqman to his son. And His saying ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾ is also a parenthetical interjection between the verb of enjoining and what is enjoined.

* * *

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, returning to the advice of Luqman: ﴿O my son, indeed, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed and be within a rock or [anywhere] in the heavens or the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted﴾ [Luqman 16].

His saying ﴿innaha﴾ (indeed it): meaning the bad deed. There is a deficiency here, because the intended meaning is ﴿innaha﴾, that is, the bad deed or the good deed; everything, good or bad, ﴿if it should be the weight of a mustard seed﴾. ﴿Mithqal﴾ means weight. The weight was called mithqal because it is measured by its heaviness, since a thing is weighed to know its heaviness from its lightness.

His saying ﴿of a mustard seed﴾: these are well-known small seeds. ﴿Then it would be in a rock﴾: in a rock in what place on earth? Because we do not know of rocks except on the earth. But those who went up to the moon brought us rocks from it, so we do not know whether this is correct or not.

In any case, ﴿in a rock﴾: it is known that rocks are on the earth. His saying ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾: could a mustard seed be in a rock? Is it possible?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Or is this by way of exaggeration?

Student: It is possible, because it sometimes grows out of rocks...

Shaykh: It appears that this plant grows in cracks, cracks that contain soil. In any case, either it is by way of exaggeration, or perhaps in this rock there is something of a different kind the size of a mustard seed, which is taken into account, or it may be said that the intended meaning is that a mustard seed may be in a crack of this rock. I have witnessed in the ghadha tree that it produces small grains the size of a fingertip (...), completely sealed. If you open it, you find in it a creature crawling on its belly, and it is sealed, and it is on the same branch. That is, you do not find an opening in it; this creature is created from it.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** ﴿Then it would be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth.﴾ That is, in the highest of the heavens, or in their lowest parts, or in the earth, at its top or its bottom. ﴿Or in the heavens or in the earth﴾: or in the most hidden place of all that. ﴿Allah will bring it forth.﴾ ﴿Will bring it forth﴾: what is the one that dropped the *yā'*?

**Student:** The answer to the condition.

**Shaykh:** Because it is the answer to the condition in His saying ﴿if it is﴾. ﴿In﴾ is conditional, and ﴿taku﴾ is a present-tense verb in the jussive (*jazm*), governed by the conditional *in*, and its sign of jussive is the sukun on the deleted *nūn*, for lightness.

**Students:** The letter of weakness was dropped.

**Shaykh:** ﴿In taku﴾, so its sign of jussive is the sukun on the deleted *nūn*, for lightness. And His saying ﴿yati﴾ is the answer to the condition, in the jussive governed by *in*, and its sign of jussive is the deletion of the *yā'* (...).

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** (...), the deletion of the *nūn*. Its original form is *in takun*, this is its original form.

He said: ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾, so He will call it to account for it. This is of the most hidden things, and yet He said ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾, and He did not say "Allah will know it," because bringing it forth necessarily entails knowing it, but bringing forth is more emphatic. Allah, glorified and exalted, brings it forth and recompenses for it.

﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle﴾ in extracting it, ﴿Acquainted﴾ with its place. The author always restricts the general meaning according to the context, but what is known among the scholars is that the consideration is the generality of the wording. Here He said ﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle and Acquainted﴾, and He made subtlety here to be in extracting it and knowledge of its place. The correct view is that it is more general than that, for *al-Latīf* (the Subtle) is one of the names of Allah. Ibn al-Qayyim said:

*"He is Al-Latīf toward His servant, and to His servant..."* ∗∗∗ ........................

So Allah, exalted, is Subtle toward His servant and Subtle to His servant.

*"......................... ∗∗∗ and subtlety in His attributes is of two kinds."*

The first subtlety: perceiving the secrets of affairs and their hidden aspects. The second: subtlety at the points of benevolence, which is kindness to the servant, meaning He treats him gently by providing him with benevolence and warding off harm of which he is unaware. So *laṭīf* is transitive with *bi* and transitive with *lām*. If it is transitive with *bi*, it means knowledge of hidden affairs; and if it is transitive with *lām*, *laṭīf lahum*, it means benevolence by bringing about what is desired and warding off what is disliked or feared. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾ [Yūsuf 100]. Who said this? Yūsuf: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, meaning, from His subtlety is that He facilitated your reunion after separation. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾.

So the upshot is that *al-Latīf* is one of His names, and it has two meanings according to what it is transitive with: if transitive with *lām*, ﴿Subtle in what He wills﴾, its meaning is benevolence; and if transitive with *bi*, its meaning is knowledge of hidden things. He is Subtle because of the perfection of His knowledge; everything is known to Him. There is a third meaning, but does it apply to the attributes of Allah or not? *Laṭīf* among people is the delicate one; they say "so-and-so is *laṭīf*," meaning gentle, of good character.

In my view, this is included in our saying ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, because it is transitive with *lām*, meaning benevolence. Benevolence is more specific than good character, more specific, because it includes bestowing favour upon the one to whom one is gentle.

As for His saying ﴿Acquainted﴾: *al-Khabīr* is the All-Knowing of inner realities. It accompanies *al-Latīf* as an emphasis of it. We said that knowledge of inner realities is *khibra*, taken from *al-khibār*, meaning soft ground into which seeds are sown and buried. So He is Acquainted, glorified and exalted, knowing the inner realities of affairs.

Among its lessons: this grain of mustard seed that may be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** ﴿Will bring it forth﴾ means that it cannot escape Him or flee from Him. He must bring it forth and call it to account for it, or bring it forth to demonstrate His power over it.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** The meaning is if it is an evil deed. Now the author says that it is in the matter of a single act. ﴿If it is the weight of a mustard seed, and it were in a rock or in the heavens or in the earth﴾ [Luqmān 16], He will bring it forth.

**Student:** From the deeds.

**Shaykh:** From the deeds which are of the weight of this thing.

* * *

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Luqmān 17]. These are four commands. ﴿O my son, establish prayer.﴾ Note that the first was prohibitions: ﴿O my son, do not associate others with Allah. Indeed, association is a great wrong﴾ [Luqmān 13], a prohibition. Then a warning in His saying ﴿if it is the weight of a mustard seed﴾, then after that a command: ﴿O my son, establish prayer.﴾ Hence it is said: clearing comes before adorning, meaning: remove the impurities, then bring the perfecting elements. So His saying here ﴿O my son, establish prayer﴾ is a command to establish prayer. Establishing it means that a person performs it complete with its pillars, conditions, obligations, and complements. His saying ﴿prayer﴾ includes both obligatory and voluntary prayers.

﴿And enjoin what is right﴾: enjoin what is right. Where is the object of *"enjoin"*? It is omitted; the implied meaning: people or others. Enjoin others to what is right, that is, with righteous speech and righteous action. *Al-ma'rūf* is what the Sharī'ah has commanded; this is *al-ma'rūf*, because what the Sharī'ah has commanded has been affirmed by the Sharī'ah and affirmed by sound natural disposition. So *al-ma'rūf* is then everything that has been commanded by the Sharī'ah, is that so? *Al-ma'rūf* is everything the Sharī'ah has commanded, whether it relates to the right of Allah or the rights of the servants.

And His saying ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾: *al-munkar* is everything the Sharī'ah has disapproved of, that is, forbidden, whether it relates to the right of Allah or the rights of the servants.

Is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong an individual obligation (*fard 'ayn*) or a communal obligation (*fard kifāya*)? It is a communal obligation, because of His saying: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 104]. If we take *min* (from) as partitive, that is what it is. But if we take *min* as explanatory of the category, meaning: "let you be a community that enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong," then it would be an individual obligation. But the correct view is that it is a communal obligation, because the purpose of it is the reform of others. When the reform of others is achieved by others, the purpose is achieved. But if it is not achieved, then it becomes obligatory on you to command. So if we find people neglectful and lax in this matter, it becomes an obligation upon us. But if we see that people have become upright in this and have begun to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, then it is a communal obligation upon us.

And His saying ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾: even your parents? Even your parents: you enjoin them to what is right and forbid them from what is wrong. Indeed the right of the parents is greater than the right of others, because enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a benefit to the one commanded and forbidden, not an injury. If that is so, then the ones most deserving of your kindness are your parents.

**Student:** Is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong the same as admonition, or...?

**Shaykh:** No. We mentioned previously that the meant three things: explanation and calling, command and prohibition, and change. Explanation and calling are obligatory upon everyone. Everyone must explain when the need for explanation arises or when he is asked about knowledge, and each person must convey when the situation requires it. As for commanding, it is more specific than calling, because commanding means directing a command to a specific person, not that you explain and stand among the people and say: "this is lawful, and this is unlawful." That is considered admonition. As for change, it is that you change with your hand: you take this wrong and break it, for example, or you say with your tongue if you are unable to act, you change with the tongue, either by referring the matter to someone who can change it, or by rebuking, reproaching, and restraining until it is achieved. If you cannot do this or that, then change is with the heart, which is disapproval and hatred. In reality, this does not bring about complete change, meaning that if you disapprove of the wrong in your heart it does not disappear. But this is the lowest degree of change. Hence the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: *"And that is the weakest of faith."*[[Reported by Muslim (49/78) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, it is not possible.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** No, it is not that it is forbidden in itself. That is, if there is for example something whereby, if we forbid the wrong (...). And this is a condition for every obligation, because of His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾.

Among the conditions also: that one not fear a certain harm. If he fears harm to his wealth or body, it does not oblige him. If he fears harassment, is it obligatory or not? If he fears harassment, it is obligatory, because there must be some harm, but harassment that does not involve damage. Hence He said: ﴿and bear patiently what befalls you﴾. This is a preparation and introduction, as if He is saying to him: if you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, harm will necessarily befall you, so be patient with it. This is what happens in reality: the one who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is usually harmed, by the one commanded and forbidden, either by words, or by mockery, and sometimes the situation reaches the point where he is pelted with stones, and sometimes the situation reaches the point where his car is wrecked or his house is broken, or something similar. But the last is harm to property, though it must be a definite harm. If it is an imagined harm, it is nothing.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** It is not, because it may harm him and it may not harm him. And He said: ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾. ﴿Indeed, that﴾ refers to what preceded of the four matters: ﴿establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you﴾ [Luqmān 17]. He said: that is, ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾, that is, the things that are required, which are determined upon because they are obligatory. ﴿Matters﴾ means affairs and circumstances, and *al-'azm* here is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, that is, the things resolved upon, which are determined upon because they are obligatory. And Allah knows best.

* * *

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them﴾ [Luqmān 15].

* Among the lessons of the verse: the prohibition of obeying the parents if they command association, because of His saying ﴿do not obey them﴾. By analogy, every act of disobedience they command, they are not to be obeyed, because of the Messenger's, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: *"There is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator."*[[Reported by Ahmad in al-Musnad (1095) from the hadith of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.]]

* And among the lessons of the noble verse: that the wickedness and disbelief of the parents do not cancel their right to kindness. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿and accompany them in this world with kindness﴾, for He commanded accompanying them with kindness even though they are disbelievers and command disbelief.

* And among the lessons of the noble verse: the obligation of following the path of the believers, because of His saying ﴿and follow the way of one who turns to Me﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers, We will leave him in what he has taken and drive him into Hell, and evil it is as a destination﴾ [al-Nisā' 115].

* And among the lessons of the noble verse: that all creatures, believers and disbelievers, will return to Allah, because of His saying: ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾.

* And among its lessons: that judgment among creation belongs to Allah, because of His saying ﴿to Me is your return﴾, for the placing of the predicate first indicates restriction.

* And among its lessons: Allah's comprehensive knowledge of everything, because of His saying ﴿then I will inform you of what you used to do﴾, for informing about what we did can only be from knowledge.

* And among the lessons of the noble verse: the affirmation of speech for Allah, because of His saying ﴿then I will inform you﴾, and informing is an act of telling.

* And among its lessons also: warning a person against evil deeds, for His saying ﴿then I will inform you﴾ indicates warning, so that we do not fall into a matter that Allah has forbidden us.

* And among the lessons of the noble verse also: the reaching of the utmost limit of eloquence in the Noble Qur'an, because of His saying ﴿then I will inform you﴾ and not "then I will recompense you." That is because a person may be informed on the Day of Resurrection of what he did, and then be forgiven. So Allah mentioned informing because it is emphatic. As for recompense, Allah, exalted, may pardon the sinner without (...).

Can it be derived from the noble verse the obligation of obeying parents in what is not disobedience to Allah? From where does the obligation of obeying them come?

**Student:** Because He only forbade association.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but He forbade obeying them.

**Student:** He forbade obeying them, not in association.

**Shaykh:** Yes, so He forbade obedience, He did not forbid obedience. So from where do we know that it is obligatory?

**Student:** ﴿Accompany them in this world with kindness﴾.

**Shaykh:** His saying ﴿accompany them in this world with kindness﴾, meaning, originally the discussion is whether it is derived from the noble verse.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** In any case, if they command something other than disobedience, the verse is silent about that. It forbade obedience in disobedience, and was silent about everything else. But it may be said: His saying ﴿and accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ indicates the obligation of obeying them in what is not disobedience, because there is no doubt that among accompanying them with kindness is carrying out their command. On this basis, one may derive from the general wording of His saying ﴿and accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ the obligation of obeying them in what is not disobedience. But it has been mentioned previously during the exegesis that Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said: obedience to them is obligatory in what benefits them and does not harm him. As for what harms him, obedience is not obligatory for him. Hence, when the scholars mentioned that a father may take from his child's wealth whatever he wishes, they said: on condition that it does not harm the child. If it harms the child, he may not take it. Rather, they said: on condition that it does not harm him, and that his need for it is not connected to it. If his need is connected to it, he may not take it.

**Student:** His need is connected.

**Shaykh:** No, his specific need, meaning, for example, he does not find another, nor for example a need, everything he needs. But for example a vessel he needs (...). But a concubine he needs, we do not say to the father that he may take her, because that would deprive the son of his need and enjoyment of her.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, but without the verse.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, without the verse... from other evidences.

**Student:** (...) ﴿When they said to their people: "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship besides Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever"﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 4].

**Shaykh:** Yes, all of this contradicts (...), because accompanying them with kindness does not mean that you show them love and loyalty. Rather you hate what they are upon of disbelief and association, and you hate them for these attributes they have acquired, but you give them what is due to them.

**Student:** By smiling in their faces, by cheerfulness toward them, with the kindness that people are accustomed to.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but this is not caused by religion. It is not caused by religion that (...) from his religion. This is a matter demanded by natural disposition, while enmity and hatred are in the heart, and disbelief, because enmity is the opposite of loyalty.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, nothing prevents this (...), but we do not harm them, meaning that we (...), and similar things.

Then it is also said: every situation has its speech. For example, if the parents or others boast of disbelief and take pride in it, then we may declare this disavowal, enmity, and hatred. If they are silent and peaceful, we do not confront them, but we disavow in a general way what they are upon of religion. The important thing is that Allah says: ﴿accompany them in this world﴾. But as for what concerns religion, do not accompany them with kindness at all. In matters of religion, you must dislike them, keep away from them, and oppose them.

* * *

Then the Exalted said, in the remaining part of Luqman's counsel: ﴿O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or in the heavens or on the earth, Allah will bring it forth﴾ [Luqman 16] and so on to the end. In this counsel there is a benefit, which is warning the son against disobedience; by His saying: ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾, so nothing escapes Him and nothing eludes Him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, the completeness of His power. From where do we derive the generality? From His saying: ﴿or within a rock or in the heavens or on the earth﴾, and what is manifest on the earth, and what is in the desert, is so by greater right. Thus there is derived from it the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge and His encompassing of all things, and also the completeness of His power, by His bringing it forth.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of these two names from the names of Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, Acquainted﴾ (al-Latif, al-Khabir), and the affirmation of the attributes they contain.
* Among its benefits: that the heavens are multiple, by His saying: ﴿or in the heavens﴾. Their number is known, and they are seven. As for the earth, it is not mentioned in the plural in the Qur'an; everything in the Qur'an that mentions the earth does so in the singular. However, Allah the Exalted indicated that it is plural in His saying: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. His saying ﴿the like thereof﴾ means likeness in number, since likeness in modality is impossible, so it necessarily means likeness in number only.

* * *

Then the Exalted said, from the rest of Luqman's counsels: ﴿O my son, establish prayer and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you﴾ [Luqman 17].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: fathers should counsel their sons with these four qualities (...).
Because ﴿'azm﴾ (resolve) means "that which is resolved upon," i.e., obligatory, and ﴿al-umur﴾ means affairs.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the father should combine his admonition to his son with encouragement and warning, for His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve﴾ is an emphasis, and it is a duty upon the son to carry out these four counsels.

* Student: (...) In Surah al-Shura: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring resolve﴾. This (...) what is feared (...) in the decree and predestination of Allah, what agrees?
* The Shaykh: It needs reflection.
* Student: Gentleness, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Yes, we have taken this before, from all the counsels. ﴿O my son﴾: from it is derived the gentleness of a person in addressing his son, especially in the context of admonition. Following from this is also the explanation of the poor treatment by some fathers: when they want to admonish their son, they deal with him by violence and harshness, and this is an error. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah gives through gentleness what He does not give through violence"[[Narrated by Muslim (2593/77) from 'Aishah radiyallahu 'anha, with the wording: "and He gives for gentleness what He does not give for violence."]]. When you act upon this, you will deal gently, for the Messenger informed that Allah gives through gentleness what He does not give through violence. If your aim is achieved through violence, its achievement through gentleness is by greater right. Accordingly, gentleness is to be practised in matters, especially in the context of admonishing those sons who do not comprehend what they are upon. As for the obstinate and the arrogant, they have a different state; but our discussion is in the context of da'wah and in the context of guidance and instruction, where gentleness and avoiding violence is to be preferred.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Each one... until upon... yes.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is not constant. ﴿So when you are secure, establish prayer. Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾ [al-Nisa' 103]. ﴿Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand devoutly before Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 238]. It is not constant.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people﴾. This is conjoined to His saying: ﴿establish prayer﴾, so it is among Luqman's counsels to his son. ﴿And do not turn your cheek﴾, and in one reading ﴿and do not turn away﴾ (wa la tusa'ir), ﴿toward people﴾. The author says: (Do not turn your face away from them out of arrogance). Ta'sir is inclination, and from it is "sa'r fi al-wajh" (a twisting of the face), which is inclination, such that the neck is twisted, leaning either to the right or to the left.
And His saying ﴿khaddaka﴾ means your face; it is the mention of a part to mean the whole. The author's words "out of arrogance": yes, this is the object of the prohibition, that one does it by way of arrogance. As for if one does it by way of turning away from what it is not permissible to look at, such as when a woman meets you and you turn away and avoid her, this does not fall under the verse; for this reason He said: ﴿And do not turn your cheek toward people﴾. But if I turn my face or my cheek so that I do not see something forbidden, this does not fall under this verse.
As for His saying ﴿And do not turn your cheek toward people﴾: is the lam here for specification as in its original sense, or is it in the meaning of "from" (ʿan)?
* Students: "From."
* The Shaykh: ﴿Do not turn your cheek toward people﴾ means "away from them," but forbidden when out of arrogance. His saying ﴿lin-nas﴾ (toward people) is general, including the believer and the disbeliever; but the disbeliever is not treated in such matters as the believer is treated. It may be said that our law has come with something different, and that the disbeliever may be turned away from and avoided. It may also be said that if a disbeliever approaches you, face him, for this is from the reconciliation (ta'lif) toward Islam; but if he turns away, then turn away from him.
﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: He said ﴿wa la tamshi﴾ is jussive by deletion of the yā'. ﴿fi al-ard﴾ means upon the earth. ﴿Marhan﴾: the author said: (i.e., with pride). Marah means insolence and haughtiness, and khuyala (self-conceit) is of this kind. So do not walk arrogantly in your gait, exalting yourself in your soul; rather walk the walk of one who humbles himself and submits to Allah the Exalted, not one who exalts himself over the servants of Allah.
And His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾. Here He mentioned ﴿do not turn your cheek toward people and do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. The first concerns the treatment of people ﴿do not turn your cheek toward people﴾, and the second concerns his bearing in himself, that he not walk upon the earth exultantly, but walk as the servants of the Most Merciful walk: ﴿those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾.
﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every self-deluded boaster﴾: ﴿mukhtal﴾ is one who walks arrogantly in his gait; ﴿fakhur﴾ is one who boasts over people. ﴿Mukhtal﴾ means one who practises khuyala, and ﴿fakhur﴾ means one who takes pride in himself. The difference between them is that self-deluded pride is in the self, and boasting is in speech. This man has self-conceit within himself and arrogance over the servants of Allah, and he has boasting in his tongue, taking pride in himself and saying: "I am so-and-so son of so-and-so," and praising himself. But this, as stated in the benefits, is not so in war; if it is in war, there is no harm in a person boasting, as the Prophet ﷺ said:
"I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib."
And he saw one of his companions walking with a proud swagger, and said: "Indeed this is a walk that Allah dislikes except in this situation"[[Narrated by al-Tabarani (6508) from the hadith of Khalid ibn Sinan ibn Kharasha, from his father, from his grandfather.]]. So in the context of war it is permissible for a person to boast, and it is permissible for him to magnify himself within, because he stands before the enemies of Allah whom it is fitting to humiliate.
﴿And be moderate in your pace﴾: be moderate in it between plodding and hastening, and let there be tranquillity upon you. ﴿And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice﴾. The author (...): (﴿lower﴾: reduce ﴿your voice; indeed, the most disagreeable of voices﴾: the most repugnant ﴿is the voice of donkeys﴾: its beginning is an exhalation and its end is an inhalation).
﴿Be moderate in your pace﴾: qasd means the middle in affairs; the middle in affairs means that a person is moderate in his walk, between one who walks hurriedly and one who walks slowly. Moderation in everything is the middle; for this reason it is reported in the transmitted supplication: "And I ask You for moderation in poverty and in wealth"[[Narrated by al-Nasa'i (1305) from the hadith of 'Ammar ibn Yasir.]]. The meaning of (qasd) is moderation in affairs: ﴿those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but between that is a moderate stance﴾ [al-Furqan 67].
And His saying ﴿and be moderate in your pace﴾: be moderate in it between plodding and hastening, with tranquillity and dignity upon you; that is, do not plod as you walk, nor hasten in a way that undermines manliness; rather let your walk be moderate between these, showing strength and vitality, as the Messenger ﷺ used to do in his walk.
﴿And lower your voice﴾: ﴿min﴾ here is for partiality. He did not say "lower your voice" but "from it" (min sawtika). This is because a person is not praised for raising his voice excessively nor for lowering it excessively. Among people there is one whose voice is loud, so that when he speaks it is as though he is addressing a group far away; and among people there is the opposite, who speaks to you, and perhaps you understand from him only word after word. All of this is not good; for this reason He said ﴿lower from your voice﴾ and did not say "lower it entirely." So neither this nor that is to be done, but rather moderation between raising the voice and lowering it.
And His saying ﴿lower from your voice﴾: is the intended meaning during address? Yes, during address. Then ﴿min﴾ here conveys partiality in manner and likewise in quantity. Sometimes it is better that you raise your voice, is it not so? Suppose you are calling a people far-flung, wanting to urge them to fight or the like; raising the voice is permissible, or not? It is permissible; for this reason al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, in the sound hadith, when the people dispersed, the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to call out, and he cried with his highest voice: "O people of the tree! O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!"[[Narrated by al-Humaydi in his Musnad (464) from al-'Abbas radiyallahu 'anhu; the wording is: "O companions of the samurah, O companions of Surat al-Baqarah."]] with his highest voice. There is no doubt that this is not lowering the voice; for Allah the Exalted says ﴿lower from your voice﴾. So lowering the voice is in terms of quantity and in terms of manner. How so? We say: if you are addressing someone beside you, do not raise your voice, nor lower it so that he cannot hear; this is in terms of manner. In terms of quantity, meaning sometimes you may be compelled to raise your voice; for this reason He said ﴿lower from your voice﴾, meaning sometimes. But at some times the situation demands that you raise your voice to the extent that it makes you heard.
Then the Exalted explained, or it may be from Luqman's words, because His saying ﴿indeed the most repugnant﴾ may be from Luqman's words, since that is the original; and it may be from the words of Allah, with which Allah concluded the verse.
And His saying ﴿indeed the most repugnant of voices﴾ is a justification for His saying ﴿lower from your voice﴾. ﴿The most repugnant of voices﴾ means the most ugly and hideous, not the loudest; for among animals there is one with a louder voice than the donkey, but in ugliness there is nothing uglier than the donkey's voice. And His saying ﴿the most repugnant of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾: this sentence is emphasized with two emphatics, namely ʾinna (indeed) and the lam; and the reason for this is what the author mentioned, that its beginning is a zafir and its end is a shahiq. How so? What is the difference between zafir and shahiq? What is it?
* Student: The zafir is the expulsion of air, and the shahiq...
* The Shaykh: Yes, the shahiq is inward in the chest, and the zafir is outward; for this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring (zafir)﴾ [al-Furqan 12].
* Student: ﴿For them therein is zafir and shahiq﴾.
* The Shaykh: And likewise the second verse: ﴿For them therein is zafir and shahiq﴾; this is in regard to its inhabitants. And in another verse He said: ﴿They hear from it shahiq while it boils﴾. So Allah the Exalted mentioned for the Fire zafir and shahiq, just as for its dwellers there is also zafir and shahiq; we seek refuge in Allah from it.
He said: ﴿Indeed the most repugnant of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾. The beneficial counsels that are from the wisdom Allah gave to Luqman have ended.
Then Allah the Exalted said, affirming what Allah has bestowed upon His servants: ﴿Have you not seen﴾, that is, know, O you addressed, ﴿that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens﴾, such as the sun, the moon and the stars, for you to benefit from them, ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾, such as fruits, rivers and animals. ﴿And has completed for you His favors, apparent and hidden﴾: ﴿asbagha﴾ means made abundant and complete. ﴿Apparent﴾ is soundness of form, the proper proportion of limbs, and other things. ﴿And hidden﴾ is knowledge and other things. In this verse Allah establishes what He has bestowed upon the servants, saying: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. I said "establishes" because when the interrogative hamzah enters upon "lam," it conveys affirmation, so the present verb becomes a past in meaning, emphasized with "qad." For example, ﴿Have you not seen﴾ means "you have indeed seen." ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ means "We have indeed expanded for you your breast." So the meaning is affirmation; and for this reason in the Surah "Alam Nashrah," Allah said: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾, followed by? ﴿And We removed﴾, thus joining a past verb to what precedes it, since what precedes it has the meaning of a past verb.
And His saying ﴿that Allah has subjected for you﴾: ﴿sakhkhara﴾ means made subservient; He made them subservient to you, or for your interests and benefits. ﴿Whatever is in the heavens﴾: the author says: from the sun, the moon and the stars. This is by way of example; otherwise He has also subjected to us the winds, which are between heaven and earth, and subjected to us the clouds, as Allah said: ﴿and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾, and they are for us. So it is general for all that Allah has subjected for our interests.
﴿And whatever is on the earth﴾: from fruits, rivers and animals, and others as well; even minerals and the like, Allah has subjected them to us and made them subservient to us. So all that is on the earth is subjected and made subservient, but some of it is subjected by its nature, and some by means. Iron, minerals and the like are subjected but by means; animals, rivers and trees are subjected without intermediary, the human finds them prepared in full.
And His saying ﴿asbagha﴾: the author explained it with two meanings, expansion and completion; that is, made abundant and complete. From it comes: "ishbagh al-wudu' 'ala al-makarih" (completing the ablution despite hardships), meaning completing the ablution. So the meaning of "asbagha" is made abundant and complete. As for "complete," its example is what I mentioned: completing the ablution despite hardships; and as for "abundant," from it is His saying: ﴿that make full coats of mail﴾ (sabighat), that is, wide coats of mail; and also the saying "thawb sabigh," meaning wide garment. It also includes completion. The point is that ishbagh encompasses two things: completing a thing, and providing it abundantly. The favors Allah has bestowed upon us encompass both, so they are abundant ﴿and if you were to count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾, and they are also complete, lacking no deficiency; everything a person needs in his life, and indeed everything he needs in his religion, Allah the Exalted has perfected, and praise be to Allah.
And His saying ﴿apparent and hidden﴾: the author explained apparent as the sensory and evident, and hidden as knowledge and other things.
* Student: It is the known (al-ma'ruf).
* The Shaykh: No, knowledge is knowledge, and that is the apparent. Allah made the favors apparent and hidden: apparent to the eyes; the author mentioned among their examples beauty of form, soundness of character, and the like. As for the hidden, he says: "it is knowledge," because it is unknown in the heart. This is undoubtedly a very deficient explanation, and the apparent is more general...
* Student: He says: al-ma'rufah (the known).

The Shaykh: The knowledge of [blessings] is not just knowledge in the heart. The correct view is that it is more general than that. Blessings are either apparent to everyone, or hidden and not recognized by everyone. That is one division. Another is that a blessing may be apparent, so that everyone knows it is a blessing, or hidden, so that a person only recognizes it as a blessing through its effects. Some things, when they happen, do not seem to be blessings, but when their effects become known, one finds that they are blessings. This is like the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:216]. A person may be afflicted by something decreed by Allah and not see it as a blessing until he learns its effects later. The main point is that blessings, praise be to Allah, are either clear and evident to the eye and general and encompassing of all creation, or hidden and known only to the one upon whom Allah has bestowed them. Likewise, something may be clearly a blessing, or something hidden may not become clear as a blessing until later (...).

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt, nor walk arrogantly upon the earth. Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [Luqman 31:18].

From this noble verse it is derived: the condemnation of these two traits, turning the cheek away from people out of arrogance and self-importance, and walking proudly on the earth. Other verses show that both are among the prohibited acts, as in Surah al-Isra.

Also derived from this verse: when a person speaks with others, he should face them with his face, because the prohibition of turning the cheek away indicates the command of its opposite, which is facing the person directly.

It is also derived: when walking, one should be as Allah, mighty and majestic, said afterward: ﴿And be moderate in your walk and lower your voice﴾ [Luqman 31:19].

Among the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation that Allah loves, from His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ The point of evidence is that the negation of Allah's love for these people indicates its affirmation for others.

Among the benefits of this noble verse is the prohibition of ikhtiyal (self-conceit) and fakhr (boasting), because Allah negated His love for one who does them. The difference between ikhtiyal and fakhr has already been explained: fakhr is by speech, and ikhtiyal is by action.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And be moderate in your walk and lower your voice﴾.

From this noble verse it is derived: a person should walk moderately, neither with a harmful haste nor with a slow, crawling pace. Hurrying that involves recklessness, rush, and frivolity is blameworthy, and slowness and dragging the feet are also blameworthy. Thus it is derived that a person should walk in a moderate manner between hurrying and dawdling.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And be moderate in your walk and lower your voice﴾ [Luqman 31:19].

From this noble verse it is derived: a person should walk moderately, neither with a harmful haste nor with a slow, crawling pace. Hurrying that involves recklessness, rush, and frivolity is blameworthy, and slowness and dragging the feet are also blameworthy. Thus it is derived that a person should walk in a moderate manner between hurrying and dawdling.

Also among its benefits: it may be said that if this applies to physical walking, then likewise it applies to the walking of moral and ethical conduct.
