He related this to us so that we might be warned and fear, and so that we would not remain silent about one we see altering and corrupting the earth. Here He related to us the story of Luqman so that we might take lessons from these wisdoms and follow his example in advising our children and families.

* * *

Then, mighty and majestic, He said: ﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾ [Luqman 31:20].

﴿Among the people﴾: this ﴿min﴾ is for partitive meaning. The grammarians have differed over the partitive (min): is it a noun, meaning "some," or is it a particle indicating this meaning?

Upon this difference the difference in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is built. If we say min is a noun meaning "some," we say: min is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿who argues﴾ is its predicate. If we say it is a particle, we say: min is a preposition, and the prepositional phrase is related to an omitted predicate that comes first, and ﴿who argues﴾ is a postponed subject.

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾.

﴿And among the people﴾: the author said: (i.e., the people of Makkah). This is based on his principle, may Allah have mercy on him, that in all the Meccan surahs, generality in such a context is to be understood as what? As specificity: the people of Makkah.

The correct view is that this is general. That is, ﴿among the people﴾ includes the people of Makkah and others.

﴿who argues about Allah without knowledge﴾: al-mujadalah (argument) is derived from al-jadl, which is twisting a rope to strengthen it. From this comes the word jadaʾil (the braids) of a woman, meaning the twisting and tightening of her hair. This is its linguistic meaning.

But in technical usage, al-mujadalah is contention, meaning that each of the two debaters strengthens his proof in order to defeat his opponent. So it is the strengthening of proof to refute and defeat the opponent. This is argument: strengthening proof to refute the opponent and render him helpless.

If argument is with knowledge and wisdom, it is praiseworthy without doubt, and it may sometimes be obligatory, as in His words: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125]. If it is without knowledge, it is blameworthy, like one who argues by presenting arguments and causes that are fabricated to defeat his opponent and support his own view, even by falsehood. This is among the prohibited evils: ﴿And they argued with falsehood to refute thereby the truth, so I seized them﴾ [Ghafir 40:5].

﴿Among the people is one who argues about Allah﴾, he said: (i.e., the people of Makkah).

﴿who argues about Allah﴾: ﴿about Allah﴾, is the intended meaning about His essence, may He be exalted, or about His lordship, or His divinity, or His names and attributes, or His rulings and actions?

The answer: it includes all of this. Among people there is one who argues about the essence of Allah, denying the existence of Allah altogether, and arguing about His essence. Among people there is one who argues about His oneness, acknowledging Him but denying His unity. Among people there is one who argues about His divinity, that is, about His exclusive right to worship. Among people there is one who argues about His names and attributes.

The most frequent arguments among Muslims occur in the field of the names and attributes. Among Muslims there are disputes beyond those between Muslims and disbelievers. But the Muslims who ascribe themselves to Islam and are called the people of the qiblah, among them arguments about the names and attributes of Allah have multiplied.

Likewise, among people there is one who argues about the rulings of Allah. How many argue about the rulings of Allah! You find him arguing: you say, "This thing is forbidden," and then he comes and argues with you: "What forbids it? What is the difference between it and such-and-such? Bring the evidence." This evidence is refuted, this reasoning is invalid, and so on, without knowledge. But if it is with knowledge, there is no blame in it. The blame is only when it is without knowledge.

Likewise, among people there is one who argues about the actions of Allah, may Allah protect us, saying: "Why did Allah grant these disbelievers many blessings while among the Muslims there is one in severe hardship, sickness, poverty, ignorance, and similar things?" This one argues about the actions of Allah.

Likewise, one argues about the actions of Allah in the matter of qadar (divine decree). For example, he says: either Allah has decreed a person's deeds for him or He has not. If He decreed them, how does He punish him? If He did not decree them, then it means the person is independent in them, so he would be a sole agent in events and a partner with Allah in them. Other arguments like this are made without knowledge. For this reason, a person should, in matters of the Sharia and in matters of qadar, submit to what the Book and the Sunnah indicate, and not argue. If he opens for himself the door of argument, his foot will never be firm.

For this reason, Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said: rational matters have no place in matters of reported information, because if we tried to refer these matters to reason, reason might permit what is absolutely impermissible by the Sharia, just as it might forbid what is permissible. By "reason" is meant what its claimant says is reason. As for sound, clear reason, it must agree with sound transmitted text. If you wish to make this clear to yourselves, read the book of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, if you can bear it, called Dar' ta'arud al-'aql wa'l-naql, or: The Agreement of Clear Reason with Sound Transmitted Text.

The main point is that the scope of argument is wide. The discussion here is about blameworthy argument, which is argument without knowledge.

So, ﴿about Allah﴾ means: about His essence, and what else? His lordship, His divinity, His names and attributes, His rulings, His actions.

﴿without knowledge﴾ means: he has no knowledge of his own, but only obstinacy and opposition.

(﴿and without guidance﴾ from a messenger.) That is: he has no following of another to guide him. He has no knowledge within himself by which he is guided, and no knowledge from another by which he is guided. ﴿and without guidance﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 15–25 (part 5 of 6):

(﴿And there is no book giving light﴾ sent down by Allah, but rather by imitation.) He has no knowledge and no guidance from the Messenger's way, nor a book sent down by Allah from which he could be guided. So why does he dispute? He disputes with falsehood.

The author said: (by imitation), due to His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down,"﴾. This is what compelled the author to say: (but rather by imitation), because he said it based on His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down,"﴾. ﴿It is said to them﴾: ﴿it is said﴾ is in the passive voice. Who is the speaker? Allah, the Messenger, the believers; all of this is possible. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other than Him as allies﴾ [al-A'raf 3]. The Prophet ﷺ urged the Ummah to follow him, and the believers likewise call people to follow what Allah has sent down. So here the agent is omitted to indicate generality.

﴿When it is said﴾ like this? This is more general than if He had said: "When Allah says to them," or "When the Messenger says to them," or "When the believers say." So His saying ﴿when it is said﴾ is more comprehensive.

﴿Follow what Allah has sent down﴾: ﴿what﴾ is the object of ﴿follow﴾, and ﴿Allah has sent down﴾. What is meant by it? The Qur'an, undoubtedly, because Allah sent it down. The Sunnah?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, how? ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾ [an-Nisa' 113]. The scholars said: wisdom is the Sunnah.

So: ﴿what Allah has sent down﴾ includes the Qur'an and the Sunnah, because the Sunnah is revelation if Allah inspired it to His Messenger; otherwise, His approval of it is equivalent to revelation. For this reason the scholars said: the Prophet's ﷺ approval is equivalent to his saying.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾. ﴿Rather﴾ is it for annulling (idrab ibtal) or for transition (idrab intiqal)? For annulling: meaning, "Rather, we do not follow what Allah has sent down, but we follow what we found our fathers upon." This is opposing truth with falsehood, because they have now turned away from what Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent down to mere opinions and desires.

﴿What we found our fathers upon﴾, even if it was shirk? Even if it was shirk. Well, even if it was obedience? We say: yes, they say: even if it was obedience. So their following what their fathers were upon is not because it is sharia, but because their fathers were upon it. In that case, their following their fathers in this state is neither following the sharia nor praiseworthy following.

Based on this, we say: concerning one who is called to the Book and the Sunnah and says, "I want to follow such-and-such imam or such-and-such scholar," despite the Sunnah being clear and manifest, is he resembling these polytheists? Yes, he resembles them.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Even though Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ [Luqman 21]. ﴿Even though﴾: this is an interrogative followed by a conjunction particle. We have mentioned many times before that when a conjunction particle follows the interrogative, there are two opinions regarding its i'rab (grammatical analysis):

The first: the interrogative hamza entered upon an omitted element, and what follows the conjunction particle is coordinated with it. This omitted element is estimated according to context. On this view, the interrogative hamza is in its proper place, and the thing asked about (i.e., what the interrogative governs) is omitted.

The second: the waw is a conjunction particle, the element it coordinates with is what came before, and the position of the hamza is after the conjunction particle.

We said that this is easier than the first. The first is more eloquent in terms of rules, but this is easier, and its ease is that with the first, a person may not know what to estimate, and sometimes it is difficult to estimate something appropriate. As for this one, nothing needs to be estimated; you say: it is coordinated with what came before.

As for the author, which of the two opinions did he follow? (﴿Do they follow them?﴾ ﴿"Even though Satan﴾ ... ?) He followed the first: that the interrogative particle entered upon an omitted thing, and the conjunction particle coordinates with that omitted thing.

﴿Even though Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ (i.e., its causes. No).

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: Do they follow their fathers rather than what Allah has sent down, even in this state, namely that Satan is calling them? Is he calling the fathers, or calling these? I think it includes both these and the fathers.

﴿To the punishment of the Blaze﴾: meaning, to what necessitates the punishment of the Blaze, such as deeds of shirk, disbelief, and others. The interrogative: the apparent meaning of the author's words is that it is for denial and negation, based on his saying: (No). But for negation there is a problem, because there is no doubt that they are following him. As for denial, yes: Allah the Mighty and Majestic denounced them for following their fathers while Satan calls them to the punishment of the Blaze.

His saying: ﴿punishment of the Blaze﴾ is the punishment of Hell, and it is idafa to (...).

His words: (﴿"To Allah while he is a muhsin"﴾ monotheist ﴿"he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold"﴾).

(Whoever) here is conditional; its answer is His saying: ﴿he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾, and the answer is joined with the fa' because it is connected with (qad). The answer is joined with the fa' when it is one of six matters:

Nominal, imperative, and rigid ...
and with "mā," "qad," "lan," and with the future marker (tanfis), seven.

This one is connected with (qad) in an answer, so it must be joined with the fa'.

His saying: ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ means: he submits completely to Him, to the extent of surrendering himself to Him, and this is the utmost of humility and reliance.

﴿Submits his face to Allah﴾: He did not say "for Allah," because ﴿to Allah﴾ is more eloquent; as if he gave himself to Allah the Mighty and Majestic and reached his goal in arriving at Allah.

His saying: ﴿his face﴾: what is meant by his face? Is it the face of his heart or the face of his body? What is meant is the face of his heart; that is, his orientation, so it is from the direction (wijha), i.e., one who turns toward Allah intentionally, with reliance and dependence.

His saying: ﴿while he is a muhsin﴾: this clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (yuslim), meaning: while he is a muhsin. The author says that ihsan means tawhid, but the correct view differs from his words, because tawhid is understood from His saying: ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾. Rather, His saying ﴿while he is a muhsin﴾ means: a muhsin in following the Sharia, a muhsin in following His Sharia, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus the verse alludes to the two fundamental rulings of worship: sincerity (ikhlas) and following (mutaba'a).

His saying: ﴿while he is a muhsin﴾: in what? In following the Sharia; that is, following His Sharia in the manner of ihsan.

﴿He has grasped the handhold﴾: ﴿istamsaka﴾ means "tamassaka," but it came in this form istaf'ala for emphasis, i.e., for emphasis in holding fast, because "istamsaka bi-kadha" is stronger than "tamassaka bihi," since they say that an increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning; so when the letters of istamsaka increased, it became stronger in meaning than tamassaka.

His saying: ﴿with the most trustworthy handhold﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿with the most trustworthy handhold﴾ with the most secure end, which is not feared to break).

The handhold: when a person holds a rope, sometimes he holds it at its end with no loop; sometimes he holds it at its end when it is knotted; sometimes he holds its end when it is folded like a loop. Which is more eloquent? The loop is more eloquent, because when a person holds the end, he may slip and fall; likewise, the end taken is not as firm as when it is a loop.

﴿The most trustworthy﴾ is the feminine of ﴿awthaq﴾, meaning the handhold that is the most trustworthy thing. There is no doubt that whoever submits his face to Allah while being a muhsin will be saved from every hardship and attain every desired goal, because this is the ideal path that leads to Allah the Mighty and Majestic: that you submit your face to Him while you are a muhsin. Has the like of "grasped the most trustworthy handhold" appeared in the Qur'an?
﴿Whoever disbelieves in false deities and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah 256].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is: his persistence when he has tied its end (...).

﴿And to Allah is the outcome of matters﴾. When He explained that the one who submits his face to Allah while being a muhsin has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, and that the human being in the state of Islam toward Allah and ihsan may be beset by matters that make him doubt whether he holds the most trustworthy handhold or not, such as victory being delayed on some day and the like, and so he fears he may be upon something other than truth, Allah the Exalted explained that the outcome of matters belongs to Allah. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah will surely support whoever supports Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Exalted in Might. Those who, if We give them authority in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the outcome of matters﴾ [al-Hajj 40–41]. Because a person may say: what is the value of these things compared to bombs and missiles and the like? So Allah the Exalted explained that the outcome belongs to whom? The outcome of matters belongs to Allah. So as long as you have taken the means of victory that Allah has shown you, let not the material strength given to the enemies of Allah deceive you, because this material strength shrinks before a word from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. When He wills to sink them all into the earth or ruin their equipment, He says "Be," and it is. For this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of matters﴾ [al-Hajj 41], so that a person does not consider Allah's victory unlikely because of the strength given to His enemies, since the outcome belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Likewise, so that the human being submits his face to Allah while being a muhsin, and sometimes doubts overtake him: is he upon truth or not, and is this true holding or not? Allah the Exalted explained that the outcome of matters is to Allah, and that whenever you submit your face to Allah while being a muhsin, you will certainly be saved.

His saying: ﴿And to Allah is the outcome of matters﴾: ﴿ilā﴾ indicates what? What is its meaning? It indicates the end point: the end of the outcome of matters is to Allah and not to other than Him. He is the One who manages matters as He wills, until they reach what He desires, the Exalted.

His saying: ﴿al-umūr﴾ is the plural of amr (matter). The matters, all affairs, religious and worldly, general and specific, all their outcome is to Allah. This is one category of people: those who submit their face to Allah while being a muhsin.

The second: the disbeliever. He said: (﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿his disbelief﴾: do not be concerned with his disbelief, ﴿to Us is their return﴾) and so on.

He said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not grieve you﴾: (whoever) here is conditional, the conditional verb is ﴿disbelieves﴾, and its answer is His saying: ﴿then let not grieve you﴾, and it is joined with the fa' because the clause is nominal: ﴿then let not grieve you﴾.

His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ is general, covering relatives and non-relatives, because the Messenger ﷺ grieves over the disbelief of disbelievers, whether they are his relatives or not.

His saying: ﴿then let not grieve you﴾ (O Muhammad): the author, may Allah have mercy on him, made clear that the address in His saying ﴿then let not grieve you﴾ is to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ. It may also be directed to the Messenger ﷺ and to everyone whose address is valid and whose nature is to grieve when the servants of Allah disbelieve. So in this meaning it is more general than what the author said.

His saying: ﴿then let not grieve you his disbelief﴾: what is grief? Grief is the opposite of joy. When it is said "grief and fear," grief refers to the past and fear to the future. Grief may also be used for fear, as in His saying: ﴿When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us"﴾ [at-Tawbah 40], meaning: ﴿do not grieve﴾, i.e., do not fear, for Allah is with us. However, it is possible that the meaning of ﴿do not grieve﴾ is over what we did in going to this cave, so it stays on its original sense.

His saying: ﴿then let not grieve you﴾: the author said: (do not be concerned with his disbelief). The apparent meaning of his words is that grief here means concern with something, i.e., let not their affair concern you. But grief is more specific than concern. So keeping the verse on its apparent meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ grieves when people disbelieve, and likewise whoever is sincere to Allah and His Messenger grieves when people disbelieve. Or rather, taking it on its apparent meaning is more preferable.

Indeed, the sincere person grieves when people disbelieve, for two reasons:
First: mercy on those who disbelieve. Second: grief over what Islam has lost of its numerous followers, because the multitude of Islam's followers is a might for Islam, is it not so? What is the evidence that multitude is might?
* Student: The saying of the Messenger (...).
* Shaykh: And from the Qur'an? Is there in the Qur'an two verses showing that multitude is might?
* Student: The verse in al-Anfal.
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps in al-Anfal there is: ﴿And had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost courage﴾ [al-Anfal 43]; perhaps this indicates it.

Shu'ayb said to his people: ﴿And remember when you were few and He increased you﴾ [al-A'raf 86], and Allah the Exalted, reminding the Children of Israel of favor: ﴿And We made you more in number, greater in manpower﴾ [al-Isra' 6]. So multitude is might by both legislative and empirical evidence.

Now communist China, in terms of industrial strength, cannot be compared with Russia or America, and yet they fear it. Why do they fear it? Because of its multitude, as the saying goes: (...). And the enemies of the Muslims now want the Muslims to reduce their offspring: sometimes they say: if you increase offspring, provision becomes tight, like the disbelievers who kill their children for fear of poverty; sometimes they say: if children increase you will be unable to raise them, which is an ill opinion of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; and sometimes they say: if pregnancies increase, the woman weakens and weakness befalls her, and this is inevitable, the woman must weaken, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾ [Luqman 14]. The summary is that the multitude of nations is a might for them.

His saying: ﴿then let not grieve you his disbelief, to Us is their return﴾ is a declarative sentence in which the predicate was placed first to indicate restriction: ﴿to Us﴾, meaning We, Allah the Mighty and Majestic, not other than Him.

His saying: ﴿their return﴾ is a verbal noun (...), i.e., their returning, so their return is to Allah the Mighty and Majestic and not to other than Him. He is the One who will call them to account for their deeds. For this He said: ﴿then We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. ﴿We will inform them﴾: We will tell them.

When they are informed of it, are they recompensed for it? Yes: the disbeliever must be recompensed for his sin, but he is recompensed with justice; for this reason the Fire has levels according to the crimes of the disbelievers, and the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire.

So His saying ﴿We will inform them﴾ means: We will tell them, as a form of rebuke and humiliation, then We will recompense them according to what they deserve.

His saying: ﴿to Us﴾ and ﴿We will inform them﴾ is a plural pronoun, but what is meant by it?
* Student: Glorification (ta'lil).
* Shaykh: Glorification, without doubt. The meaning is the glorification [of Allah].

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [Luqman 23]: this completes the warning; that is, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts. And what are "what is within the breasts"? "What is within the breasts" are the hearts, because He said: ﴿But it is hearts that grow blind which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj 46].

So the meaning of (dhāt al-ṣudūr) is: the owners of the breasts, which are the hearts.

He said: ﴿dhāt al-ṣudūr﴾ here means the hearts, because what is inside the chest is hidden from creation and only Allah the Mighty and Majestic knows it; for this He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾.

In His saying: ﴿Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ there is evidence that the disbeliever is held accountable for the deeds of the heart, and this is so: the disbeliever is held accountable for it, because if he were not to be held accountable, His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ would have no great benefit.

* Student: His saying ﴿then let not grieve you his disbelief﴾: the second conditional's answer, is it not a request (talabiyya)?
* Shaykh: It is not a request, because (lā) is a prohibitive. Correct: ﴿then let not grieve you﴾ is a prohibition; it is not a request.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verses 15–25 (part 6 of 6):

Then He said: ﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little, then We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾ [Luqman 24]. I seek refuge in Allah. ﴿We will let them enjoy themselves﴾ means: We will make them enjoy themselves, eating what they wish, wearing what they wish, riding what they wish, dwelling where they wish, and taking pleasure in every delight of this world. But this is little, little, little. The Messenger ﷺ said: "The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it" [al-Bukhari (2892), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd]. The place of a whip is better than the world. What is the world? With all its people, from its beginning to its end, that is "the world and all that is in it." These people, and we seek refuge in Allah, enjoy themselves for a little while, and how little is the world and its enjoyment! Everything that has passed of the world up to this present hour of yours is as though it had never been, as if it were a jumble of dreams. A person may live in it as long as he lives, yet ﴿On the Day they see what they are promised, it will seem to them they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf 35]. So they enjoy themselves a little, and the littleness here is considered both in terms of the kind of enjoyment and in terms of its duration. So, the kind of enjoyment, compared to what is in the Hereafter, is it little or much?

* Students: Little.

* Shaykh: Very little, and it cannot even be compared. Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in the Hereafter except the names" [al-Bayhaqi, al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur (332)].

Likewise with regard to its duration: the duration is short, is it not? And it cannot be compared to the everlasting time of the Hereafter.

﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little﴾. Allah, exalted is He, has explained the nature of this enjoyment in another verse, when He said, glorified is His remembrance: ﴿Those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their abode﴾ [Muhammad 12]. This is the description of this enjoyment: they are slaves of desire, having no concern except the desire of the belly and the desire of the private parts, just as cattle do exactly.

He said: ﴿Then We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾ [Luqman 24]. ﴿Then﴾ means: after this little enjoyment, (﴿We will drive them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿to a harsh punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire, from which they will find no escape).

﴿We will drive them﴾ means: We will compel them. ﴿But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah 173], meaning: whoever is forced. This is originally derived from being compelled into harm, because (idtarra, "to be compelled") originally comes from nudtarru ("we compel"). Therefore, everything that compels a person is called a darurah ("necessity"), because it compels him toward that thing.

As for His saying ﴿We will drive them to a harsh punishment﴾, it is because they do not want it. They do not want the Fire, nor do they want this punishment, but they are forced into it, and we seek refuge in Allah, because they performed its causes.

As for His saying (﴿We will drive them﴾ in the Hereafter): what is meant by "the Hereafter"? Is it what comes after the Day of Resurrection, or even the grave?

* A student: Even the grave.

* Shaykh: Even the grave. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah: "Among what enters into belief in the Last Day is everything the Prophet ﷺ informed about that occurs after death. All of it is from the Last Day." So after this enjoyment they will be driven to punishment, and we seek refuge in Allah.

As for His saying ﴿We will drive them to a punishment﴾: "punishment" means chastisement. The author says "harsh" means: "it is the punishment of the Fire." What is the opposite of "harsh"? Its opposite is "gentle." The harshness of the punishment of the Fire is in its manner and in its kind, and we seek refuge in Allah.

As for its manner: Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa' 56]. And He says regarding what they are punished with: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra' 97]. And we seek refuge in Allah, this is regarding its manner.

As for its kind: it does not occur to the mind, nor can imagination grasp it. They are given to drink boiling water. When they cry for help and die of thirst, and seek relief, what are they given for relief? They are given water like molten brass, which is melted lead, and we seek refuge in Allah. It scorches the faces: when it approaches the face, it scorches the face. When it descends into the intestines, they are given boiling water which cuts their intestines to pieces. Sometimes they are given drink of pus: ﴿They gulp it down but can hardly swallow it, and death comes to him from every direction, yet he will not die, and before him is a harsh punishment﴾ [Ibrahim 17]. This punishment, and we seek refuge in Allah, with its severe, great kinds, deserves to be described as a harsh punishment, without any gentleness or kindness. Rather, it is harsh and severe.

As for His saying ﴿They will find no escape from it﴾ [al-Nisa' 121]: this is how it is in the Qur'an, meaning they will find no place of flight. ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are about to fall into it, and will find no escape from it﴾ [al-Kahf 53]. Not even this; rather, they, and we seek refuge in Allah, will come to it as thirsty herds rushing to water, and it will appear to them as a mirage. The thirsty person, when he sees water, even if it is a mirage, thinks it is water, due to his intense longing for water. So they will approach it in this manner, and we seek refuge in Allah, and they will fall into it.

﴿And if﴾: the lam of oath. ﴿If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman 25].

Regarding His saying ﴿And if﴾: he says "lam of oath" is joined with what? With the conditional ("in," "if"). Was the answer of the condition omitted, or the answer of the oath? The answer of the condition was omitted and the answer of the oath remained. Where is the answer? ﴿They would surely say, "Allah"﴾. Ibn Malik's saying has already passed us:

"When the condition and the oath come together, omit the answer of whichever is placed later, and it is what is required."

And His saying ﴿If you asked them﴾: does it mean the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or whoever may be addressed? It may be either.

﴿Who created the heavens﴾: this is the form of the question. Who created the heavens and the earth? Did al-Lat create them? Al-'Uzza? Manat? Hubal? Who?

The answer: ﴿They would surely say, "Allah"﴾. They acknowledge that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, mighty and majestic.

As for His saying ﴿They would surely say﴾: it is the answer of the oath. (The nun of the nominative was deleted because of the succession of similar letters, and the waw of the pronoun because of the meeting of two quiescent letters.) Its original form is: liyaqulunanna, correct? Because this is a present-tense verb of the "five verbs," which must include the waw and the nun. So we say: (liyaqulun), then add the emphatic nun with it: (liyaqulunanna). Now three nuns have gathered, all of them additional. Do we draw lots among them, or distinguish between them by a ruling? We distinguish between them by a ruling. We say: if we delete the nun of the nominative, the emphatic nun remains; if we delete the emphatic nun, the nun of the nominative remains. Which one? We delete the nun of the nominative, for two reasons.

The first reason: the nun of the nominative is customarily deleted when the verb is in the subjunctive or the jussive, is that correct? Rather, it may also be deleted outside the two states of subjunctive and jussive, deleted for lightness, as in the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise until you believe" [Abu Dawud (5193), al-Tirmidhi (2688), Ibn Majah (68), and it is originally in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise." "You will not enter" here has neither a governing particle nor a jussive particle, and it was deleted for lightness. Its original form is: "you will not enter Paradise" (la tadkhuluna al-jannah), so the nun was deleted for lightness.

The nun is also often deleted together with the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah). So it is more deserving of deletion, and the emphatic nun remains. For if we deleted the emphatic nun, the intended purpose would be lost, while we want to emphasize the verb. And the emphasis of the verb here, and we have studied this in a new lesson in grammar, is it obligatory or not obligatory (liyaqulunanna)?

* A student: Obligatory.

* Shaykh: Obligatory, because it affirms a future oath.

* A student: It is not separated.

* Shaykh: It is not separated. Nothing separates its lam from its verb, so its emphasis is obligatory.

So we keep the nun. If the nun of the nominative says, "Let us all remain," and we all become (liyaqulunanna), can we keep what contradicts it?

We say: it is not possible, because the nun of the nominative is additional and the emphatic nun is additional, so three letters, all additional, cannot gather in one place. We can bear one letter or two letters at most.

So we say: one of you must be deleted, and you, O nun of the nominative, are more deserving of deletion. Go! Then the waw comes together with the emphatic nun. The waw here is quiescent. You say: quiescent, and the emphatic nun is doubled, so the first of them is quiescent. Two quiescent letters have come together, and two quiescent letters cannot come together. Why? Because quiescence and vowel are opposites, so one quiescent letter and another quiescent letter cannot come together. Therefore we must perform an action that frees us from the meeting of two quiescent letters. What is the action? If the letter before the quiescent letter is sound, what do we do with it? We vowel it with kasrah. If the letter before the quiescent letter is not sound, but a soft letter (harf layn), then we delete it. Ibn Malik said:

"If two quiescent letters meet, vowel what precedes them with kasrah. If it is a soft letter, deletion is deserved."

So here, is the first quiescent letter (the waw) a soft letter or a sound one?

* A student: A soft letter.

* Shaykh: Then we delete it, so the lam meets the nun: (liyaqulunna). So in this verb there are now two deletions: deletion of the nun, with the reason being the succession of similar letters; deletion of the waw of the nominative, with the reason being the meeting of two quiescent letters. On this basis the author says: "The nun of the nominative was deleted because of the succession of similar letters, and the waw of the pronoun because of the meeting of two quiescent letters."

What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying ﴿Allah﴾ in ﴿They would surely say, "Allah"﴾? It is the subject of a deleted verb. The estimate is: "Allah created them." This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 9]. "They would surely say: created them." So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the verb. So here, what is the deleted element?

* A student: A verb.

* Shaykh: The verb? Yes. Is it correct to say the deleted element is a noun, with the estimate "He is Allah"? It is correct, but it is contrary to what is preferable, because the question is in conflict with the answer. And the question was in the form of a verb: "Who created?" So it requires that the answer be like the question in verb form: "He created them, such-and-such."

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾ [Luqman 25]. ("Say") means: when they acknowledge and confess. ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾. ﴿The praise﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿to Allah﴾ is its predicate. Praise be to Allah for what? For the clarity of the proof and the clarity of the way. Now they have confessed to what? That they are in error in their polytheism.

So ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ here is for the clarification and manifestation of the proof, and that they have been refuted by it. For when they acknowledge and confess that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, and that these idols do not create, then they have testified against themselves that these idols do not deserve worship. For this reason, ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾. Also, the praise here may be understood as: "Praise be to Allah for creating the heavens and the earth, that He is the Creator, mighty and majestic, alone, and therefore He is praised for His attributes of perfection and His beautiful acts."

He says: (﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ for the manifestation of the proof against them).

﴿The praise﴾ has been mentioned here many times, and it is the description of the one praised with perfection, together with love and exaltation.

The lam in His saying ﴿to Allah﴾ is the lam of entitlement and exclusivity. Entitlement, because He is the one entitled to praise, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Possessor of praise and glory" [Muslim (477/205), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Second, exclusivity: because who is the one who deserves absolute praise? He is Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾. ("But" here) is the transitional retraction (idrab intiqali), not the cancelling retraction (idrab ibtali). It is a transition from what preceded to recording their complete ignorance. For this reason he says: (﴿But most of them do not know﴾) its obligation upon them, meaning tawhid (monotheism). The negation of knowledge from them is because of what? Because its benefit is absent, and a thing may be negated because its benefit is absent. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21]. He negated hearing from them, because its benefit is absent with regard to them.

So His saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ negates knowledge from them, although they acknowledge that Allah is the Creator, but they did not benefit from this knowledge. And which of the two is more abominable: an ignorant person who does not know, or a knowledgeable person who did not benefit?

* Students: The latter.

* Shaykh: The latter is more severe and more abominable, because he is a compound ignorant person, while the other is a simple ignorant person. And because he is stubborn and arrogant, while the other is a misguided person who is not stubborn. Compound ignorance is more abominable, and stubbornness born of knowledge is worse than stubbornness born of ignorance. A poet said two verses:

"Whoever seeks the sciences without a teacher will go astray from the straight path,
and the sciences will become confused for him until he becomes more misguided than Tuma the sage."

Tuma is a compound ignorant person whom they called "the sage." But what deceived him is that they called him "the sage," and he began to issue rulings on everything, until he ruled that whoever gives his daughter in charity to a man will enter Paradise. He said, (the third verse):

"He gave away daughters in charity to men,
desiring by that the gardens of bliss."

Is this ignorance or not?

* A student: Is this like fornication?

* Shaykh: Yes. You are a young man in need of marriage and you have no dowry or anything, so if I gave you charity, [they say] yes indeed. Ignorance may measure with its mind and say: instead of giving him dirhams and having him go to propose, we cut the road, saying: this one is without dirhams.

* A student: We want an explanation of this compound and simple.

* Shaykh: Listen to the compound and the simple in the next two verses:

"The donkey of the sage Tuma said..."

Did he not say: more misguided than Tuma the sage?

"The donkey of the sage Tuma said: If fate were just, I would be the one riding.
Because I am a simple ignorant one, and my companion is a compound ignorant one."

Did you understand the difference now?

* A student: Yes, it is known, the verse, that is...

* Shaykh: Fine, it is known, finished.

* The student: I am saying: what is the difference...?

* Shaykh: The donkey says: he is a simple ignorant one, and his companion, who is Tuma, is a compound ignorant one. The compound ignorant one is the one who does not know that he is ignorant: ignorant and unaware that he is ignorant, this is compound. And the simple one is the ignorant one who knows that he is ignorant. It becomes clear through an example: someone says to you, "When was the Battle of Badr?" and you say, "I do not know." What is this called?

* A student: Simple.

* Shaykh: This is simple ignorance. The person does not know, and he knows that he does not know, and he says: "I do not know."

Another man says to someone else, "When was the Battle of Badr?" He says, "Praise be to Allah who has opened [knowledge] to the ignorant. The Battle of Badr was in Jumada al-Akhirah in the ninth year after the Hijrah (...)."

Did you understand the difference now?

* A student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...).

* The student: No, I am saying: what is the difference...

* Shaykh: The donkey says he is a simple ignorant one, and his companion, who is Tuma, is a compound ignorant one. The compound ignorant one is the one who does not know that he is ignorant: ignorant and unaware that he is ignorant, this is compound. And the simple one is the ignorant one who knows that he is ignorant. It becomes clear through an example: someone says to you, "When was the Battle of Badr?" and you say, "I do not know." What is this called?

* A student: Simple.

* Shaykh: This is simple ignorance: the person does not know, and he knows that he does not know, and he says, "I do not know."

Another man says to someone else, "When was the Battle of Badr?" He says, "Praise be to Allah who has opened [knowledge] to the ignorant. The Battle of Badr was in Jumada al-Akhirah in the ninth year after the Hijrah." What do you say about this?

* A student: This is compound ignorance.

* Shaykh: Now, he is ignorant, and he does not know that he is ignorant. For this reason he began with his saying: "Praise be to Allah who has opened [knowledge] to the ignorant." It is said to him: "Allah has not opened [knowledge] to you, because you are ignorant."

* A student: I mean "compound." What is the meaning of "compound"?

* Shaykh: It is compounded of two ignorances: his ignorance of the reality and his ignorance of his own state. The compound ignorant one is ignorant of the reality and ignorant of his own state. Clear?

* A student: Yes.

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 26–29 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 26]. The sentence here is declarative (khabariyyah): ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. It contains restriction (hasr), and its method is the fronting of the predicate, because placing before its place what should be delayed conveys restriction. So ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ means: not to other than Him, and it belongs to Him alone, glorified and exalted is He.

His saying ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ means: whatever exists in them, ﴿and the earth﴾ likewise. He used (mā), which is used for non-rational beings, because it is intended to denote ownership of essences and attributes. When ownership of essences and attributes is meant, (mā) is used because it is more comprehensive, since every essence has an attribute; and also not every essence is rational, for beasts, animals and the like belong to the category of non-rational beings.

His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾: the author said: (dominion, creation and servitude). (Dominion, creation) — and dominion (mulk) includes ownership of essences and disposal over those essences; for this reason he said (and servitude). The servitude intended here is general servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-'ammah), not specific servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-khassah), because specific servitude is restricted to the obedient who have humbled themselves before Allah the Exalted in obedience in the legal sense; general servitude, however, includes all creation, because all creatures are humbled before Allah the Mighty and Majestic in terms of His cosmic ordinance and decree. No one can oppose the decree and destiny of Allah, but the disbelievers can oppose the law of Allah, and for this reason they opposed it, denied the law, and were arrogant toward the truth.

He said: (and servitude, so none in them deserves worship other than Him). In the heavens and the earth, nothing deserves worship except Allah; because by the requirement of reason and innate nature, the Owner, the Creator, the Disposer must be the one who is worshipped. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic argues for the obligation of worship on what basis? On lordship: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. And it has passed us: ﴿If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾ [Luqman 25]. This is evident: whoever has creation must be the one to whom worship is due alone.

(﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from His creation ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ who is praised in His work). The sentence here is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), to explain what Allah the Mighty and Majestic possesses of these two names and the attribute they contain.

﴿Indeed, Allah is﴾: the pronoun is the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and the pronoun of separation has three benefits:
The first benefit: emphasis (tawkid).
The second: restriction (ḥaṣr).
The third: distinguishing the predicate from the adjective.

So if you say: (Zayd is the virtuous), then (Zayd) is the subject, and (the virtuous) may well be an adjective of Zayd, and the predicate has not yet come, and the estimate is: Zayd the virtuous is beloved, for example. But if you say: (Zayd is he the virtuous), is it possible that it is an adjective or not?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: No, it is the predicate, and for this reason it is called the pronoun of separation.

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾: the author said: (from His creation). He is also free of need in Himself, free of need of others: free of need in Himself because of the abundance of what He has, since everything belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and this is the completeness of independence; and He is free of need of His creation, so He needs no one. The evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97]. As for others, they are in need. In need of whom? Of Allah the Mighty and Majestic before everything else. Then people are in need of one another, as He said: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in this worldly life, and raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some may take others in service﴾ [al-Zukhruf 32]. People are in need of one another, and sometimes in dire necessity; and all are in need of Allah and in dire necessity, whereas the Lord the Mighty and Majestic is free of need of others, just as He is self-sufficient.

So His independence includes two things:
Essential independence: meaning the abundance of what He possesses, the Exalted; for everything is His possession.
Second: independence from others, such that He does not need anyone while others need Him.

His saying ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ who is praised in His work). He fell short in the explanation in two respects:
First: he said ﴿al-Ḥamīd﴾ means "the one praised". The correct view is that it means both "the one praised" and "the one who praises"; He, glorified and exalted, praises those who deserve praise, and how much praise of those who deserve it there is in the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. And He is also praised for the perfection of His attributes and the completeness of His bounty; He is praised for two things: the perfection of His attributes and the completeness of His favours.
The second respect in which the author fell short is that he said: (who is praised in His work). The correct view is that He is praised in His work and also in His law, for His law, glorified and exalted is He, is the most perfect of laws and the most beneficial to the servants. Whoever lays down for creation a path by which their affairs are set right deserves praise. Now, if someone guided you to the road to a town on one of your journeys, would you praise him or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: You would praise him. How much more so one who guides you to the path of the Hereafter in everything you need! So the correct view is that (Ḥamīd) means both "the one who praises" and "the one praised," and that He is praiseworthy in His work and in His law. His work, which is creation, is to be praised for bringing it into being, for preparing it, and for sustaining it. He is also praiseworthy in His law, for the justice, wisdom and mercy in His law, which have no equal.

How great is the benefit of the conjunction of ﴿al-Ḥamīd﴾ with ﴿al-Ghanī﴾! For, as has passed us, the names of Allah are all most beautiful and indicate a most beautiful meaning; but two names may indicate a third attribute that arises from what? From their conjunction. Independence together with praiseworthiness increases in perfection, for a free-of-need one may be free of need but in a way that is not praised; like what? 
* Student: The miser.
* The Shaykh: Like the miser. The miser is rich, but he is not praised for his wealth, because his money is not benefited from, and he has deprived himself of the benefit of his wealth. But Allah the Mighty and Majestic has independence conjoined with praiseworthiness, because of the completeness of His beneficence to His creation from this independence: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea [were ink], with seven more seas to supply it, the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27] (...). Let us look at the grammatical analysis (i'rab).

﴿And if [wa-law anna mā]﴾: (law) here is conditional, and its protasis (fi'l al-shart) is omitted; i.e., "and if it were established that whatever is on the earth of trees ... to the end." And (mā) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which."

﴿on the earth﴾ is a prepositional phrase, related to an omitted element that is the complement (ṣilah) of the relative pronoun; meaning: and if that which is established on the earth.

﴿of trees﴾ is a prepositional phrase serving as a clarification (bayān) of (mā), the relative pronoun, because the relative pronoun is vague and needs clarification; so ﴿of trees﴾ clarifies it; meaning: if what is on the earth of trees.

His saying ﴿were pens﴾: is the predicate of (anna), meaning: if what is on the earth of trees were pens — this is the meaning — they would be pens with which to write.

﴿and the sea﴾: he says: (conjoined to the noun of anna). ﴿and the sea﴾. In another reading ﴿and the sea [is]﴾ [with nominative].
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Here it is ﴿and the sea﴾ in the Mushaf, but the author (...) in the accusative; he said: (conjoined to the noun of anna).
If it is in the nominative ﴿and the sea﴾ it is the subject (mubtada'). Ibn Malik said:
"And it is permissible to raise what is conjoined to the accusative of (inna) after it has been completed;
And (lakinna) and (anna) are attached to (inna) ..."
This (anna), he said: (﴿and the sea﴾ is conjoined to the noun of anna), so it is in the accusative. ﴿and the sea [is] drawing it, with seven more seas after it﴾ [Luqman 27]. Where is the predicate?
* Students: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27].
* The Shaykh: No, that is the response of the condition. The predicate is omitted, which the author estimated by his saying: (ink) — meaning: if what is on the earth of trees were pens and what is in it of seas were ink. (Midād) means the ink with which one writes.

The response of the condition is ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ (expressed by them about His knowledge ...) to the end.

﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ (exhausted): what is its meaning?
* Student: Ended.
* The Shaykh: Ended and finished.

﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾: ﴿words﴾ is the subject of ﴿exhausted﴾. The cosmic and legal words do not run out. The reason is that He, glorified and exalted, has never ceased and never ceases to speak. And creation: does it have an end or does it not have an end?
* Students: No.
* Other students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: No, creation has no end; for when people enter Paradise or Hell, what is it? Eternal, everlasting, perpetual abiding. So everything Allah creates, He creates by what? He creates it by the word "Be," and it is. If creatures do not end, and likewise the acts of Allah in eternity have no end, they can never be exhausted, even if it were supposed that the sea and seven more seas supply it, and all the trees on the earth were pens with which one writes; the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic would not be exhausted. The reason is clear: creatures do not end, and every creature comes into being by the word; ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].

Thus the wisdom of this declarative sentence being pure truth becomes clear to us; it is truth beyond doubt, the report of Allah is truth. But someone may say: how? What is the reasoning behind this? We say: this is its reasoning. A person may find it hard to imagine that the ocean, and seven seas beyond it, become ink, and all the trees on the earth become pens with which to write, and yet the words are not exhausted. He may find this extraordinary, but when he knows the perfection of Allah's power and greatness, he will not find it extraordinary.

His saying ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾: he said: (expressed by them about His knowledge, by writing them with those pens and that ink, and not more than that, because His knowledge, exalted is He, is not finite). May Allah pardon the author; this is a distortion. He says that the intended meaning of "words" is "known things" — the things known by Allah; i.e., what He knows would not be exhausted. But this is a clear distortion of the Qur'an. Allah says: "His words would not be exhausted," and the words are what is written; as for knowledge, it may or may not be written. Do you write down all your knowledge? But when you want to express your words to others, you speak them and write them. So the meaning: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, that is, His words in truth, in reality; the true words, if they were dictated to someone and the seas became ink for them and the trees pens for them, would not be exhausted. The meaning is evident, and this indicates the greatness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and the perfection of His power.

(﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾ nothing overcomes Him ﴿Wise﴾ [Luqman 27] nothing goes beyond His knowledge and wisdom).

His saying ﴿Mighty﴾: he says (nothing overcomes Him). Sometimes the author himself says: ﴿Mighty﴾ (nothing overpowers Him); this is because might, as has been mentioned, is divided into three kinds: might of rank (ʿizzat al-qadr); second, might of dominance (ʿizzat al-qahr), which is overpowering; and third, might of inaccessibility (ʿizzat al-imtinaʿ), which means that nothing can reach Him with harm, ever; He is inaccessible to all harm, by His own strength, glorified and exalted is He.

As for His saying ﴿Wise﴾, he here said: (nothing goes beyond His knowledge and wisdom), so he interpreted wisdom as knowledge. It has already been mentioned for us that (al-Ḥakīm) is derived from judgment (ḥukm) and wisdom (ḥikmah); so He is Wise, nothing goes outside His dominion and His judgment, and He is Wise, nothing goes beyond His wisdom; He is the Judge who perfects, all of this is taken from the word (Ḥakīm).

Joining (ʿAzīz) with (Ḥakīm) establishes a third attribute besides might and wisdom, namely that His might, may He be exalted, is conjoined with wisdom, so it becomes a more perfect might, and a more perfect wisdom. For a mighty person among creatures may be seized by pride in sin and so not be wise in his conduct, isn't that so?
* Student: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: But Allah the Mighty and Majestic, His might is conjoined with wisdom; it is impossible for His actions to go outside wisdom, which is conformity to what is correct.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said, showing the perfection of His power after mentioning the generality of His dominion and the perfection of His words: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ [Luqman 28], in creation and resurrection, because it is by the word "Be" that it is. For He means creation and resurrection: He did not create all of you except as a single soul, and did not resurrect all of you except as a single soul. So multitude does not overwhelm Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for multitude and few are equal to Him; all are within the reach of His power, and all is easy for Him, because it happens by what word? By the word "Be." When Allah the Mighty and Majestic created the heavens and the earth, did He need workers and tools?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Here we say: if the building is large, is it harder, and if it is small, is it easier? No, it is by the word "Be," and whatever is by the word "Be," there is no difference between it being many or few. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic said in another verse: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer﴾ [al-Nahl 77], meaning: it is even nearer than the blink of an eye. And He said: ﴿And Our command is but one, like the blink of an eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50], this is the utmost of speed and accomplishment. And He said: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will be on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 13–14]. All of this indicates the perfection of the Mighty and Majestic's power.

If someone says: if the matter is so, why did He create the heavens in six (...)?
How is it conjoined with wisdom? Because this creation requires things: preliminaries and causes by which the perfection of creation is achieved. Is Allah not able to create the fetus in its mother's womb without a man touching her?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, as happened with 'Isa. Nevertheless, Allah the Exalted has made causes for this: the transfer of the man's water to the woman, then the fetus develops little by little until it reaches its end; then, when it is ready to come out into the world, it comes out; then, even so, it grows little by little; it does not reach full intellect at once, nor does it reach full growth at once, but it is in accordance with wisdom. This is the answer to what comes to the mind or is raised to a person: why did Allah create the heavens and the earth in six days? And why does He create the fetus in its mother's womb for nine months? And other such questions. The answer is that His actions are conjoined with wisdom, and that He, glorified and exalted, has linked for you the causes to their effects, so there must be a cause and from it an effect, and this cause must be fitting and suitable, so that creation is completed in its perfection.

﴿but as a single soul﴾ (﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ who hears every thing heard, ﴿Seeing﴾ [Luqman 28] who sees every thing seen; nothing preoccupies Him from anything).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Seen.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, every thing seen; and everything seen is created; there is none but Creator or created. As if you were saying that (...) does not see itself.
* Student: (...) the sensible seen things.
* The Shaykh: No, every thing seen means everything that can be the object of sight. (...) I do not see it, but Allah the Mighty and Majestic sees it. Now, we differ: something Zayd sees and Amr does not see.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾: it has been mentioned that (al-Samī') is divided into two kinds: one kind in the sense of "responding" (mujīb), and one kind in the sense of "hearing" (sāmi'), that is, perceiving sounds.

The Mighty One who is All-Hearing, in the sense of the One who answers, is like Ibrahim's saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39], meaning the One who answers it. It is also known that He does not answer it unless He has heard it with a hearing of perception (sam' idrak). But the benefit of supplication is the answering of the one who supplicates. As for merely hearing his supplication, there is no benefit in that unless it is answered.

It has already been mentioned that the hearing of perception is divided into three categories. What are they? That which conveys a warning (tahdid), that which conveys support (ta'yid), and that which conveys the vastness of Allah's hearing, the Exalted and Glorified, and His perception of everything that is heard.

Among what conveys a warning is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, writing﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80]. What is the purpose of this? What is it? A warning.

Among what conveys support is His, the Exalted, saying to Musa and Harun: ﴿Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha 46].

Among what conveys comprehensiveness, the comprehensiveness of Allah's hearing, the Mighty and Majestic, of everything that is heard, is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujadila 1]. For this reason 'A'isha said: "Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses all voices. I was at the side of the room, and some of their conversation was hidden from me."[[Recorded by al-Nasa'i (3460) and Ibn Majah (188) from the hadith of 'A'isha.]] Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from above the seven heavens, hears this conversation and all this dialogue, and nothing escapes Him, the Glorified and Exalted.

As for His saying: ﴿Basir (All-Seeing)﴾, then al-Basir...

* Student: The second meaning of al-Sami'.
* Shaykh: This means perceiving what is heard.
* Student: We said: in the sense of the One who answers.
* Shaykh: In the sense of the One who answers, and in the sense of the One who perceives sounds; the hearer of sounds. And the hearing of sounds, we said, is divided into three categories. Is it clear?

As for al-Basir: al-Basir means the One who sees, i.e., He perceives with His sight, the Glorified and Exalted. Allah, the Exalted, has a sight with which He sees the things that are seen, as came in the authentic hadith: "His veil is light; if He were to unveil it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches."[[Recorded by Muslim (179 / 293) from the hadith of Abu Musa.]]

Al-Basir may also indicate knowledge, as in: ﴿And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqara 265], meaning, All-Knowing of it. Among people now, when they say: "So-and-so is knowledgeable (basir) about things," they mean he has knowledge and expertise in them.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, to the end of the verse [Luqman 29]. The hamzah here is the interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri). The meaning of ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is "you have indeed seen." He, the Glorified and Exalted, is affirming this matter, which is observed and known by everyone. The address in His saying ﴿you see﴾ is either to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The second meaning is broader and more general, so it includes everyone who is fit to be addressed.

﴿Have you not seen﴾, O seeing addressee? ﴿That Allah causes to enter﴾ makes enter ﴿the night into the day and causes the day﴾ to enter ﴿into the night﴾. This causing to enter cannot be except by great power.

How is the "causing to enter" in ﴿causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾? Does it mean the approach of the night and the approach of the day? Because you see the night, when it approaches, its darkness enters into the day, entering upon the day and driving it away; and you see the day, when it approaches, entering into the night and driving it away. So this is an expression for the establishing of the break of dawn, and what else? And the approach of the night.

Allah, the Exalted, has sworn by this in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And by the night when it retreats, and by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir 33-34]. And He does not swear by any created thing except for its greatness. So the meaning of "causing to enter" is making one enter the other: making the night enter the day or the reverse. When? At every morning and every evening. This is one aspect.

Or the meaning is: ﴿causes the night to enter into the day﴾ in the sense that the day increases in duration until it enters into the night, and the night increases in duration until it enters into the day. That is, the day lengthens, and when it lengthens it takes from the night; so this means it has entered upon it. And the night lengthens, and when it lengthens it takes from the day, so it has entered upon it and taken from it by stealth. This too is a meaning of the word "causing to enter."

Both are correct meanings. In the approach and retreat of the night there is a great sign of Allah's signs, and in the fact that this increases while that decreases there is also a sign of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For if all creatures were to gather together to bring the night into the day or the day into the night, they could not do it. If they all gathered together to add one minute to the day or one minute to the night, could they do it or not?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: They cannot, however much strength they are given. So this is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then, in causing the night to enter into the day according to the second meaning, it is the reverse: it is evidence of Allah's mercy, because the alternation of night and day in increase and decrease contains enormous benefit. When the night lengthens, cold and winter occur, the trees of winter appear, and the insects die whose continued existence may be harmful to humans and plants. Likewise, when the day increases, heat increases, fruits ripen, and vapor leaves the earth. Many insects die because of the heat, which, had they remained and multiplied, would have harmed people. So this too is evidence of the perfection of wisdom and mercy together with power.

The author says: (﴿causes to enter﴾ makes enter ﴿the night into the day and causes the day﴾ to enter ﴿into the night﴾, so each increases by what the other has lost, ﴿and He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾). That is, He made them subservient. For what? For the benefit of the servants. The evidence for this is His saying in the general, all-encompassing verse: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾ [al-Jathiya 13]. ﴿He has subjected to you﴾: notice the word ﴿to you﴾. So everything mentioned of subjugation in the universe is for the children of Adam. For this reason it is said in some reports: "O son of Adam, I created you for My sake, and I created everything for your sake."[[We have not located it; al-Abshihi mentioned it in similar wording in al-Mustatraf (1 / 78).]] And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 56], and He says: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqara 29], and: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...). ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning He made them subservient for the benefit of the servants. The sun and moon are mentioned after the night and day because the sun is the sign of the day and the moon is the sign of the night, as His saying: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs; then We effaced the sign of the night﴾, which is the moon, ﴿and We made the sign of the day as a means of sight﴾ [al-Isra 12]. Therefore the moon has no light of its own; it is effaced, and it derives its light from the sun. Whenever it faces the sun, its light increases; when the facing between it and the sun is complete, on the nights of the full moon, its light is perfected. Then, as the facing weakens, its light weakens.

* Student: Shaykh, the verse seems to indicate entering, "causing to enter" (...) lengthening (...).
* Shaykh: Each is valid; all of it is causing to enter.
* Student: Lengthening is causing to enter! How (...)?!
* Shaykh: Because the day enters into the night (...). If we suppose that we are now at the equality of night and day, how long is the night?
* Student: Twelve hours.
* Shaykh: And the day?
* Student: Twelve hours.
* Shaykh: Good. The day lengthens, so it becomes thirteen hours, and the night?
* Student: Eleven.
* Shaykh: Eleven. So the day has entered into the night; that is, into the time of the night.
* Student: Meaning in time, the time of the night.
* Shaykh: In the time of the night, and likewise the reverse.

(﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each﴾ of them ﴿running﴾ in its orbit ﴿for a designated term﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.)

﴿Each running﴾: this tanwin (nunation) of ﴿kullun﴾, the grammarians say, is a substitute (ʿiwad) for an omitted word. That is: each one of the sun and the moon runs until a designated term.

Remarkably, it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "The sun and the moon run in their orbits during the day, and run in their orbits beneath the earth at night."[[Recorded by Ibn Mandah in al-Tawhid (58) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] This indicates that Ibn 'Abbas held that the earth is spherical, because if it runs beneath the earth, it means that the earth is round. And so it is, because the sun and the moon at night run beneath the earth, as he, may Allah be pleased with him, said.

* Student: Which earth?
* Shaykh: This earth of ours; it will be beneath it.
* Student: And the remaining earths?
* Shaykh: (...)..
* Student: I mean the remaining earths, the remaining six; they are below.
* Shaykh: Yes, the remaining six are beneath us. That is, the earths are layers, (...), layers one above another. Have you not looked at the egg? It has the uppermost shell, then the second shell, (...) then the white next to it, then the white, then a thin membrane, then the yolk, and the yolk too has layers. The earth is like the egg in this way. Likewise the heavens, the same thing: layers, curved.

* Student: So they are not separate?
* Shaykh: (...) separate?
* Student: I mean the earths are not separated from one another.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a difference of opinion. Some scholars say that there is a separation and air between them, just as the heavens have air and separation between them. And some say there is no separation between them.

* Student: We said that the sun and moon revolve beneath all the earths, the seven earths.
* Shaykh: Now, the seven earths are the mass, this mass of earth which they call the terrestrial globe. It contains the seven, the seven are within its core. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, will have it hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2452) and Muslim (1610 / 137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]] For if he wrongs the upper earth on which we now stand, he has transgressed against those beneath it, and those beneath it, and those beneath it, down to the seventh. For this reason, the common people now say: (...).

* * *

.. ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes...﴾; that is, "And have you not seen that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?" Here, seeing means knowing in both places, as the author estimated: that is, "Do you not know that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?"

If someone says: my knowledge that Allah causes the night to enter the day and that He has subjected the sun and moon is knowledge whose path is sense perception; I witness it. But ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Luqman 29], what is the path of this knowledge? Is it witnessed sense perception or true report?

True report, without doubt. We know that Allah is Acquainted with what we do because He has informed us of that, the Glorified and Exalted, and He is the most truthful of speakers.

But do we also know this through witnessed sense perception, or not?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: How so? We say: yes, we know it from what we observe of the punishments for sins, for example, and of the rewards of the obedient, and from what happens to a person himself from the effect of obedience and the effect of disobedience. The believer experiences an evil effect in himself from sin, to the point that some people's chests become constricted and they do not know the reason, but its cause is a sin that has remained hidden from them. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed my heart is covered over, and I seek Allah's forgiveness a hundred times a day."[[Recorded by Muslim (2702 / 41) from the hadith of al-Aghurr ibn Yasar.]] Or as he, peace and blessings be upon him, said. So a person senses the knowledge and awareness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding what he does, through its effects.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From its effects. So the summary now is that ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: we say we know it through two paths: true report and witnessed sense perception. We sense it through what we see of the effects of our good deeds or the effects of our evil deeds.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is also among the signs. So the conclusion from this is that this affirmation, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, meaning "do you not know," is an affirmation of a matter that is actual, witnessed, and perceived, and of a matter known through true report (...).

* * *

.. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 26].

* It is derived from this verse that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone. And the path of benefit from it is?
* Student: The path of benefit is that everything in the universe (...) belongs to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.
* Shaykh: (...) but it is specific to Allah. So what is the indicator that Allah, the Exalted, is specifically the owner of it from the sentence?
* Student: (...) the restriction.
* Shaykh: Yes, what is its means?
* Student: Fronting of the prepositional phrase.
* Shaykh: Fronting of the predicate.
* Student: Fronting of the predicate over the subject (...).
* Shaykh: So in the noble verse... among its benefits: that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is specific to Him. From where do we take that it is specific? From the fronting of the predicate, because fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction and exclusivity.
* And it is derived from this noble verse: that people do not own their wealth with absolute ownership. You say, for example: "I own my house, my car, and similar things," but your ownership of them is not absolute, is it? Because absolute ownership belongs to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason, your disposal of them is according to what Allah has permitted, not according to what you want. With this the objection that is raised is removed, which says: If you say that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth is specific to Allah, has not Allah attributed ownership to humans? ﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. So how is the answer? We say: this ownership is not absolute ownership.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, (...) we do not see it in the Qur'an, but we say: it is not absolute ownership, by the proof that it is restricted by Allah's permission, by what Allah has permitted.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Ghani (the Free of need) and al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy), and what they indicate of the attribute of free-of-need-ness and praise, and what their combination indicates of an attribute as well: that Allah's freedom from need is joined with His being praiseworthy, which indicates that it is an essential freedom from need (ghina dhati), and that He, the Glorified and Exalted, despite being free of need, is generous and gives of what He has. Or not? For not every free-of-need person is praiseworthy.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification that Allah's ownership of the heavens and the earth is an ownership that includes bounty and praise. From where do we take it? Because He mentioned it after His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾. So His being free of need, through which the Glorified and Exalted praises Himself after mentioning the ownership of the heavens and the earth, indicates His bounty through this freedom from need, and His being praised for this ownership, that it is an ownership built upon praise. This is like His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha 2]. He praised Himself for being Lord of the worlds, because His lordship, the Glorified and Exalted, is a lordship for which He is to be praised, due to the perfection of bounty, kindness, and justice it contains (...). Have you understood this? What did we say about it, what is the benefit? The affirmation that the ownership of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is built upon bounty and praise; because He mentioned it after His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾.
* And it is derived from the noble verse: the poverty (iftiqar) of whatever is in the heavens and the earth to Allah. From where is it taken?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 26–29 (part 3 of 3):

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes; because His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need (al-Ghaniy), the Praiseworthy﴾ is evidence that whatever is in the heavens and the earth is in need of Him and poor (in need) before Him, as the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor (in need) before Allah, and Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15].
