* Student: And the remaining earths?
* Shaykh: (...)..
* Student: I mean the remaining earths, the remaining six; they are below.
* Shaykh: Yes, the remaining six are beneath us. That is, the earths are layers, (...), layers one above another. Have you not looked at the egg? It has the uppermost shell, then the second shell, (...) then the white next to it, then the white, then a thin membrane, then the yolk, and the yolk too has layers. The earth is like the egg in this way. Likewise the heavens, the same thing: layers, curved.

* Student: So they are not separate?
* Shaykh: (...) separate?
* Student: I mean the earths are not separated from one another.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a difference of opinion. Some scholars say that there is a separation and air between them, just as the heavens have air and separation between them. And some say there is no separation between them.

* Student: We said that the sun and moon revolve beneath all the earths, the seven earths.
* Shaykh: Now, the seven earths are the mass, this mass of earth which they call the terrestrial globe. It contains the seven, the seven are within its core. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, will have it hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2452) and Muslim (1610 / 137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]] For if he wrongs the upper earth on which we now stand, he has transgressed against those beneath it, and those beneath it, and those beneath it, down to the seventh. For this reason, the common people now say: (...).

* * *

.. ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes...﴾; that is, "And have you not seen that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?" Here, seeing means knowing in both places, as the author estimated: that is, "Do you not know that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?"

If someone says: my knowledge that Allah causes the night to enter the day and that He has subjected the sun and moon is knowledge whose path is sense perception; I witness it. But ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Luqman 29], what is the path of this knowledge? Is it witnessed sense perception or true report?

True report, without doubt. We know that Allah is Acquainted with what we do because He has informed us of that, the Glorified and Exalted, and He is the most truthful of speakers.

But do we also know this through witnessed sense perception, or not?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: How so? We say: yes, we know it from what we observe of the punishments for sins, for example, and of the rewards of the obedient, and from what happens to a person himself from the effect of obedience and the effect of disobedience. The believer experiences an evil effect in himself from sin, to the point that some people's chests become constricted and they do not know the reason, but its cause is a sin that has remained hidden from them. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed my heart is covered over, and I seek Allah's forgiveness a hundred times a day."[[Recorded by Muslim (2702 / 41) from the hadith of al-Aghurr ibn Yasar.]] Or as he, peace and blessings be upon him, said. So a person senses the knowledge and awareness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding what he does, through its effects.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From its effects. So the summary now is that ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: we say we know it through two paths: true report and witnessed sense perception. We sense it through what we see of the effects of our good deeds or the effects of our evil deeds.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is also among the signs. So the conclusion from this is that this affirmation, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, meaning "do you not know," is an affirmation of a matter that is actual, witnessed, and perceived, and of a matter known through true report (...).

* * *

.. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 26].

* It is derived from this verse that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone. And the path of benefit from it is?
* Student: The path of benefit is that everything in the universe (...) belongs to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.
* Shaykh: (...) but it is specific to Allah. So what is the indicator that Allah, the Exalted, is specifically the owner of it from the sentence?
* Student: (...) the restriction.
* Shaykh: Yes, what is its means?
* Student: Fronting of the prepositional phrase.
* Shaykh: Fronting of the predicate.
* Student: Fronting of the predicate over the subject (...).
* Shaykh: So in the noble verse... among its benefits: that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is specific to Him. From where do we take that it is specific? From the fronting of the predicate, because fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction and exclusivity.
* And it is derived from this noble verse: that people do not own their wealth with absolute ownership. You say, for example: "I own my house, my car, and similar things," but your ownership of them is not absolute, is it? Because absolute ownership belongs to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason, your disposal of them is according to what Allah has permitted, not according to what you want. With this the objection that is raised is removed, which says: If you say that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth is specific to Allah, has not Allah attributed ownership to humans? ﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. So how is the answer? We say: this ownership is not absolute ownership.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, (...) we do not see it in the Qur'an, but we say: it is not absolute ownership, by the proof that it is restricted by Allah's permission, by what Allah has permitted.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Ghani (the Free of need) and al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy), and what they indicate of the attribute of free-of-need-ness and praise, and what their combination indicates of an attribute as well: that Allah's freedom from need is joined with His being praiseworthy, which indicates that it is an essential freedom from need (ghina dhati), and that He, the Glorified and Exalted, despite being free of need, is generous and gives of what He has. Or not? For not every free-of-need person is praiseworthy.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification that Allah's ownership of the heavens and the earth is an ownership that includes bounty and praise. From where do we take it? Because He mentioned it after His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾. So His being free of need, through which the Glorified and Exalted praises Himself after mentioning the ownership of the heavens and the earth, indicates His bounty through this freedom from need, and His being praised for this ownership, that it is an ownership built upon praise. This is like His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha 2]. He praised Himself for being Lord of the worlds, because His lordship, the Glorified and Exalted, is a lordship for which He is to be praised, due to the perfection of bounty, kindness, and justice it contains (...). Have you understood this? What did we say about it, what is the benefit? The affirmation that the ownership of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is built upon bounty and praise; because He mentioned it after His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾.
* And it is derived from the noble verse: the poverty (iftiqar) of whatever is in the heavens and the earth to Allah. From where is it taken?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 26–29 (part 3 of 3):

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes; because His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need (al-Ghaniy), the Praiseworthy﴾ is evidence that whatever is in the heavens and the earth is in need of Him and poor (in need) before Him, as the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor (in need) before Allah, and Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that "the heavens" is plural and that their number is seven; this is taken from His saying: ﴿what is in the heavens﴾. As for specifying the number as seven, it comes from other verses.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens and the sea (were ink), replenished thereafter by seven seas, the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27].
* Derived from this noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, speaks; from His saying: ﴿the words of Allah﴾.
* And derived from it: that His words are audible, because they are written, and only what is audible is written. Is this so? Is there any consideration in this benefit?
* Student: There is consideration in it.
* The Shaykh: How so?
* The student: Because it is not possible to write sound (...).
* The Shaykh: Fine, meaning a person can write his own words without them being heard by others.
* The student: But no one else writes them.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but is it necessary that someone else writes them? Is it necessary, for something to be written, that someone else writes it?
So this benefit is open to consideration, but what is derived is the affirmation that Allah speaks with a voice; speech is not called speech except where it is a sound, whereas what is merely in the soul is not speech.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the words of Allah the Exalted have no end. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾. The basis for this was explained earlier in the tafsir: Allah, the Exalted, has not ceased and does not cease to be the Creator, the Doer of what He wills, and it follows from this that He is a speaker, as in His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since He is capable of a speech that does not end.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of might (al-'Izzah) and wisdom (al-Hikmah), from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Wise﴾; and the affirmation of wisdom also from His saying: ﴿Wise﴾; and the affirmation of these two names: ﴿Almighty﴾ and ﴿Wise﴾.
* Among its benefits also: what is indicated by the combination of might and wisdom among the attributes of perfection, or not? That is, we have said that a name may have a meaning in itself and a meaning when combined with others; the combination of might with wisdom conveys a greater perfection than if might or wisdom stood alone, namely that the might of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is tied to wisdom.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as (that of) a single soul﴾ [Luqman 28].
* Derived from this noble verse: the affirmation of creation and resurrection, from His saying: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection﴾.
* And derived from it: the perfection of Allah's power, since He, may His majesty be exalted, made the creation and resurrection of all creatures like a single soul, and this is the utmost of power.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of resurrection, from His saying: ﴿nor your resurrection﴾.
* Among its benefits: deducing the unseen (al-ghaib) from the seen. From where? And what is the intended benefit?
* Student: Deducing the promised from the witnessed.
* Another student: The creation (...).
* The Shaykh: The witnessed is creation, and the promised is resurrection; Allah has joined them both, affirming each of them, and that just as He was able to create at first, He is able to resurrect a second time.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of two names of Allah: (As-Sami') (the All-Hearing) and (Al-Basir) (the All-Seeing), and the affirmation of the attributes they indicate, and the affirmation of perfection through their combination: hearing and sight; for not every hearer is seeing, and not every seer is hearing. The meanings of As-Sami' and Al-Basir have already been mentioned for us, so there is no need to repeat them.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ to its end [Luqman 29].
* In this verse: the affirmation of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in causing the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night.
* Among its benefits also: the demonstration of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since this interchange contains many benefits, some observed and known, and some not known.
* Among them: the demonstration of the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon His servants in subjecting the sun and the moon; from His saying: ﴿and He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the sun and the moon run; from His saying: ﴿each runs to a specified term﴾.
* Among them: the demonstration of the perfection of order in the acts of Allah; from His saying: ﴿to a specified term﴾, fixed, not varying, neither advancing nor delaying.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of those who say that the sun and the moon are stationary; from His saying: ﴿each runs﴾. This is a report from their Creator, glorified and exalted, who is most knowing of what He created. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14]. Thus there is a clear refutation in it of those who say that they are stationary and do not run.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every existing creature has an end (ghayah), from His saying: ﴿each runs to a specified term﴾, except Paradise and Hellfire, for they are enduring forever without end, by Allah's sustaining them; their permanence is not intrinsic, because whatever may be brought into existence may be annihilated; or in other words: whatever may come into being may cease to be. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has decreed the everlastingness of Paradise and Hellfire, as the clear and authentic evidences indicate.
* Student: Every existing (...).
* The Shaykh: You mean that every existing thing has an end. We suppose there is an analogy here: the running of the sun and the moon, although they are constantly and perpetually so, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses﴾ [Ibrahim 33]. Thus, despite their being constant in their courses, they have an end; so whatever else is like them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the name (Al-Khabir) (the All-Aware) as one of the names of Allah; ﴿and that Allah is Aware of what you do﴾.
* Among them: warning a person against opposition; from His saying: ﴿Aware of what you do﴾; meaning, beware of opposing (...) in your deeds, for Allah the Exalted is Knowing of it.
Now, His saying: ﴿Aware of what you do﴾ — is restriction (al-hasr) derived from it? Because He placed the object first, ﴿of what you do﴾; its original form would be: "And that Allah is Aware of what you do." We say this restriction is relative (idafi); its purpose is warning. It is as if He said: Were He not aware of anything, He would still be aware of your deeds. So the affirmation of restriction here serves to complete the warning; it is as if He said: were He not aware of anything, He would still be aware of your deeds, so beware of opposition.
* Student: ﴿And that Allah is Aware of what you do﴾.
* The Shaykh: This is well known in its interpretation. We passed by it a short time ago, that awareness (al-khibrah) is knowledge of the inner realities of matters. Did we not pass it in the admonitions of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, All-Aware﴾ [Luqman 16]?!

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 26–29 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 26]. The sentence here is declarative (khabariyyah): ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. It contains restriction (hasr), and its method is the fronting of the predicate, because placing before its place what should be delayed conveys restriction. So ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ means: not to other than Him, and it belongs to Him alone, glorified and exalted is He.

His saying ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ means: whatever exists in them, ﴿and the earth﴾ likewise. He used (mā), which is used for non-rational beings, because it is intended to denote ownership of essences and attributes. When ownership of essences and attributes is meant, (mā) is used because it is more comprehensive, since every essence has an attribute; and also not every essence is rational, for beasts, animals and the like belong to the category of non-rational beings.

His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾: the author said: (dominion, creation and servitude). (Dominion, creation) — and dominion (mulk) includes ownership of essences and disposal over those essences; for this reason he said (and servitude). The servitude intended here is general servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-'ammah), not specific servitude (al-'ubudiyyah al-khassah), because specific servitude is restricted to the obedient who have humbled themselves before Allah the Exalted in obedience in the legal sense; general servitude, however, includes all creation, because all creatures are humbled before Allah the Mighty and Majestic in terms of His cosmic ordinance and decree. No one can oppose the decree and destiny of Allah, but the disbelievers can oppose the law of Allah, and for this reason they opposed it, denied the law, and were arrogant toward the truth.

He said: (and servitude, so none in them deserves worship other than Him). In the heavens and the earth, nothing deserves worship except Allah; because by the requirement of reason and innate nature, the Owner, the Creator, the Disposer must be the one who is worshipped. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic argues for the obligation of worship on what basis? On lordship: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. And it has passed us: ﴿If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾ [Luqman 25]. This is evident: whoever has creation must be the one to whom worship is due alone.

(﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from His creation ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ who is praised in His work). The sentence here is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), to explain what Allah the Mighty and Majestic possesses of these two names and the attribute they contain.

﴿Indeed, Allah is﴾: the pronoun is the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and the pronoun of separation has three benefits:
The first benefit: emphasis (tawkid).
The second: restriction (ḥaṣr).
The third: distinguishing the predicate from the adjective.

So if you say: (Zayd is the virtuous), then (Zayd) is the subject, and (the virtuous) may well be an adjective of Zayd, and the predicate has not yet come, and the estimate is: Zayd the virtuous is beloved, for example. But if you say: (Zayd is he the virtuous), is it possible that it is an adjective or not?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: No, it is the predicate, and for this reason it is called the pronoun of separation.

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾: the author said: (from His creation). He is also free of need in Himself, free of need of others: free of need in Himself because of the abundance of what He has, since everything belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and this is the completeness of independence; and He is free of need of His creation, so He needs no one. The evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97]. As for others, they are in need. In need of whom? Of Allah the Mighty and Majestic before everything else. Then people are in need of one another, as He said: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in this worldly life, and raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some may take others in service﴾ [al-Zukhruf 32]. People are in need of one another, and sometimes in dire necessity; and all are in need of Allah and in dire necessity, whereas the Lord the Mighty and Majestic is free of need of others, just as He is self-sufficient.

So His independence includes two things:
Essential independence: meaning the abundance of what He possesses, the Exalted; for everything is His possession.
Second: independence from others, such that He does not need anyone while others need Him.

His saying ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ who is praised in His work). He fell short in the explanation in two respects:
First: he said ﴿al-Ḥamīd﴾ means "the one praised". The correct view is that it means both "the one praised" and "the one who praises"; He, glorified and exalted, praises those who deserve praise, and how much praise of those who deserve it there is in the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. And He is also praised for the perfection of His attributes and the completeness of His bounty; He is praised for two things: the perfection of His attributes and the completeness of His favours.
The second respect in which the author fell short is that he said: (who is praised in His work). The correct view is that He is praised in His work and also in His law, for His law, glorified and exalted is He, is the most perfect of laws and the most beneficial to the servants. Whoever lays down for creation a path by which their affairs are set right deserves praise. Now, if someone guided you to the road to a town on one of your journeys, would you praise him or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: You would praise him. How much more so one who guides you to the path of the Hereafter in everything you need! So the correct view is that (Ḥamīd) means both "the one who praises" and "the one praised," and that He is praiseworthy in His work and in His law. His work, which is creation, is to be praised for bringing it into being, for preparing it, and for sustaining it. He is also praiseworthy in His law, for the justice, wisdom and mercy in His law, which have no equal.

How great is the benefit of the conjunction of ﴿al-Ḥamīd﴾ with ﴿al-Ghanī﴾! For, as has passed us, the names of Allah are all most beautiful and indicate a most beautiful meaning; but two names may indicate a third attribute that arises from what? From their conjunction. Independence together with praiseworthiness increases in perfection, for a free-of-need one may be free of need but in a way that is not praised; like what? 
* Student: The miser.
* The Shaykh: Like the miser. The miser is rich, but he is not praised for his wealth, because his money is not benefited from, and he has deprived himself of the benefit of his wealth. But Allah the Mighty and Majestic has independence conjoined with praiseworthiness, because of the completeness of His beneficence to His creation from this independence: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea [were ink], with seven more seas to supply it, the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27] (...). Let us look at the grammatical analysis (i'rab).

﴿And if [wa-law anna mā]﴾: (law) here is conditional, and its protasis (fi'l al-shart) is omitted; i.e., "and if it were established that whatever is on the earth of trees ... to the end." And (mā) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which."

﴿on the earth﴾ is a prepositional phrase, related to an omitted element that is the complement (ṣilah) of the relative pronoun; meaning: and if that which is established on the earth.

﴿of trees﴾ is a prepositional phrase serving as a clarification (bayān) of (mā), the relative pronoun, because the relative pronoun is vague and needs clarification; so ﴿of trees﴾ clarifies it; meaning: if what is on the earth of trees.

His saying ﴿were pens﴾: is the predicate of (anna), meaning: if what is on the earth of trees were pens — this is the meaning — they would be pens with which to write.

﴿and the sea﴾: he says: (conjoined to the noun of anna). ﴿and the sea﴾. In another reading ﴿and the sea [is]﴾ [with nominative].
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Here it is ﴿and the sea﴾ in the Mushaf, but the author (...) in the accusative; he said: (conjoined to the noun of anna).
If it is in the nominative ﴿and the sea﴾ it is the subject (mubtada'). Ibn Malik said:
"And it is permissible to raise what is conjoined to the accusative of (inna) after it has been completed;
And (lakinna) and (anna) are attached to (inna) ..."
This (anna), he said: (﴿and the sea﴾ is conjoined to the noun of anna), so it is in the accusative. ﴿and the sea [is] drawing it, with seven more seas after it﴾ [Luqman 27]. Where is the predicate?
* Students: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27].
* The Shaykh: No, that is the response of the condition. The predicate is omitted, which the author estimated by his saying: (ink) — meaning: if what is on the earth of trees were pens and what is in it of seas were ink. (Midād) means the ink with which one writes.

The response of the condition is ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ (expressed by them about His knowledge ...) to the end.

﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ (exhausted): what is its meaning?
* Student: Ended.
* The Shaykh: Ended and finished.

﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾: ﴿words﴾ is the subject of ﴿exhausted﴾. The cosmic and legal words do not run out. The reason is that He, glorified and exalted, has never ceased and never ceases to speak. And creation: does it have an end or does it not have an end?
* Students: No.
* Other students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: No, creation has no end; for when people enter Paradise or Hell, what is it? Eternal, everlasting, perpetual abiding. So everything Allah creates, He creates by what? He creates it by the word "Be," and it is. If creatures do not end, and likewise the acts of Allah in eternity have no end, they can never be exhausted, even if it were supposed that the sea and seven more seas supply it, and all the trees on the earth were pens with which one writes; the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic would not be exhausted. The reason is clear: creatures do not end, and every creature comes into being by the word; ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].

Thus the wisdom of this declarative sentence being pure truth becomes clear to us; it is truth beyond doubt, the report of Allah is truth. But someone may say: how? What is the reasoning behind this? We say: this is its reasoning. A person may find it hard to imagine that the ocean, and seven seas beyond it, become ink, and all the trees on the earth become pens with which to write, and yet the words are not exhausted. He may find this extraordinary, but when he knows the perfection of Allah's power and greatness, he will not find it extraordinary.

His saying ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾: he said: (expressed by them about His knowledge, by writing them with those pens and that ink, and not more than that, because His knowledge, exalted is He, is not finite). May Allah pardon the author; this is a distortion. He says that the intended meaning of "words" is "known things" — the things known by Allah; i.e., what He knows would not be exhausted. But this is a clear distortion of the Qur'an. Allah says: "His words would not be exhausted," and the words are what is written; as for knowledge, it may or may not be written. Do you write down all your knowledge? But when you want to express your words to others, you speak them and write them. So the meaning: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, that is, His words in truth, in reality; the true words, if they were dictated to someone and the seas became ink for them and the trees pens for them, would not be exhausted. The meaning is evident, and this indicates the greatness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and the perfection of His power.

(﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾ nothing overcomes Him ﴿Wise﴾ [Luqman 27] nothing goes beyond His knowledge and wisdom).

His saying ﴿Mighty﴾: he says (nothing overcomes Him). Sometimes the author himself says: ﴿Mighty﴾ (nothing overpowers Him); this is because might, as has been mentioned, is divided into three kinds: might of rank (ʿizzat al-qadr); second, might of dominance (ʿizzat al-qahr), which is overpowering; and third, might of inaccessibility (ʿizzat al-imtinaʿ), which means that nothing can reach Him with harm, ever; He is inaccessible to all harm, by His own strength, glorified and exalted is He.

As for His saying ﴿Wise﴾, he here said: (nothing goes beyond His knowledge and wisdom), so he interpreted wisdom as knowledge. It has already been mentioned for us that (al-Ḥakīm) is derived from judgment (ḥukm) and wisdom (ḥikmah); so He is Wise, nothing goes outside His dominion and His judgment, and He is Wise, nothing goes beyond His wisdom; He is the Judge who perfects, all of this is taken from the word (Ḥakīm).

Joining (ʿAzīz) with (Ḥakīm) establishes a third attribute besides might and wisdom, namely that His might, may He be exalted, is conjoined with wisdom, so it becomes a more perfect might, and a more perfect wisdom. For a mighty person among creatures may be seized by pride in sin and so not be wise in his conduct, isn't that so?
* Student: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: But Allah the Mighty and Majestic, His might is conjoined with wisdom; it is impossible for His actions to go outside wisdom, which is conformity to what is correct.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said, showing the perfection of His power after mentioning the generality of His dominion and the perfection of His words: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ [Luqman 28], in creation and resurrection, because it is by the word "Be" that it is. For He means creation and resurrection: He did not create all of you except as a single soul, and did not resurrect all of you except as a single soul. So multitude does not overwhelm Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for multitude and few are equal to Him; all are within the reach of His power, and all is easy for Him, because it happens by what word? By the word "Be." When Allah the Mighty and Majestic created the heavens and the earth, did He need workers and tools?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Here we say: if the building is large, is it harder, and if it is small, is it easier? No, it is by the word "Be," and whatever is by the word "Be," there is no difference between it being many or few. For this reason Allah the Mighty and Majestic said in another verse: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer﴾ [al-Nahl 77], meaning: it is even nearer than the blink of an eye. And He said: ﴿And Our command is but one, like the blink of an eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50], this is the utmost of speed and accomplishment. And He said: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will be on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 13–14]. All of this indicates the perfection of the Mighty and Majestic's power.

If someone says: if the matter is so, why did He create the heavens in six (...)?
How is it conjoined with wisdom? Because this creation requires things: preliminaries and causes by which the perfection of creation is achieved. Is Allah not able to create the fetus in its mother's womb without a man touching her?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, as happened with 'Isa. Nevertheless, Allah the Exalted has made causes for this: the transfer of the man's water to the woman, then the fetus develops little by little until it reaches its end; then, when it is ready to come out into the world, it comes out; then, even so, it grows little by little; it does not reach full intellect at once, nor does it reach full growth at once, but it is in accordance with wisdom. This is the answer to what comes to the mind or is raised to a person: why did Allah create the heavens and the earth in six days? And why does He create the fetus in its mother's womb for nine months? And other such questions. The answer is that His actions are conjoined with wisdom, and that He, glorified and exalted, has linked for you the causes to their effects, so there must be a cause and from it an effect, and this cause must be fitting and suitable, so that creation is completed in its perfection.

﴿but as a single soul﴾ (﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ who hears every thing heard, ﴿Seeing﴾ [Luqman 28] who sees every thing seen; nothing preoccupies Him from anything).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Seen.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, every thing seen; and everything seen is created; there is none but Creator or created. As if you were saying that (...) does not see itself.
* Student: (...) the sensible seen things.
* The Shaykh: No, every thing seen means everything that can be the object of sight. (...) I do not see it, but Allah the Mighty and Majestic sees it. Now, we differ: something Zayd sees and Amr does not see.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾: it has been mentioned that (al-Samī') is divided into two kinds: one kind in the sense of "responding" (mujīb), and one kind in the sense of "hearing" (sāmi'), that is, perceiving sounds.

The Mighty One who is All-Hearing, in the sense of the One who answers, is like Ibrahim's saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39], meaning the One who answers it. It is also known that He does not answer it unless He has heard it with a hearing of perception (sam' idrak). But the benefit of supplication is the answering of the one who supplicates. As for merely hearing his supplication, there is no benefit in that unless it is answered.

It has already been mentioned that the hearing of perception is divided into three categories. What are they? That which conveys a warning (tahdid), that which conveys support (ta'yid), and that which conveys the vastness of Allah's hearing, the Exalted and Glorified, and His perception of everything that is heard.

Among what conveys a warning is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private talk? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, writing﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80]. What is the purpose of this? What is it? A warning.

Among what conveys support is His, the Exalted, saying to Musa and Harun: ﴿Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha 46].

Among what conveys comprehensiveness, the comprehensiveness of Allah's hearing, the Mighty and Majestic, of everything that is heard, is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujadila 1]. For this reason 'A'isha said: "Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses all voices. I was at the side of the room, and some of their conversation was hidden from me."[[Recorded by al-Nasa'i (3460) and Ibn Majah (188) from the hadith of 'A'isha.]] Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from above the seven heavens, hears this conversation and all this dialogue, and nothing escapes Him, the Glorified and Exalted.

As for His saying: ﴿Basir (All-Seeing)﴾, then al-Basir...

* Student: The second meaning of al-Sami'.
* Shaykh: This means perceiving what is heard.
* Student: We said: in the sense of the One who answers.
* Shaykh: In the sense of the One who answers, and in the sense of the One who perceives sounds; the hearer of sounds. And the hearing of sounds, we said, is divided into three categories. Is it clear?

As for al-Basir: al-Basir means the One who sees, i.e., He perceives with His sight, the Glorified and Exalted. Allah, the Exalted, has a sight with which He sees the things that are seen, as came in the authentic hadith: "His veil is light; if He were to unveil it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches."[[Recorded by Muslim (179 / 293) from the hadith of Abu Musa.]]

Al-Basir may also indicate knowledge, as in: ﴿And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do﴾ [al-Baqara 265], meaning, All-Knowing of it. Among people now, when they say: "So-and-so is knowledgeable (basir) about things," they mean he has knowledge and expertise in them.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, to the end of the verse [Luqman 29]. The hamzah here is the interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri). The meaning of ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is "you have indeed seen." He, the Glorified and Exalted, is affirming this matter, which is observed and known by everyone. The address in His saying ﴿you see﴾ is either to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The second meaning is broader and more general, so it includes everyone who is fit to be addressed.

﴿Have you not seen﴾, O seeing addressee? ﴿That Allah causes to enter﴾ makes enter ﴿the night into the day and causes the day﴾ to enter ﴿into the night﴾. This causing to enter cannot be except by great power.

How is the "causing to enter" in ﴿causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾? Does it mean the approach of the night and the approach of the day? Because you see the night, when it approaches, its darkness enters into the day, entering upon the day and driving it away; and you see the day, when it approaches, entering into the night and driving it away. So this is an expression for the establishing of the break of dawn, and what else? And the approach of the night.

Allah, the Exalted, has sworn by this in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And by the night when it retreats, and by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir 33-34]. And He does not swear by any created thing except for its greatness. So the meaning of "causing to enter" is making one enter the other: making the night enter the day or the reverse. When? At every morning and every evening. This is one aspect.

Or the meaning is: ﴿causes the night to enter into the day﴾ in the sense that the day increases in duration until it enters into the night, and the night increases in duration until it enters into the day. That is, the day lengthens, and when it lengthens it takes from the night; so this means it has entered upon it. And the night lengthens, and when it lengthens it takes from the day, so it has entered upon it and taken from it by stealth. This too is a meaning of the word "causing to enter."

Both are correct meanings. In the approach and retreat of the night there is a great sign of Allah's signs, and in the fact that this increases while that decreases there is also a sign of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For if all creatures were to gather together to bring the night into the day or the day into the night, they could not do it. If they all gathered together to add one minute to the day or one minute to the night, could they do it or not?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: They cannot, however much strength they are given. So this is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then, in causing the night to enter into the day according to the second meaning, it is the reverse: it is evidence of Allah's mercy, because the alternation of night and day in increase and decrease contains enormous benefit. When the night lengthens, cold and winter occur, the trees of winter appear, and the insects die whose continued existence may be harmful to humans and plants. Likewise, when the day increases, heat increases, fruits ripen, and vapor leaves the earth. Many insects die because of the heat, which, had they remained and multiplied, would have harmed people. So this too is evidence of the perfection of wisdom and mercy together with power.

The author says: (﴿causes to enter﴾ makes enter ﴿the night into the day and causes the day﴾ to enter ﴿into the night﴾, so each increases by what the other has lost, ﴿and He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾). That is, He made them subservient. For what? For the benefit of the servants. The evidence for this is His saying in the general, all-encompassing verse: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾ [al-Jathiya 13]. ﴿He has subjected to you﴾: notice the word ﴿to you﴾. So everything mentioned of subjugation in the universe is for the children of Adam. For this reason it is said in some reports: "O son of Adam, I created you for My sake, and I created everything for your sake."[[We have not located it; al-Abshihi mentioned it in similar wording in al-Mustatraf (1 / 78).]] And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 56], and He says: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqara 29], and: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...). ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning He made them subservient for the benefit of the servants. The sun and moon are mentioned after the night and day because the sun is the sign of the day and the moon is the sign of the night, as His saying: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs; then We effaced the sign of the night﴾, which is the moon, ﴿and We made the sign of the day as a means of sight﴾ [al-Isra 12]. Therefore the moon has no light of its own; it is effaced, and it derives its light from the sun. Whenever it faces the sun, its light increases; when the facing between it and the sun is complete, on the nights of the full moon, its light is perfected. Then, as the facing weakens, its light weakens.

* Student: Shaykh, the verse seems to indicate entering, "causing to enter" (...) lengthening (...).
* Shaykh: Each is valid; all of it is causing to enter.
* Student: Lengthening is causing to enter! How (...)?!
* Shaykh: Because the day enters into the night (...). If we suppose that we are now at the equality of night and day, how long is the night?
* Student: Twelve hours.
* Shaykh: And the day?
* Student: Twelve hours.
* Shaykh: Good. The day lengthens, so it becomes thirteen hours, and the night?
* Student: Eleven.
* Shaykh: Eleven. So the day has entered into the night; that is, into the time of the night.
* Student: Meaning in time, the time of the night.
* Shaykh: In the time of the night, and likewise the reverse.

(﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each﴾ of them ﴿running﴾ in its orbit ﴿for a designated term﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.)

﴿Each running﴾: this tanwin (nunation) of ﴿kullun﴾, the grammarians say, is a substitute (ʿiwad) for an omitted word. That is: each one of the sun and the moon runs until a designated term.

Remarkably, it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "The sun and the moon run in their orbits during the day, and run in their orbits beneath the earth at night."[[Recorded by Ibn Mandah in al-Tawhid (58) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] This indicates that Ibn 'Abbas held that the earth is spherical, because if it runs beneath the earth, it means that the earth is round. And so it is, because the sun and the moon at night run beneath the earth, as he, may Allah be pleased with him, said.

* Student: Which earth?
* Shaykh: This earth of ours; it will be beneath it.
* Student: And the remaining earths?
* Shaykh: (...)..
* Student: I mean the remaining earths, the remaining six; they are below.
* Shaykh: Yes, the remaining six are beneath us. That is, the earths are layers, (...), layers one above another. Have you not looked at the egg? It has the uppermost shell, then the second shell, (...) then the white next to it, then the white, then a thin membrane, then the yolk, and the yolk too has layers. The earth is like the egg in this way. Likewise the heavens, the same thing: layers, curved.

* Student: So they are not separate?
* Shaykh: (...) separate?
* Student: I mean the earths are not separated from one another.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a difference of opinion. Some scholars say that there is a separation and air between them, just as the heavens have air and separation between them. And some say there is no separation between them.

* Student: We said that the sun and moon revolve beneath all the earths, the seven earths.
* Shaykh: Now, the seven earths are the mass, this mass of earth which they call the terrestrial globe. It contains the seven, the seven are within its core. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, will have it hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2452) and Muslim (1610 / 137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]] For if he wrongs the upper earth on which we now stand, he has transgressed against those beneath it, and those beneath it, and those beneath it, down to the seventh. For this reason, the common people now say: (...).

* * *

.. ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes...﴾; that is, "And have you not seen that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?" Here, seeing means knowing in both places, as the author estimated: that is, "Do you not know that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?"

If someone says: my knowledge that Allah causes the night to enter the day and that He has subjected the sun and moon is knowledge whose path is sense perception; I witness it. But ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Luqman 29], what is the path of this knowledge? Is it witnessed sense perception or true report?

True report, without doubt. We know that Allah is Acquainted with what we do because He has informed us of that, the Glorified and Exalted, and He is the most truthful of speakers.

But do we also know this through witnessed sense perception, or not?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: How so? We say: yes, we know it from what we observe of the punishments for sins, for example, and of the rewards of the obedient, and from what happens to a person himself from the effect of obedience and the effect of disobedience. The believer experiences an evil effect in himself from sin, to the point that some people's chests become constricted and they do not know the reason, but its cause is a sin that has remained hidden from them. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed my heart is covered over, and I seek Allah's forgiveness a hundred times a day."[[Recorded by Muslim (2702 / 41) from the hadith of al-Aghurr ibn Yasar.]] Or as he, peace and blessings be upon him, said. So a person senses the knowledge and awareness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding what he does, through its effects.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From its effects. So the summary now is that ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: we say we know it through two paths: true report and witnessed sense perception. We sense it through what we see of the effects of our good deeds or the effects of our evil deeds.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is also among the signs. So the conclusion from this is that this affirmation, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, meaning "do you not know," is an affirmation of a matter that is actual, witnessed, and perceived, and of a matter known through true report (...).

* * *

.. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman 26].

* It is derived from this verse that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone. And the path of benefit from it is?
* Student: The path of benefit is that everything in the universe (...) belongs to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.
* Shaykh: (...) but it is specific to Allah. So what is the indicator that Allah, the Exalted, is specifically the owner of it from the sentence?
* Student: (...) the restriction.
* Shaykh: Yes, what is its means?
* Student: Fronting of the prepositional phrase.
* Shaykh: Fronting of the predicate.
* Student: Fronting of the predicate over the subject (...).
* Shaykh: So in the noble verse... among its benefits: that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is specific to Him. From where do we take that it is specific? From the fronting of the predicate, because fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction and exclusivity.
* And it is derived from this noble verse: that people do not own their wealth with absolute ownership. You say, for example: "I own my house, my car, and similar things," but your ownership of them is not absolute, is it? Because absolute ownership belongs to whom? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason, your disposal of them is according to what Allah has permitted, not according to what you want. With this the objection that is raised is removed, which says: If you say that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth is specific to Allah, has not Allah attributed ownership to humans? ﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. So how is the answer? We say: this ownership is not absolute ownership.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, (...) we do not see it in the Qur'an, but we say: it is not absolute ownership, by the proof that it is restricted by Allah's permission, by what Allah has permitted.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Ghani (the Free of need) and al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy), and what they indicate of the attribute of free-of-need-ness and praise, and what their combination indicates of an attribute as well: that Allah's freedom from need is joined with His being praiseworthy, which indicates that it is an essential freedom from need (ghina dhati), and that He, the Glorified and Exalted, despite being free of need, is generous and gives of what He has. Or not? For not every free-of-need person is praiseworthy.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification that Allah's ownership of the heavens and the earth is an ownership that includes bounty and praise. From where do we take it? Because He mentioned it after His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾. So His being free of need, through which the Glorified and Exalted praises Himself after mentioning the ownership of the heavens and the earth, indicates His bounty through this freedom from need, and His being praised for this ownership, that it is an ownership built upon praise. This is like His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha 2]. He praised Himself for being Lord of the worlds, because His lordship, the Glorified and Exalted, is a lordship for which He is to be praised, due to the perfection of bounty, kindness, and justice it contains (...). Have you understood this? What did we say about it, what is the benefit? The affirmation that the ownership of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and is built upon bounty and praise; because He mentioned it after His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾.
* And it is derived from the noble verse: the poverty (iftiqar) of whatever is in the heavens and the earth to Allah. From where is it taken?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 26–29 (part 3 of 3):

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes; because His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need (al-Ghaniy), the Praiseworthy﴾ is evidence that whatever is in the heavens and the earth is in need of Him and poor (in need) before Him, as the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor (in need) before Allah, and Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that "the heavens" is plural and that their number is seven; this is taken from His saying: ﴿what is in the heavens﴾. As for specifying the number as seven, it comes from other verses.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens and the sea (were ink), replenished thereafter by seven seas, the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman 27].
* Derived from this noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, speaks; from His saying: ﴿the words of Allah﴾.
* And derived from it: that His words are audible, because they are written, and only what is audible is written. Is this so? Is there any consideration in this benefit?
* Student: There is consideration in it.
* The Shaykh: How so?
* The student: Because it is not possible to write sound (...).
* The Shaykh: Fine, meaning a person can write his own words without them being heard by others.
* The student: But no one else writes them.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but is it necessary that someone else writes them? Is it necessary, for something to be written, that someone else writes it?
So this benefit is open to consideration, but what is derived is the affirmation that Allah speaks with a voice; speech is not called speech except where it is a sound, whereas what is merely in the soul is not speech.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the words of Allah the Exalted have no end. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾. The basis for this was explained earlier in the tafsir: Allah, the Exalted, has not ceased and does not cease to be the Creator, the Doer of what He wills, and it follows from this that He is a speaker, as in His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since He is capable of a speech that does not end.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of might (al-'Izzah) and wisdom (al-Hikmah), from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Wise﴾; and the affirmation of wisdom also from His saying: ﴿Wise﴾; and the affirmation of these two names: ﴿Almighty﴾ and ﴿Wise﴾.
* Among its benefits also: what is indicated by the combination of might and wisdom among the attributes of perfection, or not? That is, we have said that a name may have a meaning in itself and a meaning when combined with others; the combination of might with wisdom conveys a greater perfection than if might or wisdom stood alone, namely that the might of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is tied to wisdom.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as (that of) a single soul﴾ [Luqman 28].
* Derived from this noble verse: the affirmation of creation and resurrection, from His saying: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection﴾.
* And derived from it: the perfection of Allah's power, since He, may His majesty be exalted, made the creation and resurrection of all creatures like a single soul, and this is the utmost of power.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of resurrection, from His saying: ﴿nor your resurrection﴾.
* Among its benefits: deducing the unseen (al-ghaib) from the seen. From where? And what is the intended benefit?
* Student: Deducing the promised from the witnessed.
* Another student: The creation (...).
* The Shaykh: The witnessed is creation, and the promised is resurrection; Allah has joined them both, affirming each of them, and that just as He was able to create at first, He is able to resurrect a second time.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of two names of Allah: (As-Sami') (the All-Hearing) and (Al-Basir) (the All-Seeing), and the affirmation of the attributes they indicate, and the affirmation of perfection through their combination: hearing and sight; for not every hearer is seeing, and not every seer is hearing. The meanings of As-Sami' and Al-Basir have already been mentioned for us, so there is no need to repeat them.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ to its end [Luqman 29].
* In this verse: the affirmation of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in causing the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night.
* Among its benefits also: the demonstration of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since this interchange contains many benefits, some observed and known, and some not known.
* Among them: the demonstration of the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon His servants in subjecting the sun and the moon; from His saying: ﴿and He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the sun and the moon run; from His saying: ﴿each runs to a specified term﴾.
* Among them: the demonstration of the perfection of order in the acts of Allah; from His saying: ﴿to a specified term﴾, fixed, not varying, neither advancing nor delaying.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of those who say that the sun and the moon are stationary; from His saying: ﴿each runs﴾. This is a report from their Creator, glorified and exalted, who is most knowing of what He created. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14]. Thus there is a clear refutation in it of those who say that they are stationary and do not run.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every existing creature has an end (ghayah), from His saying: ﴿each runs to a specified term﴾, except Paradise and Hellfire, for they are enduring forever without end, by Allah's sustaining them; their permanence is not intrinsic, because whatever may be brought into existence may be annihilated; or in other words: whatever may come into being may cease to be. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has decreed the everlastingness of Paradise and Hellfire, as the clear and authentic evidences indicate.
* Student: Every existing (...).
* The Shaykh: You mean that every existing thing has an end. We suppose there is an analogy here: the running of the sun and the moon, although they are constantly and perpetually so, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses﴾ [Ibrahim 33]. Thus, despite their being constant in their courses, they have an end; so whatever else is like them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the name (Al-Khabir) (the All-Aware) as one of the names of Allah; ﴿and that Allah is Aware of what you do﴾.
* Among them: warning a person against opposition; from His saying: ﴿Aware of what you do﴾; meaning, beware of opposing (...) in your deeds, for Allah the Exalted is Knowing of it.
Now, His saying: ﴿Aware of what you do﴾ — is restriction (al-hasr) derived from it? Because He placed the object first, ﴿of what you do﴾; its original form would be: "And that Allah is Aware of what you do." We say this restriction is relative (idafi); its purpose is warning. It is as if He said: Were He not aware of anything, He would still be aware of your deeds. So the affirmation of restriction here serves to complete the warning; it is as if He said: were He not aware of anything, He would still be aware of your deeds, so beware of opposition.
* Student: ﴿And that Allah is Aware of what you do﴾.
* The Shaykh: This is well known in its interpretation. We passed by it a short time ago, that awareness (al-khibrah) is knowledge of the inner realities of matters. Did we not pass it in the admonitions of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, All-Aware﴾ [Luqman 16]?!

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 30–34 (part 1 of 5):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ [Luqman 30]. "That" refers to what was mentioned earlier of the subjugation of the sun and the moon, and the power to resurrect and to create; that is, that aforementioned matter.

"Because Allah is the Truth": the "bi" (ba') here denotes causation (lil-sababiyyah); that is, because Allah is the Truth. By virtue of His being the Truth, these matters came into being and these systems were ordered, for He, may He be exalted, is Truth in His essence, Truth in His actions, Truth in His judgments, and Truth in His names and attributes. His Messenger is true, His Book is true, His promise is true, His reward is true, His punishment is true, and everything that proceeds from Him is true.

Al-haqq (the Truth) is the opposite of al-batil (falsehood), and al-batil is vain and idle talk or action that contains no good. So the meaning is that everything that proceeds from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is true and established good.

﴿And that what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [Luqman 30]. "And that" (wa-anna) is conjoined to "that" (anna); meaning: "and [that it is because]," conjoined to the opening "anna."

His saying "mā yad'ūn" (what they invoke): "mā" here is a relative pronoun; meaning: "and that which they invoke."

His saying "yad'ūn" (they invoke) includes both du'a' al-'ibadah (invocation of worship) and du'a' al-mas'alah (invocation of petition), because the idols that are worshipped besides Allah are called upon in the sense of being worshipped, and are called upon in the sense of being asked.

Du'a' (invocation) has two meanings: du'a' of worship and du'a' of petition. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 186] — what is meant there? It is du'a' of petition. And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord says, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation"﴾ [Ghafir 60] is du'a' of worship. Likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ [al-Ra'd 14], meaning: their worship is only in error. Thus du'a' may mean du'a' of petition or du'a' of worship, so His saying "mā yad'ūn" includes both meanings; that is, what they worship and what they ask from it for their needs.

﴿Wa-anna mā yad'ūn﴾: as for his saying "bi-l-yā' wa-l-tā'" (with the yā' and the tā'), these are two recitations, both of the seven: ﴿wa-anna mā tad'ūn﴾ and ﴿wa-anna mā yad'ūn﴾, and both are correct. But in His saying ﴿wa-anna mā tad'ūn min dūnihi al-bāṭil﴾ there is address, and it can only be addressed to the disbelievers, because address of this kind cannot be directed to the Messenger ﷺ or to the believers among his Companions.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Du'a' of petition.
* Student: Du'a' of petition, (...) du'a' of worship.
* Shaykh: He says: ﴿And that what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾. "Min dūnihi" means: from other than Him.

The author's saying "(they worship)" (...) this is deficient, and the correct wording is: they worship and they ask, as the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more astray than one who invokes other than Allah, those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. "Yad'ū" here means "yas'al" (asks) ﴿other than Allah, those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾. So here it should be added: they worship and they ask.

His saying "min dūnihi" means: from other than Him.

His saying "al-bāṭil": the author says "(al-zā'il)" (that which passes away), and this is open to scrutiny, because the intended meaning is falsehood, i.e., that which contains no good. From this is the hadith: "The truest word a poet has ever spoken is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything other than Allah is vain (bāṭil)'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3841) and Muslim (2256/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. "Bāṭil" means: it contains no good.

His saying: ﴿And that what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾: is the intended meaning the falsehood of their worshipping it, or falsehood even in itself, such that it does not deserve worship?

Both matters are intended: it is falsehood with respect to their worshipping it, and it is falsehood in itself, deserving no share of divinity whatsoever.

(﴿And that Allah is the Most High﴾ over His creation by subjugation ﴿the Most Great﴾, the Magnificent.)

﴿And that Allah is the Most High﴾: this sentence, as you see, is a declarative sentence emphasized by the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl). Where is the pronoun of separation?

* Students: ﴿Huwa﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Huwa al-'Aliyy﴾, meaning: not other than Him.

And al-'Aliyy is an attributive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah), because it is on the pattern (fa'īl), and the scholars of the Arabic language say that the attributive adjective indicates establishment and continuity (...).

* * *

﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman 34]. It is well known that "Allah," the word of majesty, is the subject of (inna), "'indahu" (with Him) is the predicate preceding, and "'ilmu" (knowledge) is the delayed subject, and the clause is the predicate of (inna). A declarative clause contains restriction (ḥaṣr), and this is derived from the fronting of the predicate: the fronting of ﴿'indahu﴾, ﴿Indeed Allah, with Him﴾ and not with other than Him ﴿is the knowledge of the Hour﴾. This restriction is confirmed by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival? Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf 187], restricted by the form ﴿innama﴾ (only): ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾. If someone claimed that the restriction here is in the predicate and not in the whole clause, we would say: the predicate is what indicated the restriction of the knowledge of the Hour to Allah, the Exalted, and what indicates and confirms it is the verse we mentioned: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival? Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾. If such an expression reaches you, ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾, the meaning is: none knows it but my Lord; this is its meaning, just as when you say: "Only Zayd is standing," meaning: there is no one standing except Zayd.

His saying: ﴿'indahu 'ilmu al-sā'ah﴾ (with Him is knowledge of the Hour): when it will occur, and at what time, and none knows it but Allah. For this reason Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying: "Tell me about the Hour." He said: "The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. Consider this: two messengers, one of them the best of the angels and the other the best of mankind, both say: "I have no knowledge," because his saying: "The one asked knows no more than the one asking" means: if you do not know, then I, by greater right, do not know. Therefore, knowledge of it is specific to Allah.

Whoever claims that he knows it has lied, especially by the means he mentioned as indicating it, as was published about a person called Rashad Khalifah. He is a man in America, a man who possesses knowledge, but he was greatly deceived by what he calls the number nineteen, claiming that the whole Qur'an is structured upon nineteen letters, and that this material he has, the nineteen, he used as evidence that he knows when the Hour will be established; he set it, I think, at a few years beyond 2000.

* Student: (...) the year 1909.
* Shaykh: 1909? 
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: 1909, how?
* Student: I mean: the year 1909 Hijri.
* Shaykh: Hijri, good. In reality, Allah knows best whether this man was a mistaken interpreter or a stubborn opponent, but whoever claims knowledge of the Hour is a disbeliever, because he denies Allah and His Messenger and the consensus of the Muslims, and the Muslims are in definitive consensus that none knows when the Hour will be established except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾: the Hour is the Resurrection. It is called the Hour (al-sā'ah) because it is the greatest event that will occur, and because in it there is a warning to the deniers; for this reason one is threatened with "the Hour." One says, for example: "Your hour is with me." If you wish to threaten a person, you threaten him with the word "the Hour," because a great event will befall in it.

Second: ﴿And He sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman 34]. He did not say "and He knows when the rain will fall"; He said "and He sends down," and the difference of expression has a great meaning. Otherwise, all five of these are from the knowledge of the unseen, for the Prophet ﷺ explained the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [al-An'am 59] with these five. The wording of the hadith is: "And none knows when the rain will fall except Allah." But the Qur'an says, in Allah's words: ﴿And He sends down the rain﴾, so how can we say that what is meant is: none knows when the rain will fall except Allah? We say: because Allah is the One who sends down the rain, none knows it except Allah, for He is the one who sends it down, and the one who sends down a thing is the one who knows it, while others do not know it.

His saying: ﴿al-ghayth﴾ [Luqman 34]: meaning the rain. It is called ghayth because by it hardship is removed, and istighathah (seeking relief) is the request for the removal of hardship; by rain the calamities are removed, the calamities of drought and the calamities of barrenness, so that people have water and have farms.

﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾ [Luqman 34]: "yaʿlamu mā" means: that which is in the wombs. He used "mā" because it is more general and comprehensive than "man" (who), since "man" is specific to what? To the rational being. This is one aspect. Another aspect is that "mā" is specific to attributes, while "man" is specific to essences. Have you not seen His saying: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 3]? He did not say "man ṭāba" (whoever is good), even though the one married is a rational being, or not? Rather He said: ﴿mā ṭāba﴾, not "man," because marriage rests upon the attribute of the woman, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "A woman is married for four [things]" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5090) and Muslim (1466/53) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. Here He said "mā" rather than "man," because knowledge of what is in the wombs in terms of attributes is more eloquent than knowledge of it in terms of essence, more eloquent than knowledge of it in terms of being male or female. The fetus in the womb is not known merely by being male or female, or tall or short, or small or large; no, there is something more significant than that, which is the attributes of this fetus: will it be wretched or happy, long-lived or short-lived? Will its deeds be righteous or corrupt? For this reason the expression came with "mā," in which what is taken into account? The attributes are taken into account, because knowledge of what is in the wombs from this standpoint is greater than knowing whether it is male or female. Therefore, today they become aware of its knowledge of being male or female; they know this before it is born, whether male or female. Thus the eloquence of the Qur'an becomes clear in that it expressed with "mā" rather than "man," because "man" specifies the person, the identity of a rational being, whereas if it is non-rational one says "mā." As for what relates to attributes (...).

The adjective al-mushabbahah, the scholars of the Arabic language say, indicates establishment and continuity, and "al-'Aliyy" means High in His essence and High in His attributes; His highness is intrinsic and permanent, whether He is High in His essence or High in His attributes.

As for His saying: ﴿He is the Most High﴾ [Luqman 30]: it has already been mentioned to us that among the people of innovation are those who deny highness, which highness? The intrinsic highness. As for the highness of meaning (exaltation of status), it is agreed upon among the Muslims.

As for His saying: ﴿al-Kabir﴾ [Luqman 30], the author said: "(the Great)." He, glorified and exalted, is Great in the sense of magnificent in His essence and in His attributes: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]. Allah informed that the heavens will be folded up in His right hand, and that the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and that He will fold up the heaven like the folding of a scroll for writings. All of this indicates the greatness of His essence, glorified and exalted, just as He is magnificent in His attributes.

* Student: His saying: ﴿jamī'an﴾ does it not indicate (...) ﴿and the earth entirely﴾ [al-Zumar 67]?
* Shaykh: No, it does not indicate that; it indicates the whole of the earth, but it does not indicate a number.
* Student: His saying: ﴿jamī'an﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, the entire earth, including the trees, as came in the hadith: "He places the trees on one finger and the moist earth on one finger" [al-Bukhari (4811) and Muslim (2786/19) on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: A rabbi came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Muhammad, we find that Allah places the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the trees on one finger, the water and the moist earth on one finger, and all other creatures on one finger, then He says, 'I am the King.'" The Prophet ﷺ laughed until his molars showed, confirming the rabbi's statement. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿They have not measured Allah with His true measure; the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand. Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate﴾ [al-Zumar 67].]

Here, when He mentioned that Allah is the Truth, and that what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, He said: ﴿And that Allah is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [Luqman 30]. Because of His highness and His majesty, blessed and exalted is He, it becomes clear that these idols are the opposite of that: they are lowly, having no highness in them, they are humiliated and insignificant, having nothing of greatness.

* Student: The explanation of al-'Aliyy (...).
* Shaykh: No, His saying: "al-'Aliyy over His creation" here by subjugation. Yes. Rather, the correct view is that He is High in His essence and His attributes.

(﴿Have you not seen that the ships﴾ are ships ﴿sail through the sea by the favor of Allah, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾ [Luqman 31] — ﴿'ibar﴾ lessons — ﴿for everyone patient﴾ in refraining from the disobedience of Allah, ﴿grateful﴾ for His blessings.)

﴿Have you not seen that the ships﴾: this interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), because this is a matter that is seen, so one is not asked about its establishment, but its establishment is affirmed. And the address in His saying ﴿tara﴾ (you see) returns to whom? Either to the Messenger ﷺ, or to everyone who is fit to be addressed; and this is more general.

As for His saying: ﴿that the ships﴾, the author said: "(the ships)," so he took it as plural, although it may be intended as singular, by His saying ﴿tajrī﴾ (sails), and "al-fulk," as has already been mentioned, is a word used for both the plural and the singular. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Until when you are in ships and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus 22]. Is "al-fulk" here singular or plural? Plural: ﴿until when you are in the ships and they sail﴾, ﴿wa-jarayna﴾ is not singular, it is plural; He did not say "wa-jarat." But here ﴿anna al-fulka tajrī﴾, the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that the singular is intended, since He did not say "yajrīna." Nevertheless, the singular may be intended to mean the plural in terms of meaning, because al-fulk is not one individual in number, but it is one in kind; as for individuals, they cannot be counted.

As for His saying: ﴿tajrī fī al-baḥr﴾ (sails in the sea), "fī" denotes location (lil-ẓarfiyyah). Is it on its original sense, or does it mean "'alā" (upon)?

* Students: It means "'alā" (upon).
* Shaykh: Is it on the sea or in it?
* Student: The submarine is in the sea.
* Shaykh: Yes, the submarine, is it?
* Student: It is a ship.
* Shaykh: But the ships that carry these cattle on their surface, yet in reality it is (...), not covering it, but its underside is covered by the water.

﴿fī al-baḥr bi-ni'mati Allāh﴾: the "bi" is connected to ﴿tajrī﴾; meaning: they sail with blessings, that is, carrying blessings. And it may be that the "bi" denotes causation, that is: they sail because of the blessing of Allah, meaning that Allah has blessed His servants with their sailing, and there is a difference between the two meanings, is there not? Yes; because on the first meaning the ships are carrying blessings, and on the second meaning the ships sail by the blessing of Allah, meaning that their sailing is among the favors of Allah upon us. The verse admits both meanings without contradiction, and we have mentioned again and again that when a verse admits two meanings without contradiction, both meanings are taken.

* Student: If there is a difference, but the apparent meaning is the latter; do we say (...) the first?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: But their sailing by the blessing of Allah carries the cattle..

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 31, verse 30–34 (part 2 of 5):

* The Shaykh: No; because it may run empty, with nothing in it. It is merely God, Mighty and Majestic, enabling these ships to run upon the water, and water, as you know, is not a solid body that bears weight; rather it is a soft body. Were it not that God, exalted is He, made it easy for these ships to move upon it, they would not move.
* A student: Sometimes they sink into the water.
* The Shaykh: Yes. If they are carrying only passengers, they are in the first sense, by God's bounty. Usually there is in them a great deal of God's provision, so they are in the second sense. We say: they are in both senses together. They run by the grace of God, meaning by God's favour upon us, that their running is one of His blessings; and they run "with blessing," meaning carrying the blessing of God.

﴿لِيُرِيَكُمْ مِنْ آيَاتِهِ﴾ ("so that He may show you of His signs"): the lam is connected to ﴿تَجْرِي﴾ ("run") and is the lam of purpose, meaning: in order that He may show you. The meaning of (يُرِيَكُم) is that He makes it manifest so that you see it, that is: so that you may see of God's signs what overwhelms your minds.

Regarding His words ﴿لِيُرِيَكُمْ مِنْ آيَاتِهِ﴾ ("of His signs"): (مِن) here is partitive, since the ships and those riding on them do not see all of God's signs, but see only some of them.

His words ﴿لِيُرِيَكُمْ مِنْ آيَاتِهِ﴾ mean: of that which indicates His perfection in power and bounty, and other things. The word (الآيات) is the plural of (آية), which linguistically means a sign, and what is intended by it is everything by which one may infer the perfection of God, Mighty and Majestic, in His essence and attributes. What are the signs that are seen in the sea?
* A student: (...) the ships.
* The Shaykh: Such as?
